events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibition: "Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations"
events.location: Worth Ryder Art Gallery, Anthropology & Art Building, Rm 116
events.description: The Department of German and the Department of Art Practice are excited to announce the opening of Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations, curated by Antonio Somaini with Hannes Bajohr and Sonja Thiel, in dialogue with the France–Berkeley research initiative The Latent Spaces of Culture, and on display at the Worth Ryder Art Gallery. This exhibition examines some of the concealed dimensions of contemporary AI culture — the planetary infrastructures of extraction and computation, the often invisible human labor, the latent vector spaces within which culture is compressed and processed, and the models' hallucinations. Hidden Layers tackles these phenomena from two different perspectives: AI Infrastructures and AI Hallucinations. Featuring works by Nouf Aljowaysir; Gašper and Nina Beguš & Metahaven; Grégory Chatonsky; Kate Crawford & Vladan Joler; Asma Kazmi & Jill Miller; Andrea Khôra; Occitane Lacurie & Barnabé Sauvage; Greg Niemeyer; and Mario Santamaria & Alex Saum-Pascual. The project is a collaboration between the Department of German and the Worth Ryder Art Gallery at the Department of Art Practice.Exhibition Dates: September 3 - October 3, 2026Opening Reception: Thursday, September 3, 4-6:30pm, Worth Ryder Art Gallery RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Artist Talk, Gregory Chatonsky: Thursday, September 3, 6:30-8:00pm, AAPB 285 RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd_OOMe7YQHw3CYbSr673UCSlQ0f4mn4lZ7g46KhRUTRpC5qQ/viewform?usp=dialog)Related programming:Film Program: September 9, 7 pm, BAMPFAWorkshop on Latent Spaces of Culture: September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days, 470 Stephens Additional events and more details to be announced. Times subject to change, please also check the campus calendar. This exhibition is supported by the France-Berkeley Fund of the Institute of European Studies, the Department of German and the Department of Art Practice, together with the Berkeley Center for New Media, the Berkeley Institute for Data Science (BIDS), Department of Rhetoric; Antikythera, the Pamela P. Fong and Family Distinguished Chair in China Studies, the Division of Arts & Humanities, the Townsend Center for the Humanities and the School of Information, the Technology Network of the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI); and the Berkeley Art, Law, and Finance Project, hosted by the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at Berkeley Law. In conjunction with the exhibition, additional programming is developed in collaboration with Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) and the Institute for Contemporary Art San Jose.

events.title: Group Actions and Dynamics Seminar: Banach Fixed Point Properties of Universal Lattices
events.description: Speaker: Izhar Oppenheim, Ben Gurion UniversityHigher-rank universal lattices and Steinberg groups over Z[t1,…,tm] can be viewed as generalizations of higher-rank algebraic lattices. In this lecture, I will discuss results showing that these groups possess the fixed point property for all affine isometric actions on uniformly convex Banach spaces. This result provides a far-reaching extension of my earlier work on Banach property (T) for SL(n,Z) that was later generalized by de Laat and de la Salle for all higher rank algebraic lattices.

events.title: Film Screening: We
events.description: We takes viewers along the suburban RER B train line of Paris, which runs physically from north to south yet metaphorically ranges across the entire breadth of Parisian, French, and global humanity. The film introduces writers, nurses, cleaning ladies, garage mechanics, and more, all representing the many disparate communities that ring Paris, yet each unique enough to remind us that no one—and no one film, book, or song—could ever represent such a wide array of voices and lives. "A tender homage to the unnoticed" (The Guardian).

events.title: CNMAT Concert: Matteo Cesari & Simone Conforti
events.description: Matteo Cesari & Simone Conforti play works for flute and electronics from Kaija Saariaho, Eva Reiter, Simone Conforti, & Marco Stroppa.Matteo Cesari Flutes Simone Conforti Flute and Electronics ProgramInTheEventThatDuskMeetsDawn, Simone Conforti For two flutes, world premiere NoaNoa, Kaija Saariaho For flute and electronics Konter (transcription for contrabass flute in C - Matteo Cesari), Eva ReiterFor contrabass flute and electronics PastiCity, Simone Conforti Fixed media Little i, Marco Stroppa For flutes and chamber electronics Matteo Cesari is internationally recognised as one of the leading interpreters of contemporary flute repertoire. Recipient of the Kranichsteiner Musikpreis at Darmstadt, he has performed at venues including the Philharmonie de Paris, Elbphilharmonie Hamburg, Pierre Boulez Saal Berlin and Teatro Colón Buenos Aires. His activity combines performance, creation, artistic research and pedagogy, with long-term collaborations including Salvatore Sciarrino, Alberto Posadas, Georges Aperghis and Brian Ferneyhough. He has contributed to more than thirty premieres and participated closely in projects including the rewriting of Sciarrino's L'Opera per flauto, vol. 3. A permanent member of Ensemble Multilatérale and faculty at IRCAM / Pôle Sup'93, his recent work increasingly focuses on contrabass flute, electronics and new artistic formats linking interpretation, technology and listening. Born in Winterthur, Switzerland, Simone Conforti is a composer, Computer Music Designer, wind instrument performer, and software developer. He holds a Ph.D. in Media Studies, as well as degrees in Flute and Electronic Music Composition. He currently serves as Computer Music Designer and Professor at IRCAM in Paris. He has previously taught Electroacoustic Composition and Computer Music at the Conservatories of Cuneo and Florence, and worked as a Computer Music Designer and tutor at the CIMM of the Venice Biennale. His research activity has taken him to institutions across Europe, including the University of Basel, HEM Geneva, HEMU Lausanne, and MARTLab in Florence. Driven by a deep curiosity for emerging music technology, has founded several companies pioneering automatic music generation and algorithmic approaches to 3D sound diffusion and sound masking. His work has been published by Suvini Zerboni, Da Vinci Classics, Mode, Stradivarius, Die Schachtel, Third Man Records, Cramps, Audiomat, Mudima Music, ET'CETERA, A14, Nardini Editore, Kehrer Verlag, Dissonance, SAGE Publishing, AIB – Associazione Italiana Biblioteche, Artestampa, and Transcript.

events.title: Film Screening: Breathless
events.description: Jean-Luc Godard's films of the 1960s are rich in intellectual references, gorgeous visuals, and music by Michel Legrand—classically French, in their postmodern way. But scrappy, jazzy, black-and-white Breathlessremains what Russell Merritt called "the outlaw artifact of the nouvelle vague." A very young Jean-Paul Belmondo plays the outlaw hero Michel Poiccard (alias Laszlo Kovacs), who kills a cop and hides in plain sight in Paris. An even younger Jean Seberg announces herself loudly as an American student working for the New York Herald Tribune. "A thrilling reminder of how playful Godard could be" (Ella Taylor, Village Voice).

events.title: Film Screening: Mean Streets
events.description: Set during the Feast of San Gennaro in the Italian neighborhood where Martin Scorsese grew up, and populated with characters and situations based on the neighborhood's inhabitants, Mean Streets is an early distillation of the themes that would define the director's career. Charlie (Harvey Keitel) is torn between his devout Catholicism, his commitment to his volatile friend Johnny Boy (Robert De Niro), a romantic entanglement with Johnny's cousin Teresa, and opportunities offered by his crime boss uncle. Crackling with creative energy, this now iconic neo-noir is inflected with influences from French New Wave, cinema verité, and American independent filmmakers like Kenneth Anger, John Cassavetes, and Shirley Clarke.

events.title: Exploration of Forms: Movement as Creative Practice, a three-part workshop with Randee Paufve
events.description: About Exploration of Forms: Exploration of Forms is a public workshop series that centers embodiment, transformation, and creativity. All workshops are free for students. Guests are encouraged to make a donation of $25 at the door, but no one will be turned away for lack of funds.Signups are available here: https://tdps.link/explorationAbout This Workshop:This workshop series investigates movement not as a set of skills to acquire, but as a creative and expressive practice to inhabit and sustain. Drawing on modern/contemporary and jazz dance techniques and performance practices, each session builds on the last — offering dancers a framework for thinking about their relationship to technique, expression, and the long arc of a life in movement.September 6th - Session 1:Technique as a Tool for Expression - What is technique for? This session uses rigorous contemporary movement — warmup, floor progressions, combinations — as a lens for examining how technical training shapes (and can liberate) individual expression. Dancers are invited to bring their bodies and their questions. September 13th - Session 2:Performance Presence and the Moving Body - How does a dancer inhabit a moment rather than execute it? This session explores performance technique not as a set of presentational skills but as a practice of attention — to space, to music, to other bodies, and to the intelligence moving through your own. September 20th - Session 3: Sustaining a Creative Practice - What keeps us dancing? This session addresses the longer questions beneath the work: how dancers build and maintain a creative practice over time, how they stay curious, how they metabolize influences, and how they find their own movement voice. Includes movement work alongside structured reflection. About the Teacher: Randee Paufve is a choreographer, dancer, teacher, and Artistic Director of Paufve Dance. A 2019 Fulbright Scholar and recipient of the Isadora Duncan Dance Award for Outstanding Individual Performance, she has been featured on NPR's All Things Considered and honored with the inaugural Della Davidson Prize for Innovations in Dance-Theater. Her work has been presented nationally at ODC Theater, SFMOMA, the Mondavi Center, On the Boards, and the Portland Institute for Contemporary Art, and internationally in India, Austria, and Portugal. She has taught on the faculties of UC Davis, CSU Sacramento, St. Mary's College of California, University of San Francisco and Lewis and Clark College, and Shawl-Anderson Dance Center. Accessibility: If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact us with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7–10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Film Screening: A Woman is a Woman
events.description: Jean-Luc Godard's third feature was conceived "within the framework of a neorealist musical," with nods to René Clair and Ernst Lubitsch. Anna Karina is Angela, an occasional stripper in a shabby club called the Zodiac. She is determined to have a baby and soon; when her lover Emile (Jean-Claude Brialy) won't, she turns to his friend Alfred Lubitsch (Jean-Paul Belmondo), who will. There is magic in this film, from actual hat tricks to the famous egg-frying gag to the mesmerizing traveling shots. Godard's sense of woman as mystery is a part of that magic. (Even the title throws up its hands.)

events.description: A departure from the urban underworld of Mean Streets, Martin Scorsese's first studio film, set in the Southwest with a female lead, afforded him the opportunity to show his versatility. Alice earned Academy Award nominations for writer Robert Getchell and actress Diane Ladd, as well as a Best Actress win for Ellen Burstyn for her nuanced performance as a widowed mother who hits the road with her preteen son in the hope of finding work as a singer. Scorsese and Burstyn bonded over Alice's emotional journey while leaving space for the rest of the excellent cast��including Jodie Foster, Harvey Keitel, and Kris Kristofferson—to shine.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Hao Xu, Professor of Chemistry, Brandeis UniversitySearching for New Reactivity: Merging Enzymatic Catalysis with Iron Catalysis for Highly Stereoselective Glycosaminoglycan AssemblyComplex glycans are directly involved in essential life processes, but it is challenging to precisely assemble them in sufficient quantities with high homogeneity. One major hurdle is that the stereoselectivity in glycosylation often varies with substrates, thus it is difficult to develop an exquisitely selective glycosylation method that is also broadly effective. In particular, searching for a general solution for stereoselective assembly of 1,2-cis-glycosidic bonds is an unsolved challenge. The lecture will focus on the discovery of a mechanistically unique and generally applicable approach for exclusively 1,2-cis-selective glycosylation. In this lecture, we will also discuss a generally applicable glycosaminoglycan (GAG) assembly strategy by merging the catalytic power of sulfotransferases (SULTs) with two distinct iron-catalyzed glycosylation reactions that have been recently discovered in our lab. Every glycosidic linkage in heparan sulfate (HS) was assembled by one of these iron-catalyzed, entirely stereoselective glycosylation reactions. An array of sulfate groups that are essential to the functions of HS were installed at their desired locations via the SULT-controlled sulfation reactions.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Reconciling Treatment Effects Estimates across Levels of Aggregation"
events.description: Abstract: Empirical researchers often estimate treatment effects at different levels of aggregation to address confounding shocks or to detect violations of the stable unit treatment value assumption. Using eight widely used datasets on trade, employment, syndicated loans, patents, and stock holdings, we document that disaggregated data share common properties that complicate comparisons across aggregation levels. We show that, under standard specifications, these properties can lead treatment effect estimates to differ across levels of aggregation even in the absence of shocks or SUTVA violations. These gaps arise mechanically from implicit weighting across levels of aggregation, entry and exit, and Jensen's inequality. We characterize the conditions under which they become quantitatively important and propose simple approaches that are not sensitive to these sources of bias. Using practical examples, we show how aligning estimates across levels of aggregation can help researchers separately identify confounding shocks, spillovers, and extensive-margin changes at little additional cost.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics: Alex Rees-Jones "Style over substance: The oversized role of presentation details in school-choice matching systems"
events.description: Abstract: Since Abdulkadiroğlu and Sönmez (2003), economists have assessed school-choice systems nearly universally through the lens of mechanism design. In this paper, we experimentally assess this practice using the model completeness approach of Fudenberg, Kleinberg, Liang, and Mullainathan (2022). We present 10k experimental subjects with a simulation of a school choice decision, varying both the actual mechanism used and the manner in which the mechanism is communicated. Our presentations span a large number of potential versions of the most common lab-experimental paradigm as well as the presentations actually in use in US school districts. We find that respondents' propensity to either truthful or optimally report their preferences responds to the mechanism used and to the preference and priorities that are randomly assigned, as is predicted by any standard economic model. However, a significant portion of explainable variation remains unexplained by these factors, instead being determined by potentially complex details of how the mechanism is presented. We use our data to demonstrate that estimates of the causal effect of a mechanism that come from comparing two markets can change dramatically as presentation details vary (as they do in real-world comparisons). In contrast to the view where determination of the mechanism is the sole substantive issue and presentation is a second-order detail, our results suggest that presentation is a lever of comparable and at times greater importance than mechanism choice itself. We further discuss how our approach can be used to assess the external validity of field-oriented experimental literatures. Paper Link: [TBD]

events.description: Abstract: My laboratory combines experiments and computation to develop a predictive understanding of metabolism—how it is regulated, why it is organized the way it is, and how it breaks down in aging and disease. events.title: Operator Algebras Seminar: The Lima Bean Law
events.description: Speaker: Todd Kemp, University of California, San DiegoR-Diagonal elements are the most rotationally-invariant operators in free probability: a is R-diagonal if a has the same law as ua (and au) for any Haar unitary u freely independent from a. Examples include circular elements and Haar unitaries. They are the large-N limits of the most general kind of matrix with totally random eigenvectors; i.e. the (*-distribution) model is an ensemble of the form UAV where A is any matrix and U,V are Haar-distributed random matrices with {A,U,V} independent. One of the biggest modern theorems in random matrix theory, the Single Ring Theorem [Guionnet–Krishnapur–Zeitouni, 2011], proved that the density of eigenvalues of such a random matrix model converges to the Brown measure of the corresponding R-diagonal.In this talk I will discuss my recent work on "random walk" models of the form $(1+a_1)…(1+a_k)$ for freely independent R-diagonal elements $a_j$. We prove convergence of the density of eigenvalues for all these models as well. This talk will focus on the Brown measure of such shifted products, which we are able to describe quite precisely thanks to a surprising result (which I will discuss) on operator-valued freeness vs. scalar-valued freeness in the context of a symmetry we call "circulant invariance".Our main result is that, under diffusion rescaling, the Brown measure of any such k-step random walk superconverges to the large-N limit law of the standard Brownian motion on GL(N,C), yielding a very strong kind of Berger-Donsker scaling limit law (very strong because it holds even when the covariance of the terms is "wrong"). We call this scaling limit theorem The Lima Bean Law, for reasons that will become clear from pictures.This is joint work with Driver, Hall, Ho, Nemish, Nikitopoulos, and Parraud.

Observing Christian women's activism from grassroots networks to conservative academies and law school to public politics and jobs at the White House today���as they borrow feminist rhetoric to "lean in" to their executive skills while rejecting liberal feminism—Gaddini reveals how these women have turned being underestimated into a strategic force.Katie Gaddini is Associate Professor of Sociology at University College London. events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Ahmad Omar, Assistant Professor, UC BerkeleyThe Statistical Mechanics of Active Interfaces, Bubbles, and Membranes Thermodynamics is among the most successful frameworks in the physical sciences because it explains how and why systems at or near equilibrium undergo dramatic transformations. Yet many living and active systems are sustained far from equilibrium, where the usual thermodynamic framework need not apply. In this talk, I will provide a broad overview of my group's efforts to develop a statistical-mechanical description of interfacial phenomena in such systems. Starting from microscopic dynamics and systematically coarse-graining to continuum fields, we recover analogues of familiar concepts such as surface tension and nucleation barriers, while revealing how activity and nonconservative forces modify them. I will show how this mechanical framework can describe the formation, fluctuations, and stability of active interfaces, bubbles, and membranes, comparing its predictions with simulations and experiments. Together, these results help clarify which equilibrium concepts remain useful far from equilibrium and how they must be generalized when they do.

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market"
events.description: Abstract: We use advances in natural language processing to construct new measures of workers' tasklevel exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning from 2010 to 2023, capturing variation across firms, occupations, and time. Tasks with higher AI exposure subsequently experience reduced labor demand. To interpret these patterns, we develop a model that separates direct substitution from indirect reallocative effects of labor-saving technologies. Two variables summarize the impact of AI on within-firm labor demand: the mean exposure of an occupation's tasks, which depresses demand, and the concentration of exposure in a few tasks, which offsets losses by enabling workers to reallocate effort. Using an instrument based on historical university hiring networks, we find causal evidence consistent with these predictions. Despite strong substitution at the task level, overall employment effects are modest, as reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.

events.title: Stop the Race to Superintelligence
events.description: Nate Soares, MIRI Machines are resolving long-standing mathematical conjectures, generating novel scientific research, and carrying out cyberattacks on their own initiative. The leading AI laboratories say that their goal is to build AI systems that surpass humans at every cognitive task. Drawing on his book with Eliezer Yudkowsky, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, Nate Soares (President, Machine Intelligence Research Institute) argues that the current AI trajectory would predictably end in human extinction, not because the AI will hate us but because it simply won't care, and will pursue other strange drives. But all is not lost: the dangerous sort of AI does not exist yet, and there is ample time to change the trajectory and avert catastrophe.

events.title: Tania Ketenjian & Philip Wood // Sound Made Public: The Art of Listening
events.description: Join the Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation on Tuesday, September 8th for a talk with Tania Ketenjian and Philip Wood, co-founders of SOUND MADE PUBLIC, a San Francisco and New York -based studio that creates audio experiences, sound installations, and immersive cultural programming for institutions around the world. ​Award-winning journalist and producer Tania Ketenjian has spent over two decades interviewing the world's leading artists and thinkers with unique conversations that reveal intimate understandings of creativity, inspiration and the journeys that shape us. She has produced nationally and globally for NPR, the BBC, the BBC World Service and many others. Philip is a designer, maker, and cultural provocateur whose work spans branding, spatial design, furniture, and live events, and the founder of CITIZEN:Citizen, with pieces in the permanent collections of MoMA. Together, they've built SOUND MADE PUBLIC into a studio agnostic to scale and medium, producing everything from podcast series to public installations for institutions including the Guggenheim, the Met, MoMA, the Whitney, The Brooklyn Museum, The Studio Museum in Harlem and The Rubin Museum, amongst others. ​In this talk, Tania and Philip will share how they translate place, story, and sound into experiences that move fluidly from audio and recorded media into live, physical space. Drawing on projects like their work capturing the Guggenheim's architecture as an auditory experience for blind and low-vision visitors, and their Webby-honored podcast collaborations, they'll reflect on what it means to design for the ear as much as the eye, and how sound can make cultural spaces and stories more accessible, resonant, and public. ​This event is free and open to the public. ���…………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Buchanan Lecture with Jennifer Brophy | Programmable memory as a tool for plant genome engineering
events.description: Transkingdom transfer of DNA from Agrobacterium to plants is a stunning biological feat and the basis of the most widely used tool for introducing new DNA into plants. Yet despite decades of use, fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of Agrobacterium-mediated DNA transfer, particularly the dynamics and mechanisms of transferred DNA (T-DNA) integration into the plant genome. These gaps have limited our ability to reliably control transgene insertion. We developed T-SWITCH (T-DNA Sensing With Integrase CHassis), a transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana line that can be used to independently measure T-DNA delivery and integration after Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, to dissect these processes. Using T-SWITCH, we found that most transformation variables, including DNA repair factors, Agrobacterium virulence proteins, promoter choice, and vector architecture, act on T-DNA delivery, not integration. We find that ~17% of T-DNA delivery events do not result in T-DNA integration. Building on this insight, we use T-SWITCH to achieve integration-free genome editing, producing heritable mutations without Cas9 T-DNA in the genome in a single generation. In a related project we build synthetic genetic circuits that can sense and record specific biological events to achieve greater control over gene expression across the Arabidopsis root system. In Arabidopsis, a single primary root gives rise to secondary (lateral) roots, which subsequently branch into tertiary roots to form an increasingly complex root network over the plant's life. But because these branch types share the same core regulatory machinery, they have been impossible to control independently. We developed a synthetic genetic "counter" that can record repeated developmental events and enable independent control over gene expression across root types. The system successfully counts to two in heterozygous plants, and we discuss ongoing work to apply it for manipulation of root traits. Together, these systems show how synthetic circuits that record biological events can be used to understand or engineer previously inaccessible plant processes.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Mathew Hauer and Tyler McCormick: "AI in Demography"
events.description: Mathew E. Hauer is the Charles B. Nam Associate Professor of Sociology at Florida State University, Assistant Director of the Center for Demography and Population Health, and the Head of AI Agent Development at Aaru, a company focused on artificial intelligence and simulation (https://aaru.com/). His research lies at the intersection of demography, migration, population projections, and climate change, with particular expertise in modeling future population dynamics under climate stress. His work on climate migration and population vulnerability has earned numerous prestigious accolades, including the 2024 Early Achievement Award (https://www.populationassociation.org/about/annual-awards/early-achievement-award#:~:text=The%20Early%20Achievement%20award%20recognizes,scholars%20who%20received%20their%20Ph.) from the Population Association of America and the 2023 Cozzarelli Prize (http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/pnas-cozzarelli-2022.html) from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, and is a finalist for the 2025 Cozzarelli Prize and the Max Planck-Humboldt Research Award. He is a two-time recipient of the E. Walter Terrie Award (https://www.sda-demography.org/Terrie-Award) for excellence in applied demography, and his dissertation on sea-level rise and human migration has accumulated over 1,500 citations since 2016. Dr. Hauer's research has significantly shaped our understanding of climate change's demographic impacts, from sea-level rise displacement to temperature extremes and coastal flooding. His work has been featured in over 800 media outlets worldwide, including the New York Times, The Guardian, Time Magazine, National Geographic, and the Washington Post. Before joining FSU, he spent nearly a decade directing the Applied Demography Program at the University of Georgia. Tyler McCormick's work develops statistical models for inference and prediction in scientific settings where data are sparsely observed or measured with error, with a particular focus on measuring and understanding human behavior. His recent projects include estimating features of social networks (e.g. the degree of clustering or how central an individual is) using data from standard surveys, inferring a likely cause of death (when deaths happen outside of hospitals) using reports from surviving caretakers, and quantifying & communicating uncertainty in predictive models for global health policymakers. He holds a Ph.D. in Statistics (with distinction) from Columbia University and is the recipient of the NIH Director's New Innovator Award, NIH Career Development (K01) Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Program Award, and a Google Faculty Research Award. Currently, he is a Professor of Statistics and Sociology at the University of Washington, where he is also a core faculty member in the Center for Statistics and the Social Sciences and a Senior Data Science Fellow at the eScience Institute. During the 2019-2020 academic year Tyler was a Visiting Faculty Researcher at Google People+AI Research (PAIR). Tyler is the former Editor of the Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics (JCGS) and a Fellow of the American Statistical Association. Tyler is currently a member of the Committee on Applied and Theoretical Statistics at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, & Medicine. More information on Tyler's work is here: https://thmccormick.github.io (https://thmccormick.github.io/).

events.title: Eva Odzuck | Plato's Critique of Democracy
events.description: This lecture reconstructs Plato's critique of the democratic concept of freedom in Books 8 and 9 of the Republic and argues that this critique is more context-sensitive, complex, and constructive than is generally assumed in current scholarship. The lecture argues that, in his analysis of democracy, Plato sheds light on the psychological, institutional, and conceptual dimensions of populism and its connection to tyranny—dimensions that could also be relevant to understanding the problems facing democracies today. Eva Helene Odzuck is Professor of Political Philosophy at the University of Regensburg. Her research focus is on ancient and early modern political thought and on liberal democracy. Eva Odzuck's monographs include „Thomas Hobbes' körperbasierter Liberalismus" (2016) and „Keimbahneingriffe im Namen der Freiheit?" (2026). Her research has been published in journals such as Hobbes Studies, History of European Ideas, Zeitschrift für Politikwissenschaft, Zeitschrift für praktische Philosophie, and The Review of Politics.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Rosa Cao: Computational triviality and scaffolded intelligence
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain gives rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, August 26, 2026 Time: 12:00 pm Location: 101 Weill hall Speaker: Rosa Cao Affiliation: Stanford University (https://philosophy.stanford.edu/people/rosa-cao)

events.title: Seminar 291, Department Seminar: Suresh Naidu (Columbia University) - The Economic Geography of American Slavery
events.description: Abstract: What would the antebellum American economy have looked like without slavery? Using new micro-data on the U.S. economy in 1860, we document that where free and enslaved workers live and how much they earn correlates strongly—but differently— with geographic proxies for agricultural productivity, disease, and ease of slave escape. To explain these patterns, we build a quantitative spatial model of slavery, where slaveholders coerce enslaved workers into supplying more labor, capture the proceeds of their labor, and assign them to sectors and occupations that maximize owner profits rather than worker welfare. Combining theory and data, we then quantify how dismantling the institution of slavery affected the spatial economy. We find that the economic impacts of emancipation are substantial, generating welfare gains for the enslaved of roughly 1,200%, while reducing welfare of free workers by 0.7% and eliminating slaveholder profit. Aggregate GDP rises by 9.1%, with a contraction in agricultural productivity counteracted by an expansion in manufacturing and services driven by an exodus of formerly enslaved workers out of agriculture and into the U.S. North. See paper here (https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/rda051o16fkz03tlfg5h1/ACN-The-Economic-Geography-of-American-Slavery.pdf?rlkey=y8g9410q8chb15o5i6haucriy&e=1&dl=0).

events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Shigehiro Oishi, "Specialization and Its Discontent: Implications for Curiosity and Well-Being"
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Shigehiro OishiMarshall Field IV Distinguished Service ProfessorDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of Chicago;2026-27 FellowCenter for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS)Stanford UniversityWednesday, September 9, 202612:10 pm to 1:30 pmRoom 11022121 Berkeley WaySpecialization and Its Discontent: Implications for Curiosity and Well-BeingDivision of labor (specialization) is widely considered a cornerstone of modern productivity, yet its potential psychological costs are not well understood. We examined whether division of labor reduces curiosity–the motivation to explore and learn new things. Across four experiments (N = 821), participants who work, or are expected to work, in divided labor settings showed lower curiosity than those who work in undivided settings. Analyses of three large cross-sectional datasets and one longitudinal panel (N = 320,119) showed that similar patterns generalized across countries, industries, economic contexts, and personality profiles. Together, these findings suggest that, as work becomes more divided, people's motivation to explore and learn new things may diminish. Shigehiro Oishi is the Marshall Field IV Distinguished Service Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago. He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2023). He received his B.A. at International Christian University in Tokyo, Ed. M at Teachers College, Columbia University, and Ph.D. at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 2000. He taught at the University of Minnesota (2000-2004), Columbia University (2018-2020), and the University of Virginia (2004-2018; 2020-2022) before joining UChicago (2022-). He won the 2017 Society of Experimental Social Psychology Career Trajectory Award, the 2018 Carol and Ed Diener Award from the Society for Personality and Social Psychology, and the 2021 Outstanding Achievement Award for Advancing Cultural Psychology. His research focuses on culture, social ecology, and well-being. His lab is particularly interested in asking questions surrounding the concept of well-being (e.g. "what is a good life?"), the predictors of well-being (e.g. "what are the predictors of a good life?"), and the consequences of well-being (e.g. "are there benefits to a happy/meaningful/psychologically rich life?"). Furthermore, he is interested in how the concepts, the predictors, and the consequences of well-being might differ across cultures. Additionally, his research explores socio-ecological conditions that are detrimental or conducive to well-being (e.g., income inequality, residential mobility, walkability).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Ore Carmi [Tel:��510-642-5050; Email: orecarmi@berkeley.edu (mailto:orecarmi@berkeley.edu)] with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Dipti Nayak: CRISPR guided insights in the biology of (methanogenic) archaea
events.description: Methanogenic archaea carry out an unusual energy metabolism that culminates in the production of methane gas. No other trait is more emblematic of extant archaea, which makes methanogens an ideal system for probing foundational questions about archaeal biology. These microbes are also abundant in anoxic environments within and around us, and they account for the vast majority of methane emissions on our planet. Yet despite their importance to human and planetary health, methanogens remain poorly understood. In this talk, I will present work from my lab that uses our recently developed CRISPR genome editing toolkit to characterize the distinctive molecular biology and metabolism of methanogenic archaea. On the molecular side, I will describe the discovery of a new class of archaeal transcription factors and of an ambiguous genetic code. Turning to methanogenesis itself, I will showcase our efforts to map the energy conservation pathways of these microorganisms and the biogenesis of methyl-coenzyme M reductase, the enzyme that catalyzes the final step of biological methane production.Division(s): Department of Molecular & Cell Biology

events.title: Real Estate Populism: Urban Spectacles and the Ecological Origins of Bukelismo in El Salvador
events.description: This talk explores the geography of authoritarian populism in El Salvador. It focuses on Nuevo Cuscatlán, a semi-rural town in the periphery of San Salvador where President Nayib Bukele served as municipal mayor between 2012 and 2015. I examine how Bukele crafted his profile as a promising politician by using the urbanizing landscape as a stage for a populist media spectacle. Promoted through the name of "The New City," this spectacle portrayed the mayor as the inventor of a "new development model" capable of reconciling gentrification with longstanding working-class demands. Drawing on urban political ecology and critical agrarian studies, I argue that the political success of this strategy relied on Bukele's strategic use of land and water as a political asset. This use consisted of two main practices: 1. The increase of municipal revenue from real estate capital through rezoning and land deals, and 2. The financing and fetishization of public water infrastructure in a context of growing scarcity. The portrayal of the latter as a form of progressive redistribution obscured what was, in reality, a silent process of territorial dispossession. Dr. Julio Gutiérrez is an anthropologist and political ecologist from El Salvador. He specializes in urban political ecology and critical development studies, with a research focus on urban extractivism, land politics, and the geographies of financialization.

events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Rising Star Lecture with Neha Kamat, PhD
events.description: Harnessing Membrane-Protein Interactions to Engineer Synthetic and Cellular Lipid Membranes Abstract: Membranes play a vital role in a variety of physiological processes. Recreating these processes outside of the cell will allow us to better understand them as well as design an entirely new class of materials that can sense, transport, or target important biological signals and molecules. In this talk, I will present our recent work harnessing lipid-protein interactions to design membrane-based nanoparticles for biosensing and therapeutic applications. Our approach, bridging synthetic biology techniques and model membrane assembly, provides an innovative yet simple method to probe the role of membrane composition and biophysical properties on protein dynamics and to advance the design of nanoparticles that leverage membrane protein activity.

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Normalizing Inequality: How Californians Make Sense of the Growing Divide"
events.description: REGISTER (https://forms.gle/f4JhiHaonginYLWY6) Please join us on Wednesday, September 9th from 4-5:30pm for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Normalizing Inequality: How Californians Make Sense of the Growing Divide, by G. Cristina Mora, Professor of Sociology and Tianna Paschel, Associate Professor of African American Studies, both at UC Berkeley. Professors Mora and Paschel will be joined in conversation by Desmond Jagmohan, Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, and Lisa García Bedolla, Professor of Education at UC Berkeley. Nicholas Vargas, Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at UC Berkeley, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, the School of Education, the Othering and Belonging Institute, and the Departments of Political Science and African American Studies.A reception will follow the discussion. The Social Science Matrix Authors Meet Critics (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/authors-meet-critics/) book series features lively discussions about recently published books authored by social scientists at UC Berkeley. For each event, the author discusses the key arguments of their book with fellow scholars. These events are free and open to the public.About the Book California has long been mythologized as the quintessential land of opportunity and reinvention — a place where anyone, regardless of origin, can forge a new life and realize their aspirations. Yet beneath this gilded narrative lies a starker reality: California ranks among the most unequal states in one of the world's most unequal countries, where the middle class finds itself increasingly squeezed. Economic inequality is not an anomaly but part of a broader global phenomenon, as disparities deepen across the world. While we know a lot about its contours, its evolution over time and its intersections with race and immigration, we understand far less about how ordinary people interpret and internalize it. In Normalizing Inequality, sociologists G. Cristina Mora and Tianna S. Paschel illuminate how middle-class Californians perceive and come to accept the inequalities that surround them. Drawing on extensive interviews and surveys, Mora and Paschel uncover a profound paradox at the heart of middle-class consciousness. They find that Californians are keenly aware of the systemic causes of inequality—they recognize policies engineered to benefit the wealthy, they acknowledge how structural racism makes it hard for some groups to get ahead—yet they consistently minimize these forces. Instead, they gravitate toward explanations rooted in individualism, moral character, and the idea that things are worse in other places. Racism and racial inequality in California become palatable when framed as "not as bad as the South." Immigrant exploitation, however severe, transforms into evidence of the American Dream fulfilled simply upon arrival. Economic pressures that displace others become surmountable through personal industriousness and forbearance. These beliefs about inequality grow more troubling still. Middle-class Californians sometimes blame disempowered people for their circumstances—acknowledging structural barriers facing homeless and undocumented populations while simultaneously faulting them for insufficient drive or criminal behavior that compounds their difficulties. When contemplating California's future, interviewees envision economic prosperity propelled by technological innovation, yet remain curiously unconcerned with how present inequalities might shape that tomorrow. Their imagined future is one where White and Asian American populations thrive, while Black, Latino, and economically marginalized Californians either vanish through displacement or fade into irrelevance. As respondents use these interpretive frameworks to make sense of inequality, they lean heavily on California's foundational narratives of opportunity, sanctuary and multiracial promise.Normalizing Inequality offers an incisive examination of how ordinary citizens make sense of inequality and, through that very process of sense-making, how they tolerate and passively reproduce the conditions they often claim to deplore.Read a Berkeley News article about the book.PanelistsG. Cristina Mora (https://sociology.berkeley.edu/faculty/g-cristina-mora) completed her B.A. in Sociology at UC Berkeley in 2003 and earned her PhD in Sociology from Princeton University in 2009. Before returning to Cal, she was a Provost Postdoctoral Scholar in Sociology at the University of Chicago. Professor Mora's award-winning research focuses mainly on questions of racial and ethnic categorization, racial politics, and immigration. Her book, Making Hispanics, was published in 2014 by the University of Chicago Press and provides a socio-historical account of the rise of the "Hispanic/Latino" panethnic category in the United States. This work, along with related articles, has received wide recognition, including the Best Dissertation Award and the 2018 Early Career Award (SREM) from the American Sociological Association. Her work has also been the subject of various national media segments in venues like the Atlantic, the New Yorker, NPR, and Latino USA. At UC Berkeley, her long-term efforts towards diversity and inclusion have recently been formally acknowledged. In 2021 and 2022, she received the UCB Graduate Mentoring Award and the Chancellors Award for Advancing Equity and Excellence, and she led campus' first social-science cluster hire focused on "Latinos and Democracy." In 2023 she received a million-dollar federal grant from the Department of Education to establish a "Latino Social Science Pipeline" initiative at UC Berkeley.Tianna Paschel (https://africam.berkeley.edu/people/tianna-paschel) is an associate professor in the Department of African American Studies, and Sociology (by courtesy) and Faculty Director of the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies at UC Berkeley. Her research explores the intersection of racial ideology, politics, and globalization in the Americas and has been published in the American Journal of Sociology, the Du Bois Review, Ethnic and Racial Studies, Sociological Forum, Social Forces, and various edited volumes. She is also the author of Becoming Black Political Subjects, which draws on ethnographic and archival methods to explore the shift in the 1990s from ideas of unmarked universal citizenship to multicultural citizenship regimes and the recognition of specific rights for black populations by Latin American states. It is the winner of numerous awards including the Herbert Jacob Book Award of the Law and Society Association and the Barrington Moore Book Award of the American Sociological Association (ASA). Professor Paschel is also the co-editor of Afro-Latin@s in Movement, an interdisciplinary volume that explores transnationalism and blackness in the Americas and Co-PI of the Mellon-funded Black Studies Collaboratory.Lisa García Bedolla (https://bse.berkeley.edu/lisa-garc%C3%ADa-bedolla) is Berkeley's Vice Provost for Graduate Studies and Hitchcock Dean of the Graduate Division, and Chancellor's Professor of Education. She uses the tools of social science to reveal the causes of educational and political inequalities in the United States, considering differences across the lines of ethnorace, gender, class, geography, et cetera. She believes an intersectional and interdisciplinary approach is critical to recognizing the complexity of the contemporary United States. She has used a variety of social science methods – in-depth interviewing, survey research, field experiments, and geographic information systems (GIS), among others – to shed light on these questions. She has published six books and dozens of research articles, earning five national book awards and numerous other awards. She has consulted for presidential campaigns and statewide ballot efforts and has partnered with over a dozen community organizations working to empower low-income communities of color. Through those partnerships, she has developed a set of best practices for engaging and mobilizing voters in these communities, becoming one of the nation's foremost experts on political engagement within communities of color. Professor García Bedolla earned her PhD in political science from Yale University and her BA in Latin American Studies and Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley.Desmond Jagmohan (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/desmond-jagmohan) is Assistant Professor of Political Science at the University of California, Berkeley. He specializes in the history of American and African American political thought, American intellectual history, and the history of political thought. His research concerns political and moral agency under conditions of extreme oppression. He is completing his first book, Dark Virtues: Booker T. Washington's Tragic Realism (under contract with Princeton University Press), which draws on several years of archival research to recover Washington as a virtue theorist of the oppressed. His second book will read Harriet Jacobs's slave narrative as a work of moral and political theory that grounds the wrong of slavery in property rights in another person. His work has been published in Journal of Politics, Political Theory, Annual Review of Political Science, Perspectives on Politics, Politics, Groups, and Identities, Contemporary Political Theory, and Boston Review. Professor Jagmohan is the winner of several awards and fellowships: The APSA Best Dissertation Award from the Race, Ethnicity and Politics Section (2015), a National Fellow at the Hoover Institution, Stanford University (2018), and a Laurance S. Rockefeller Visiting Faculty Fellow at University Center for Human Values at Princeton University, and Hellman Fellowship at UC, Berkeley. Prior to arriving at Berkeley, he was Assistant Professor of Politics at Princeton University, where he delivered the 2018 Constitution Day Lecture and was awarded the Laurance S. Rockefeller University Preceptorship in the University Center for Human Values. He holds an M.A. and a Ph.D. from Cornell University.Nicholas Vargas (https://ethnicstudies.berkeley.edu/people/nicholas-vargas) (moderator) is an Associate Professor in the Department of Ethnic Studies at UC Berkeley. His scholarship examines Latinx racialization: how Latinx people are identified, perceived, and positioned within U.S. racial hierarchies, and how these processes intersect with immigration ideologies, state institutions, and higher education inequality. A central aim of his work is to clarify how racial categories and racial meaning are produced in everyday life and policy contexts, and how those dynamics shape public attitudes. Methodologically, Vargas draws on survey research, administrative and demographic data, and mixed-method strategies that connect macro-level structures to micro-level meaning-making. His work bridges ethnic studies, sociology, and education research, and he frequently collaborates with student researchers to develop data-rich projects that speak to pressing public questions and contribute to ongoing debates in Latino/Latinx social science. Vargas has served on the U.S. Census Bureau's National Advisory Committee and is Co-Director of the Latino Social Science Pipeline Initiative at UC Berkeley. He also serves as the Program Coordinator of Chicanx/Latinx Studies and co-leads UC Berkeley's Latinxs and Democracy Cluster.

events.title: Casual Conversation with Venerable Pomnyun Sunim
events.location: Sutardja Dai Hall, Banatao Auditorium, Room 310, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Venerable Pomnyun Sunim (Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhist monk) In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Note: This event will begin exactly at the scheduled time of 4:00 PM. Talk Summary: How can we live with greater clarity, resilience, and compassion in a rapidly changing world? In this interactive "Casual Conversation," Venerable Pomnyun Sunim invites students and community members to openly explore questions about stress, relationships, career uncertainty, emotional wellbeing, social conflict, and the search for meaning in modern life. Known for his practical and accessible teaching style, Venerable Pomnyun Sunim responds directly to audience questions with insight, humor, and compassion. Rather than offering abstract religious doctrine, he shares practical wisdom grounded in Buddhist philosophy and decades of humanitarian and social engagement. The conversation may also touch on broader topics including mindfulness, sustainable living, peacebuilding, social responsibility, and how individuals can contribute positively to society while maintaining inner balance and freedom. This event is open to people of all backgrounds, beliefs, and levels of familiarity with Buddhism. Speaker Bio: Venerable Pomnyun Sunim is a highly respected Korean Seon (Zen) Buddhist monk, humanitarian leader, author, and founder of Jungto Society, an international volunteer-based organization dedicated to spiritual practice, social engagement, environmental sustainability, and peacebuilding. He is widely recognized for his accessible and deeply engaging public dialogues known as "Casual Conversations" (즉문즉설), where he responds spontaneously to audience questions about everyday life challenges. His teachings focus on practical wisdom, emotional clarity, compassion, and personal responsibility, making them highly relevant across cultural, academic, and professional communities. Venerable Pomnyun Sunim has delivered talks and interactive sessions at leading academic institutions including Harvard University, Columbia University, UCLA, Johns Hopkins University, the University of Toronto, and other universities across North America and Asia. He has also spoken with professionals at organizations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank, and global technology companies including Google. In 2002, he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award, often regarded as Asia's Nobel Prize, in recognition of his humanitarian work, peacebuilding efforts, and contributions to socially engaged Buddhism.

events.title: EECS Colloquium | Pursuing a "Moore's Law" for Power Electronics
events.description: As processors and controllers of electrical energy, power electronics are key drivers of innovation in transportation, energy systems, aerospace, computing, manufacturing, healthcare, consumer electronics, and more. However, unlike information-processing circuits, power electronics are challenging to miniaturize and have yet to undergo the extreme scaling that underpins microelectronics today. While major advances have been enabled by advanced semiconductor devices and control capabilities, further progress is now primarily bottlenecked by the energy storage components they depend on, particularly magnetics (i.e., inductors and transformers). Dramatic miniaturization of power electronics will therefore require new approaches to power conversion with superior power density and performance at small sizes. This talk explores how we can leverage an alternative energy storage modality – electromechanical energy storage in piezoelectric resonators – to unlock a new era of scalability for power electronics. Unlike magnetics, piezoelectric resonators offer power densities that fundamentally improve as they shrink, among numerous other advantages in size, performance, and manufacturability. Realizing these advantages, however, will require new design strategies for both power electronic circuits and the resonators themselves. Accordingly, this talk will present recent advances in (1) circuit topologies and control for resonator-based dc-dc converters and "active inductors", and (2) piezoelectric component design concepts including isolated piezoelectric transformers and "overtone" piezoelectric resonators. These strategies enable high-performance use of piezoelectric resonators as energy storage components across a wide range of applications, laying a foundation for power electronics that scale favorably to small sizes. Jessica Boles is the Chenming Hu Assistant Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at the University of California, Berkeley, and inaugural Co-Director of the Berkeley Power and Energy Center. She received her B.S. and M.S. degrees from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville (UTK) and her Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), all in electrical engineering. Boles' research pursues major advances in the performance, size, and cost of power electronics through use of alternative passive component technologies. Her research interests span power converter circuit topologies, modeling, and control, as well as passive component design, modeling, fabrication, and characterization. Boles has received the ARPA-E IGNIITE Award, the NASA Early Career Faculty Award, the NSF CAREER Award, and the UCOP Early Career Faculty Research Excellence Award. Her work has been recognized with three IEEE prize paper awards and the IEEE PELS Ph.D. Thesis Talk Award. She currently serves on the leadership of two technical committees in the IEEE Power Electronics Society: Emerging Technologies and Control and Modeling of Power Electronics.

events.title: Combinatorics Seminar: Gröbner geometry of hybrid pipe dreams
events.description: Speaker: Gabe Udell, UC Santa CruzMatrix Schubert varieties are subvarieties of the space of all n × n matrices which are defined by rank conditions on their submatrices. The equivariant cohomology classes of matrix Schubert varieties are given by double Schubert polynomials. They can be computed in terms of either pipe dreams (introduced by Bergeron–Billey), bumpless pipe dreams (introduced by Lam–Lee–Shimozono), or any of 2^n flavors of hybrid pipe dreams (introduced by Knutson–U) which interpolate between the two. In this talk I will discuss bijective proofs that the 2^n formulas agree and commutative algebraic proofs that hybrid pipe dreams index (with multiplicity) the irreducible components of Gröbner degenerations of matrix Schubert varieties for certain term orders. The latter topic is based on joint work with Tianyi Yu and Zach Hamaker and builds on work of Knutson–Miller in the pipe dream case and Klein–Weigandt in the bumpless pipe dream case.

events.title: Fall Plant Sale Series: From the Collection and Beyond - Member Opening
events.description: Every plant tells a story. From pre-Jurassic Cycads to yerba buena tea, plants connect to human and more than human history. At the University of California Botanical Garden, we work to keep those stories alive. This plant sale features a large array of plants that we have propagated from the Garden collection, as well as some special cultivars and more. This collection of perennials, trees, shrubs, and vines displays the best of our plants grown using seeds, cuttings, and divisions. Come on our opening evening and weekend to talk with our volunteer plant propagators to ask questions and get advice.Click here for more information (https://botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/plant-nursery).Pop-up Plant Sale Sale runs Thursday, September 10 – Sunday, September 13 while supplies last. events.title: Yung Ho Chang: How a House in the Sky Landed on Earth? | Inaugural Stanley Saitowitz Alumni Lecture
events.description: Yung Ho Chang (MArch 1984), FAIA, is the founding partner and principal architect of Atelier Feichang Jianzhu (FCJZ), established with Lijia Lu in 1993. Educated in China and the U.S., Chang earned his master's degree from UC Berkeley and has practiced in China since 1992. He has received numerous honors, including First Place in the Shinkenchiku Residential Design Competition (1986), a Progressive Architecture Citation Award (1996), the UNESCO Prize for the Promotion of the Arts (2000), an Academy Award in Architecture from the American Academy of Arts and Letters (2006), and the China Architecture Media Award Excellence in Practice Prize (2016). An honorary member of AIA Hong Kong, Chang served as a Pritzker Architecture Prize jury member (2012–2017). FCJZ's design for the Jishou Art Museum won the AIA 2020 Architecture Award and the ArchDaily China Building of the Year 2020 Award. Chang was founding head of the Graduate Center of Architecture at Peking University (1999–2005), held chair professorships at Harvard GSD (2002) and University of Michigan (2004), and headed MIT's Department of Architecture (2005��2010). His work has been featured six times at the Venice Biennale. The Stanley Saitowitz Alumni Lectures, established in 2026 through a generous gift from Professor Emeritus of Architecture Stanley Saitowitz (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/stanley-saitowitz) (MArch 1977), celebrate distinguished alums of UC Berkeley College of Environmental Design and bring inspiring leaders in architecture back to Bauer Wurster Hall.

events.description: In conjunction with the exhibition Hidden Layers: AI Infrastructures and Hallucinations at UC Berkeley's Worth Ryder Gallery, Antonio Somaini, Hannes Bajohr, and Sonja Thiel present a program of works about AI and its social and technical infrastructures. Gibbs Chapman's Push Button is a dryly funny exposé of the effects of automation on twenty-first-century humans, while Inès Sieulle's The Oasis I Deserve documents affective interactions with the chatbot Replika. events.title: Workshop: The Latent Spaces of Culture
events.description: Latent spaces are a foundational concept in contemporary artificial intelligence. They enable complex data—images, texts, sounds, and other digital objects—to be represented as high-dimensional structures in which relationships, patterns, and similarities can be modeled computationally. By translating intricate datasets into compressed mathematical representations, latent spaces allow AI systems not only to analyze information but also to generate new content; often, this content is itself cultural in nature. Yet the cultural and epistemological implications of latent spaces remain comparatively underexplored, particularly their role in shaping creativity, cultural memory, and representation. This three-day workshop, part of the France–Berkeley Fund project "The Latent Spaces of Culture," brings together researchers from UC Berkeley and institutions in France to examine these questions and explore latent space as both a technical architecture and a cultural form. (September 9, 2pm-4pm; September 10/11, 9:30 am-4pm on both days)https://german.berkeley.edu/latent-spaces-culture (https://german.berkeley.edu/latent-spaces-culture)

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Yilong Hou (CTML GSR)
events.description: Continuing our CTML Seminar Series is CTML GSR Yilong Hou (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/yilong-hou)! He will be discussing "Highly Adaptive Lasso Log-Splines for Univariate Density Estimation." This seminar will take place on Thursday, September 10 at 11:00 AM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401. Abstract: Highly Adaptive Lasso is a powerful nonparametric method with pointwise asymptotic normality and uniform convergence. We use it for univariate density estimation as a log-spline method: the log-density is expanded in a truncated-power basis and a variation budget becomes an ℓ1-constrained MLE. We compare this estimator with existing univariate bounded-total-variation methods such as local adaptive splines (LAS), and with other spline approaches including trend filtering and B-splines. We then discuss algorithms for optimizing the HAL-MLE and the compactness for HAL-TMLE. The rest of the talk sketches extensions from fully observed data to right-censored (RC) and current-status (CS) data, and finally to the multivariate case. For RC data we share results from directly optimizing the observed-data loss after an IPCW warm start. Bio: Yilong Hou is currently a PhD candidate in Biostatistics at the University of California, Berkeley, working/mentored by Professor Mark van der Laan. His research interests primarily lie in HAL, NPMLE, and survival analysis. His other work research interests include TV penalty and Convex optimization. Recent work has been in HAL for density estimation.

events.description: Co-hosted by the Nazarian Center at UCLA and the Helen Diller Institute at UC BerkeleyWebinarThursday, September 10, 11:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. PTREGISTER NOW (https://ucla.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_vbYX8n1cRiGx4i5-rJhGvw)https://ucla.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_vbYX8n1cRiGx4i5-rJhGvw (https://ucla.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_vbYX8n1cRiGx4i5-rJhGvw) The upcoming elections in Israel, scheduled for Tuesday, October 27, could well be the most pivotal in the country's history. events.title: Alex Hack | The Black Body and its Many Histories: Corroborating Black Health and the Death of Medgar Evers (CRG Forum Series)
events.description: CRG Forum Series*The Black Body and its Many Histories: Corroborating Black Health and the Death of Medgar Evers withAlex Hack, UC President's & Andrew W. Mellon Postdoctoral Fellow, Departments of Gender Studies and English, University of California, Los Angeles and respondentPatrice D. Douglass, Associate Professor of Gender & Women's Studies, UC Berkeley The 1963 assassination of Medgar Evers and the many accounts that followed demonstrate the ambivalent nature of racial trauma and the ways in which patient circumstance is hidden, shaped, and dispersed via fact, feeling, and social bias. The lack of verifiability of the circumstances surrounding the death of such an influential civil rights leader speaks to a larger problem that continues within the American healthcare system: its inability to recognize more holistic and collaborative forms of evidence, especially those less interested in hegemonic knowledge, "genetic predisposition," or formulaic concerns. Taking this into account, I incorporate my father's ICU medical records, placing the supposedly "factual" nature of these documents in conversation with my own experience—ultimately looking to question the methods by which grounded understanding and familial knowledge are wiped away to make room for the "objective." Working within the rich tradition of Black feminists who have made strides to consider the body and its information, I utilize Sylvia Wynter's discussion of the programming power of language and Audre Lorde's own autotheory of illness to examine how ambiguity and a continued lack of understanding intractably remain within hegemonic health systems.Event hosted by the Center for Race and Gender (https://crg.berkeley.edu/), and co-sponsored by the Departments of African American Studies (https://africam.berkeley.edu/) and Gender & Women's Studies (https://gws.berkeley.edu/).*Lunch provided on a first-come, first-served basis. **If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

Trust is at the heart of every relationship, and it's especially critical in the workplace. events.title: Navigating the Seasons: Unraveling the Genomic Basis of Hibernation in Brown Bears
events.description: Hibernation in bears involves a suite of seasonally reversible metabolic and physiological changes. Revealing the mechanisms underlying the reversible physiology of hibernation could have applications to both human and animal health as hibernation is often associated with disease-like states. Changes in hibernation are driven in part by sweeping changes in gene expression in multiple tissues. We determined the seasonal transcriptional changes occurring in brown bears (Ursus arctos horribilis). We continue to study the higher-level regulatory mechanisms involved in the emergence from hibernation. Moreover, we explore the population genetics of brown bears in North America and discuss implications for conservation.

events.title: Adrien Peyrache: Orienting memory during wake and sleep
events.description: The head-direction (HD) circuit, an upstream provider of orientation signals for navigation, maintains coherent internal orientation memory that stays stable within each environment for weeks. During non-REM sleep, when hippocampal trajectories are replayed for memory formation, HD cells remain coordinated and directly influence this hippocampal replay. This suggests the HD system conveys a "virtual" orientation signal to support memory replay, with the thalamus appearing to play a crucial role in generating it. Overall, the HD system supplies the hippocampus and associated structures with a coherent, possibly lifelong-stable signal maintained across brain states to support spatial navigation and memory formation.

events.title: ESPM Seminar Series: Paolina Lu, "Edible Insects and the Future of Food: Capitalist Dreams, Loss, and Everyday Immigrant Practices"
events.description: In the 2010s, edible insects emerged in popular discourse as a potential "food of the future." Drawing on fieldwork and interviews conducted in the United States from 2019-2024 with entrepreneurs, farmers, and food producers, this talk traces how insects became a hopeful response to anxieties about ecological crisis, food security, and changing ways of life. I bring one Southeast Asian American family's enduring practice of foraging for grasshoppers into conversation with the emergence and transformation of the insect agriculture industry. Doing so reveals two distinct relationships to insects: one shaped by the anticipation of future loss and the desire to secure against it, the other by losses already lived through displacement and relocation. Attending to these differences while listening for what they share, the talk asks what an affective throughline of loss can reveal about the ways people imagine futures, develop relationships with other forms of life, and work to make and sustain lives through food. The weekly ESPM seminar will be held in 132 Mulford Hall and via Zoom. There will be a social hour afterwards from 4:30pm - 5:30pm in the Mulford Courtyard.
