events.title: BTS Army: Forever We Are Young - Film Screening and Conversation with Directors Grace Lee and Patty Ahn
events.location: Sutardja Dai Hall, Banatao Auditorium, Room 310, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker/s: Grace Lee (Director/Producer), Patty Ahn (University of California, San Diego) In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Note: This event will begin exactly at the scheduled time of 4:00 PM. Film Summary: From Seoul to Los Angeles, Texas to Mexico City, BTS ARMY is everywhere. BTS ARMY: FOREVER WE ARE YOUNG dives into the passionate fandom that catapulted 21st century pop icons BTS into a global household name. We meet fans at a BTS-focused ReactorCon in Lewisville, Texas, a dance instructor in Seoul who teaches BTS choreography, and fans who've been organizing since 2013 to help BTS dominate the charts. Defying stereotypes of pop fans as screaming teens, ARMY is an intergenerational, culturally savvy, and socially active movement that is as diverse as the world itself. The film captures the powerful spirit of activism and collectivity that make ARMY a symbol of hope and unity in our ever-fractured world. FOREVER WE ARE YOUNG is made BY ARMY FOR ARMY. The film centers on the fans themselves and celebrates their creativity, resilience, and deep emotional connection to the group. Though rooted in fandom, the film explores universal themes of belonging, identity, and self-love. Speaker Bios: Grace Lee recently directed and produced BTS Army: Forever We Are Young, which was released in cinemas worldwide in 2025. Other credits include Peabody winning PBS series ASIAN AMERICANS as well as And She Could be Next, about women of color transforming U.S. politics and civic engagement which aired on POV. Other credits include the Peabody-winning American Revolutionary: The Evolution of Grace Lee Boggs, The Grace Lee Project, K-TOWN'92, an interactive project about the 1992 Los Angeles civil unrest and the podcast Viewers Like Us. She co-founded Asian American Documentary Network and is a member of AMPAS Documentary branch. Patty Ahn (they/them) is a filmmaker and Associate Teaching Professor in the Communication Department at the University of California, San Diego. Their research and teaching specialize in K-Pop's growing global influence, especially in the U.S. More broadly, they work at the intersection of popular music, Media Industries, and critical race and gender studies. events.title: Seminar 242, Econometrics Seminar: Kenichi Nagasawa (University of Warwick) - Treatment Effect Estimation with Noisy Conditioning Variables
events.description: Abstract: I develop a new identification strategy for treatment effects when noisy measurements of unobserved confounding factors are available. I use proxy variables to construct a random variable conditional on which treatment variables become exogenous. I show that, under appropriate conditions, there exists a one-to-one mapping between the distribution of unobserved confounding factors and the distribution of proxies, which in turn implies that holding constant the proxy distribution controls for the unobserved confounding factors. To ensure sufficient variation in the constructed control variable, I use an additional variable, termed excluded variable, which satisfies certain exclusion restrictions and relevance conditions. I establish asymptotic distributional results for semiparametric and flexible parametric estimators of causal parameters. I illustrate empirical relevance and usefulness of my results by estimating causal effects of grade retention on academic performance. See full paper here (https://kenagasawa.github.io/covariate-measurement-error.pdf).

events.title: Erich Auerbach in Exile: Western Philology and History in His Rediscovered Turkish Essays (1938-1947)
events.description: Christian Rivoletti (FAU Erlangen-Nuremberg), ErichAuerbach in Exile: Western Philology and History in His Rediscovered Turkish Essays (1938-1947), with a response by James I. Porter (UC Berkeley, Rhetoric - Ancient Greek and Roman Studies) Although international scholarly interest in Erich Auerbach's work, and particularly in his masterpiece Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946), has remained strong over the decades, the past thirty years have witnessed a remarkable intensification and deepening of critical engagement with his work. The recent rediscovery of Auerbach's Turkish essays, written during his exile in Turkey (1936–1947), offers a new perspective on the development of his thought during the exceptional years in which Mimesis was conceived and written. In these essays, Auerbach repeatedly revisits the history of Western literature and culture from within the political, social, and intellectual circumstances of contemporary Turkey. Exile, in other words, becomes a distinctive vantage point from which he reconsiders the European past and its relation to the present. His "exile philology" connects East and West, but above all past and present, revealing how historical interpretation itself can become a form of critical reflection on contemporary political and cultural questions.Christian Rivoletti is Professor of Romance Philology at FAU Erlangen-Nuremberg. His research spans the Italian Renaissance and its European reception (Ariosto e l'ironia della finzione, Marsilio, 2014), literary utopias, and modern narrative and poetry. He has edited three volumes by Erich Auerbach: Romanticismo e realismo (Edizioni della Normale, 2010), Kultur als Politik (Konstanz UP, 2014; translated into Spanish, 2017, and Japanese, 2025), and Letteratura, guerra e storia dell'Europa (forthcoming).

events.title: Paola Bacchetta | Co-Motion: Re-Thinking Power, Subjects and Feminist and Queer Alliances
events.description: A talk by Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta), Professor and the Chair of the Department of Gender and Women's Studies, on her new book, Co-Motion: Re-Thinking Power, Subjects and Feminist and Queer Alliances (https://www.dukeupress.edu/co-motion), that offers a fresh framework for understanding how feminist and queer coalitions take shape across differences and how collective movements can transform prevailing ideas about power, identity, and political agency.AnganaP. Chatterji, Founding Chair, Political Conflict, Gender, and People's Rights Initiative, Center for Race and Gender, and Research Anthropologist, UC Berkeley, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Sept 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: In Co-Motion (https://www.dukeupress.edu/co-motion), theorist Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta) proposes a new lexicon for analyzing power, subjects and alliances. Employing what she calls 'theory-assemblages' to describe how diverse theoretical and political approaches inspire movements and produce different kinds of alliances, Bacchetta engages the inseparability of power relations—such as colonialism, capitalism, racism, caste, misogyny, and speciesism—and how their combinations, operability, and the analyses they require, shift in different contexts and lives of subjects. Focusing on France, India, Italy, and the US from the 1970s to the present, Co-Motion addresses a wide activist, artivist, and social movement archive— group statements, banners, pamphlets, graffiti, posters, poetry, sit-ins, films, art exhibits—to think and feel with the many ways that people, historically and today, come together to act. Through her expansive engagement with varied bodies of scholarship, sites of analysis, and kinds of reading, Bacchetta offers new approaches to analyze, confront, and transforming power, and to enact freedom.About the Author:Paola Bacchetta (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/paola-bacchetta) is Professor and the Chair of the Department of Gender and Women's Studies at University of California, Berkeley. She is a critical theorist whose research focuses on gender, sexuality, colonialism, race, religion, capitalism, Empire, and other relations of power, along with local, translocal to transnational feminist and queer activism. She also works on right-wing movements, gender and sexuality. Her areas of specialization are India, France, the U.S., Brazil and Italy. Dr. Bacchetta is the author or contributing co-editor of the following book length works: Co-Motion: Re-Thinking Power, Subjects and Feminist and Queer Alliances (Durham: Duke University Press, 2026); Fatema Mernissi for Our Times (with Minoo Moallem, Syracuse University Press, 2025); Global Raciality: Empire, Postcoloniality, and Decoloniality, (with Sunaina Maira and Howard Winant, New York: Routledge, 2019); Femminismi Queer Postcoloniali (with Laura Fantone. Verona, Italy: Ombre Corte, 2015); Gender in the Hindu Nation (Delhi, India: Women Ink, 2004); Right-Wing Women: From Conservatives to Extremists around the World (with Margaret Power. New York: Routledge; , 2002); Textes du Mouvement Lesbien en France, 1970-2000 (with Claudie Lesselier, DVD, 2011). Dr. Bacchetta has published over 90 professional journal articles and book chapters on her research, in English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Arabic, Brazilian Portuguese and Danish. She has lectured widely within the U.S., and in Western Europe, Eastern Europe, North Africa, Turkey, Brazil and South Asia. Dr. Bacchetta is the recipient of many awards and and grants including Fulbright, Mellon, multiple different kinds of European Union grants, Peder Sather Research Fund, and the France-Berkeley Fund. She has been a postdoctoral scholar in the USA at Harvard University and the Five College Women's Studies Research Center, in France at École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales and Université de Paris 3, and in Brazil at Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (Florianópolis) and Universidade Federal de Bahia (Salvador, Bahia). events.title: Film Screening: On Call
events.description: In a single medical office just outside Paris, a weary yet caring doctor and his colleagues are visited by a steady flow of patients, all with unique symptoms, yet all united by their status as refugees, migrants, and undocumented immigrants. Some reveal physical injuries; others hold wounds—and memories—that may never heal. All are documented by Alice Diop's steady, unblinking camera, holding fast to their stories, and their faces most of all. "That face thwarts all the political, ideological discourse you hear all day long about immigration," noted Diop. "To see On Call is a therapy against the reflexes of exclusion" (Olivier Barlet, Black Camera).

events.description: Vidhu Shekar, Chief Data and Artificial Intelligence Officer at Caltrans, will present Overview of Artificial Intelligence at Caltrans: A Framework for Enterprise Governance and Adoption at the ITS Berkeley Transportation Seminar on Sept. 11, 2026. Join us for cookie hour at 2:30 in the ITS Library, hosted by TRANSOC.Abstract: This presentation examines how the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) is adopting, governing, and scaling artificial intelligence across a large public-sector transportation enterprise. The work is based on California Executive Order N-12-23 and a CalSTA directive that establishes the Chief Data and AI Officer (CDAO). Together these authorities support an integrated model for aligning AI initiatives with organizational goals through unified data governance, ethical implementation, and cross-departmental collaboration. The presentation also elaborates on the 2026 -28 Data and AI Strategic Plan, a structured use-case framework and real-world deployments and a workforce adoption strategy aligned with the U.S. Department of Labor's AI Literacy Framework. These efforts position Caltrans as an emerging model for state-level AI governance.Bio: Vidhu Shekhar serves as Chief Data and Artificial Intelligence Officer (CDAO) at Caltrans, where he leads the department's enterprise data governance and artificial intelligence strategy. In this role, he provides executive leadership for how Caltrans manages, governs, and applies data and AI technologies to support safer and more efficient transportation systems for Californians. Prior to joining Caltrans, he served at Microsoft as the Americas Lead for Global Partnerships within Industry Solutions Delivery and previously as Government Strategy Lead for U.S. State and Local Government. His career also includes leadership roles at Workday and KPMG, as well as earlier public-sector experience spanning transportation, criminal justice, and municipal finance. He is the author of Generative Artificial Intelligence Use Cases in State & Local Government and participates in the University of Washington Mobility Innovation Center, the PacTrans-USDOT Region 10 University Transportation Center, and the National Academy of Sciences, supporting the responsible adoption of emerging technologies in the public sector. In 2025, he was named to GovTech's Center for Public Sector AI 50 and nominated for the ITS America Hall of Fame Lifetime Achievement Award. He holds a Master of Public Administration from the University of Southern California and is a Senior Executive Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School of Government.

events.title: Ken Raymond Lecture
events.description: Mike Pluth, Professor, University of OregonChemical Tool for Investigating Biological Sulfur and Selenium SpeciesSulfur and selenium occupy a unique position at the interface of inorganic chemistry, redox chemistry, and biology, where changes in oxidation state, speciation, and metal coordination can profoundly alter reactivity. Understanding the fundamental chemistry of reactive S and Se species therefore provides a framework for connecting molecular structure and bonding to their roles in complex biological environments. Biological sulfur metabolism is often framed around H2S as both a metabolic product and signaling species. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that persulfides (RSSH) and related dichalcogenides serve as central intermediates in sulfur trafficking, redox buffering, and enzymatic sulfur-transfer reactions. Despite their growing importance, the fundamental chemical properties that govern the reactivity, stability, and biological fate of these species remain poorly defined. This presentation will highlight recent efforts from our group to prepare and use isolable sulfur and selenium dichalcogenides to establish fundamental structure-reactivity relationships relevant to bioinorganic S/Se chemistry. Examples will include intrinsic dichalcogenide reaction chemistry, synthetic metal-persulfide model complexes, and studies showcasing how coordination to Lewis-acidic metal centers can modulate dichalcogenide electronic structure and reactivity. Together, these studies establish fundamental chemical principles for understanding sulfur and selenium transfer, provide molecular-level insight into metalloenzyme-mediated sulfur trafficking and oxidation pathways, and highlight how coordination chemistry can be used to interrogate the broader chemical landscape of sulfur metabolism.

events.description: Join us in celebrating the opening of the student-curated exhibition Chulas Fronteras: Narrating Sound and Space on the Border. The exhibit explores and celebrates the 50th anniversary of Chulas Fronteras. Co-directed by film director Les Blank and record producer Chris Strachwitz, Chulas Fronteras documents music and culture in the U.S.-México border. Drawing upon the archives of the Arhoolie Foundation and Les Blank Films in El Cerrito, CA, the exhibition is the product of a collaboration between students of the UC Berkeley course Musics in the US-México Borderlands and the Arhoolie Foundation. Arhoolie Foundation's archivist Clark Noone provided the students with access to the Foundation's archives along with guidance in curatorial work. The majority of the objects and their labels were produced by the course students–David Han, Ariana Jiménez, Abdi Kuri Cubillo, Melina Mendoza, and Izabella Newman–under the supervision of Assistant Professor of Music Juan David Rubio Restrepo. We will celebrate the opening with live Tejano music by Miguel Govea, tamales, and a screening of Chulas Fronteras in Morrison Hall, Room 242. The event is free and open to all.

events.title: Film Screening: Vivre sa vie
events.description: Vivre sa vie depicts Nana (Anna Karina), a naive shopgirl, at the brief, flickering moment when she takes responsibility for her life. Nana takes to the streets, becoming a prostitute and a student of human emotions. Brechtian in its use of twelve dispassionately announced tableaux, Vivre sa vie is also intensely personal. Nana's crucible is Jean-Luc Godard's existential epiphany: Nana struggles to see, and say, things as they are, bravely concluding, "All is good." In the famous scene in a movie theater, Nana's rapt attention to Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc is a tribute to another who sacrificed control to take control.

events.title: Film Screening: Modern Times
events.description: It starts with an overhead shot of sheep and cuts to the throngs coming out of a subway station. Was Charlie Chaplin a Surrealist, or just a realist? His version of modern times looks forward in equal measure to Jacques Tati and 1984. This "silent" is full of modern sounds, heard over loudspeakers and big corporate television screens (not to mention the Tramp's outburst of French-inspired gibberish). Charlie, the ever-elegant Tramp, is an industrial swashbuckler with an oilcan for a sword, but he's begun taking on the characteristics of factory machines, obsessively twisting buttons no matter where they are.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. The Berkeley Center for New Media (BCNM) invites our undergraduate students to submit presentation proposals for the 2026 BCNM Undergraduate Research Symposium. The symposium offers students an opportunity to share original research, creative projects, and works in progress with an audience of fellow students, graduate researchers, faculty, and members of the broader BCNM community. In addition to student presentations, the event will include a networking lunch and a panel on graduate school and career pathways. Selected presenters will gain experience communicating their work to an interdisciplinary audience, receive guidance as they prepare their presentations, and connect with people working at the intersections of new media, technology, design, the arts, and the humanities. All students, staff, and faculty are welcome and encouraged to attend the symposium as observers. What kinds of projects are eligible? We welcome research and creative work related to BCNM's core areas of inquiry, including media transition and emergence, critical thinking and making, and technological equity and justice. Possible topics and formats include, but are not limited to: - Social media, online communities, and digital culture - Games, interactive media, virtual reality, and immersive storytelling - Digital art, design, performance, and creative technologies - Critical approaches to data, mapping, archives, or visualization - Technology, identity, accessibility, equity, or social justice - The social and cultural effects of emerging technologies - Making, prototyping, or practice-based research - Artificial intelligence, algorithms, and digital platforms Projects may come from coursework, independent research, honors theses, internships, creative practice, or collaborative work. Both completed projects and substantial works in progress are welcome. Students enrolled in the BCNM Certificate Program, or intending to enroll in the program, will be given a strong preference.Presentation format Presentations should be approximately 10–15 minutes long and will be followed by a brief audience Q&A. Presentations may include slides, demonstrations, videos, and/or performances. Selected presenters will be required to attend a virtual pre-symposium preparation meeting on Zoom the week prior to the symposium. events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Entropy and large deviations for random unitary representations
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (daj@math.ku.dk) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Tim Austin, University of WarwickThis talk will be an introduction to "almost periodic entropy". This quantity is defined for positive definite functions on a countable group, or more generally for positive functionals on a separable C*-algebra. It is an analog of Lewis Bowen's "sofic entropy" from ergodic theory. This analogy extends to many of its properties but some important differences also emerge. I will not assume any prior knowledge about sofic entropy. After setting up the basic definition, I will focus on the special case of finitely generated free groups, about which the most is known. For free groups, results include a large deviations principle in a fairly strong topology for uniformly random representations. This, in turn, offers a new proof of the Collins-Male theorem on strong convergence of independent tuples of random unitary matrices, and a large deviations principle for operator norms to accompany that theorem.

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: "The Distribution of Federally-Insured Mortgages: 1935-1975, Evidence from Local Land Records"
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: featuring Omer Ali, Assistant Professor of Economics, University of PittsburghAbstract: This project develops a novel dataset of federally-insured mortgages from 1935 to 1975 by digitizing local land records from county recorders of deeds across a geographically diverse set of U.S. counties. Despite the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and Veterans Administration (VA) programs accounting for up to 50% of all mortgages for some years during this period, systematic borrower-level data has been unavailable due to a lack of federal records and decentralized county recording systems. Using a new pipeline that deploys large language models to digitize scanned mortgages, we identify and extract information from FHA-insured and VA-guaranteed mortgages, geolocate properties, and link borrowers to full-count Census data from 1940 and 1950. This produces the first comprehensive address- and borrower-level dataset beyond 1940. We investigate the share of Black borrowers among FHA and VA mortgage recipients, characterize the spatial distribution of mortgages across neighborhoods that vary in racial composition and HOLC ratings, and examine the demographic and socioeconomic characteristics of borrowers. The analysis enhances our understanding of how federal housing policy shaped metropolitan development and racial inequality during the New Deal and Civil Rights eras. (Joint with Jacob Faber, Andreas Ferrara, Jonathan Rose, Thomas Storrs, Katherine Thomas, Gabrielle Toborg, Randall Walsh, and Wenfei Xu)

events.title: Towards breaking the curses of dimensionality in dynamic programming (Nir Halman, Bar-Ilan University)
events.description: Title: Towards breaking the curses of dimensionality in dynamic programmingAbstract:The term "curse of dimensionality", coined by Richard Bellman in 1957, refers to various phenomena that arise when analyzing dynamic programs in high dimensional spaces that do not occur in low dimensional settings. This term was later on adopted in other domains, such as machine learning and data mining, to describe somewhat similar effects. While these phenomena do make problems harder, they sometimes leave the door open for approximation schemes. In this talk I'll survey a few classes of multidimensional Dynamic Programs that do admit approximation schemes, and mention a few promising future directions to characterize more such classes.Bio: Nir Halman is an associate professor at the faculty of Engineering, Bar-Ilan University. He received his Ph.D. degree in Mathematics from Tel Aviv University. His research interests focus on mathematical optimization in general, and in particular – on designing efficient (approximation) algorithms for subclasses of mathematical programming problems.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Verifying Secure Execution for Systems with Untrusted Components
events.description: The question of trust lies at the center of modern systems: they rely on complex components that may be compromised by an adversary. Even when one component cannot be trusted, trust in the system's behavior naturally falls apart. Techniques that enable verification of expected behavior address this challenge. To this end, we introduce new techniques for efficiently verifying secure execution across a variety of systems, from cryptographic systems to AI agents. First, we present Whisper, a system for large-scale private telemetry in the two-server setting that achieves orders of magnitude reduction in server-to-server communication when verifying that measurements are individually well-formed. After that, we look at the problem of verifiable private information retrieval, where a client privately fetches information from a remote server while verifying that the server does not cheat. We present a new protocol that reduces the client's storage by orders of magnitude for standard database sizes and a deployment mode to practically bring this technology to millions of devices. Towards the end, we transition to the world of AI agents. We present Pincer, a system that augments agents with a digital twin that verifies their actions against automatically learned user preferences.

events.title: Construction Inspection of Traffic Signals
events.description: Description Traffic signal construction is a critical component of roadway infrastructure that demands precision, adherence to standards, and proactive oversight. For inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers, success depends not only on understanding how systems are built but also on recognizing when installation deviates from plans, specifications, or best practices. Minor issues such as improper wiring, inadequate grounding, or ineffective traffic control can introduce safety risks, trigger costly rework, and increase agency liability. This intensive online course is designed to prepare participants for what they will encounter in the field when overseeing traffic signal construction. While the course does not focus on signal design, it provides essential exposure to design elements from an inspector's and owner's perspective. It is intended to help participants understand how design intent is translated into constructed systems and how to verify that the work is completed correctly, safely, and in compliance with Caltrans Standard Plans and Specifications. Participants can expect practical, field-oriented instructions on inspecting and evaluating key signal system components, including conductors and cables, signal heads, controller cabinets, grounding systems, and pedestrian and vehicle detection technologies. The course also emphasizes plan interpretation at a level appropriate for oversight roles. Participants will learn what to look for in the plans, how to identify inconsistencies, and how to apply sufficient technical understanding to assess compliance without performing design work. In addition, the course addresses coordination with contractors, construction documentation, and communication practices that support CIP delivery and protect agencies throughout project implementation. Through real-world case studies, participants will gain insight into common construction challenges, effective inspection strategies, and documentation approaches that stand up to scrutiny. Led by experienced industry professionals, this course equips inspectors, construction managers, and traffic engineers with the practical knowledge and judgment needed to confidently oversee traffic signal construction by bridging the gap between design intent and successful field execution. Topics IncludeSignal Plan Interpretation & Pre-Construction Activities Reading and understanding traffic signal plans Site assessments and preparatory inspections Electrical and Structural Installation Electrical service installation procedures Standards for pedestals, posts, and mounting hardware Bonding and grounding requirements Conduit and Cabling Systems Conduit installation and layout Cable splicing and termination Pull box installation and accessibility Traffic Signal Components Installation of signal heads, brackets, and supporting appurtenances Vehicle and pedestrian detector systems Pedestrian Safety & Americans with Disability Act (ADA) Signal controller cabinet assembly and configuration Construction Close-Out & Asset Management Maintenance considerations during and after construction Salvage and reuse of components Integration of new technology and smart signal components What You Will Learn By attending this class, participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the full lifecycle of traffic signal construction-from interpreting signal plans and preparing for construction, to installing electrical systems, conduit, and signal components. Attendees will learn industry best practices for ensuring proper bonding, grounding, and splicing, as well as techniques for setting up signal heads, controllers, and detection systems. The course also covers maintenance strategies, salvage procedures, and the integration of modern signal technologies. Through this training, attendees will be equipped with the practical knowledge and field-based insights necessary to effectively inspect, manage, and support the delivery of safe and compliant traffic signal projects. Who Should Attend Ideal for traffic signal technicians, engineering inspectors, electrical contractors, junior engineers, and traffic signal engineers involved in the design, oversight, or inspection of signal infrastructure projects.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jeffrey Seeman, Visiting Research Scientist, University of RichmondWas Plagiarism Involved in the Woodward-Hoffmann Rules? In 1981, Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry "for their theories, developed independently, concerning the course of chemical reactions". Had R. B. Woodward (1917 – 1979) lived two years longer, he would surely have received his second Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his contributions to the Woodward-Hoffmann rules. In the March 29, 2004, issue of Chemical & Engineering News, E. J. Corey wrote in his Priestley Medal Address, "On May 4, 1964, I suggested to my colleague R. B. Woodward a simple explanation involving the symmetry of the perturbed (HOMO) molecular orbitals for the stereoselective cyclobutene/1,3-butadiene and 1,3,5-hexatriene/cyclohexadiene conversions that provided the basis for the further development of these ideas into what became known as the Woodward-Hoffmann rules." Letters between Corey and Hoffmann in 1981 and 1984 and other relevant information will be shown and discussed. This seminar will focus on responsible conduct of science and the practice of science in today's complex and fast moving scientific, academic, and political environments.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. events.title: Canadian Studies Student Research Showcase
events.description: Learn about the research Canadian Studies funds through our Edward E. Hildebrand Graduate Research Fellowships (https://canada.berkeley.edu/grants-and-awards/edward-e-hildebrand-graduate-research-fellowship), as recipients present overviews of their projects.Refusing Bifurcation: Mobility, Kinship and Chinese-Indigenous Families in the Pacific Northwest Borderlands Jessica Jiang, PhD candidate, Department of Ethnic Studies In the late-nineteenth-century Pacific Northwest, colonial and transpacific migration routes overlapped and often conflicted with longstanding Indigenous geographies. This talk traces several mixed Chinese-Indigenous families on the Columbia/Interior Plateau across generations, showing how these larger forces shaped their lives and movements. These families found themselves in the crosshairs of both US and Canadian policies that sought to control the movement of Chinese and Indigenous people; however, they also found creative ways to navigate and circumvent these restrictions. Drawing on both Chinese and Indigenous knowledge, practices, and relationships, mixed-descent individuals used their dual heritage to negotiate different kinship traditions, maintain their families, and protect their connections to their homelands.The Gang Exception: Eroding Propensity Rules in Canadian Criminal LawReakash Walters, PhD candidate, UC Berkeley Law The Gang Exception demonstrates how evidence law is applied differently for race and class marginalized accused than for other accused persons. The methodology of the article pairs a systematic content analysis of reported Canadian criminal cases with a content analysis of trial transcripts involving accused with serious charges. Admissibility decisions involving gang-related charges are compared with a separate group of non-gang cases that turn on the admissibility of bad character or propensity evidence arising from a similar set of serious charges. This design helps isolate what might be particular to how courts reason about the admissibility of gang-affiliation evidence. The article argues that the reasoning through which gang affiliation evidence is admitted departs from the principled application of the propensity framework set out in R v Handy: the probative value and prejudicial effect inquiry the rule demands is often thinned or left unstated. Further, courts engage in a unique form of reasoning not present in the comparator cases to justify admission of gang-affiliation evidence. This research further illustrates how the organizational mechanisms that shape criminal legal institutions affect systemic inequality.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Robust Statistics for Monetary Non-Neutrality in Menu Cost Economies"
events.description: Abstract: The first two entries of the IRF of firm-level prices to firm-level marginal cost shocks are numerically sufficient to recover the generalized Phillips curve Jacobian in a wide class of pricing models. This result is exact in Calvo and in the Gertler-Leahy menu cost model, is numerically accurate for a broad set of CalvoPlus parameterizations, including those in Golosov and Lucas (2007) and Nakamura and Steinsson (2010), and it works in models with strategic complementarities. Our approach recovers the rigidity parameter of the synthetic Calvo model that approximates the Jacobian of the unknown true menu-cost data generating process, operationalizing the numerical equivalence results in Auclert et al. (2024). This virtual Calvo hazard may be arbitrarily different from the frequency of price changes computed in a dataset of firm-level prices.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics JMP Practice: Lucio Wasserman "Shrinkflation: What Happens When Package Sizes Change?"
events.description: Abstract: Package size is a central characteristic in consumer goods, and changes in size have implications for consumer demand, welfare, policy, and firm behavior. This paper first develops a method to identify size changes at scale. We apply it to retail scanner data and show that size reductions are considerably more common than increases. Next, we estimate the dynamic demand response to size changes using an event study approach. The demand response to size increases is immediate and stable over time. In contrast, after size decreases, demand has a sluggish response: the size elasticity is smaller in the short term than in the medium term. An incentivized shopping experiment shows that individuals deviate from optimal behavior by responding less to size than to price, and provides evidence of attention as a mechanism. With the experiment, we test policy interventions, showing that displaying unit prices and making sizes more prominent can reduce welfare losses. On the other hand, size change labels generate a bias in the opposite direction, causing individuals to over-respond to sizes and thus generating only moderate reductions in welfare losses. We explain the empirical results with a dynamic demand model that allows for inattention, paired with a supply model in which firms strategically advertise size increases but not reductions, and derive sufficient statistics for the consumer-surplus effects of inattention and related policies. In the short term, the consumer surplus losses from inattention after a median size reduction are equivalent to the consumer share of deadweight loss from a tax that increases the price by 6%. Paper Link:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view)

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Robert Baker, Timashev Professorship in Chemical Physics, Ohio State UniversityElucidating Charge, Spin, and Solvation Dynamics at Electrochemical InterfacesNearly all energy conversion and information processing technologies rely on charge and spin transport in systems that are far from equilibrium. The goal to understand and control these processes motivates the need to develop methods to probe the underlying electron dynamics in functional materials on the relevant scales of time and space. To meet this challenge, we utilize high harmonic generation to produce extreme ultraviolet (XUV) light with femtosecond to attosecond pulse durations. Like X-ray absorption, XUV spectroscopy is element specific, providing chemical details of individual elements in complex materials. To extend this technique to study electron dynamics at surfaces, we have pioneered XUV reflection as a surface sensitive analog of XUV absorption. This method now enables direct observation of interfacial charge and spin transport with surface sensitivity, ultrafast time resolution, and unprecedented chemical specificity. This talk will present recent measurements using linearly and circularly polarized XUV light, which show how spin polarized electron transport increases water splitting efficiency in yttrium iron garnet (Y3Fe5O12) by more than an order of magnitude compared to widely studied hematite (α-Fe2O3) through the formation of spin-locked magnon-polarons and how angular momentum exchange between electrons and chiral phonons generates ultrafast spin polarization in chiral semiconductors. Finally, this talk will describe nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy of interfacial electric fields, which mediate charge transfer kinetics during electrochemical catalysis, and show how together these spectroscopic methods provide a detailed understanding of the molecular features of interfaces that govern non-equilibrium reaction dynamics.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Skewed Business Cycles"
events.description: Abstract: Using Census and Compustat firm panel data, we show that the skewness of four measures — the growth rate of sales, employment, productivity, and firm value — is robustly procyclical. All four display a fat left tail of large negative outcomes during recessions and a compressed right tail. This holds across US industries and over 60 countries. Using a firm dynamics model with adjustment costs, risk aversion, and financial frictions solved in general equilibrium, we analyze the impact of first-, second-, and third-moment shocks. A second- moment shock generates a sharp downturn followed by a rapid recovery, whereas concentrating the same total variance in the left tail—a negative third-moment shock—produces a persistent recession matching the depth and slow recovery observed in US data. Modeling recessions as a combination of negative first- moment, positive second-moment, and negative third-moment shocks is critical to match both the cross-sectional moments of firm growth and the aggregate response to recessions.

events.title: Knowing better, doing better? Lessons for police reform from a developmental science law enforcement training program
events.organizer: Institute for the Study of Societal Issues
events.description: Youth commonly encounter police in their daily lives, and one of every four arrests in the United States is of a person under the age of 25. Compared to adults, interactions between youth and police more often lead to use of force and physical and emotional harm—harms that disproportionately burden the economically poor and Black youth who come into contact with police at relatively high rates. Debates over the proper role of police in managing young people have existed for over a century, yet there is little consensus as to what the ideal relationship between youth and law enforcement should be, systematic efforts to alter these relationships have had limited or even perverse results, and contemporary phenomena (e.g., social media, teen "takeovers," and changing parenting approaches) bring new challenges to youth-police relations and reform efforts. This talk brings together developmental science, historical sociology, anti-carceral perspectives, and primary research to make sense of "what works" (and doesn't work) in implementing police reform for youth. To do so, Jacobs and co-investigator Murray will draw on diverse data sources, including interviews (n = 26) and surveys with police (n = 111), and non-participant observation of police training (154 hours) in a California county, sharing preliminary findings from an ongoing, mixed methods, multi-site and multi-year impact and implementation study of a law enforcement training program that seeks to improve police-youth interactions. Implications for scholarship and intervention will be discussed.Leah Jacobs, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the School of Social Work at the University of Pittsburgh, where she leads the Anti-carceral Social Work Research Lab and the Public Social Work Research Collaborative. Her scholarship is at the intersection of social welfare, criminal legal, and community mental health policy and intervention. In these areas, she studies social problems and responses to them, with particular attention to the disproportionate involvement of Black and economically poor Americans, and people diagnosed with serious mental illnesses, in carceral and coercive systems. Her current work focuses on the relationship between social work and policing, and on life-affirming alternatives to carceral and coercive interventions, especially those that prevent system involvement and build capacity among members of minoritized groups. She holds a BS in Psychology from Northeastern University, an MA in Urban and Environmental Policy and Planning/Child Development from Tufts University, and an MSW/PhD in Social Welfare from UC Berkeley, where she was a Graduate Fellow at the Institute for the Study of Societal Issues.

events.title: Frank Bösch | The "New Jews": (Post-)Soviet Migration and the Reinvention of Jewishness in Germany since 1990
events.description: Jewish communities in East and West Germany were small and aging in the late 1980s. Only about 400 Jews remained in the Jewish communities of the GDR. This changed dramatically after 1990. Over the subsequent 15 years, about 220,000 Jews and their relatives emigrated from the former Soviet Union to Germany. Frank Bösch's presentation analyzes how the country that perpetrated the Holocaust became one of the foremost destinations for Jewish migration, alongside Israel and the United States, becoming the leading destination in the early 2000s. Based on extensive archival research and interviews, the presentation shows how German officials shaped this exceptional immigration program by granting work permits and social security benefits, and how migrants with Soviet backgrounds experienced life in Germany and reshaped their identities. The talk also examines the agency of those seeking to leave the Soviet Union, exploring the strategies they used to emigrate to Germany and how they circumvented bureaucratic rules. The migration process also generated many conflicts, including with established German Jewish communities, which led to new hybrid identities. At least in the 1990s, expectations on all sides remained unfulfilled. Jewish migration thus became a story of broken expectations. Frank Bösch is Professor of Twentieth-Century European History at the University of Potsdam and Director of the Leibniz Centre for Contemporary History Potsdam (ZZF), a leading research institute in Germany. He is the author of numerous influential books, including several bestsellers. His most recent book examines Germany's relations with autocracies (Deals mit Diktaturen, 2024). Previous publications have explored topics such as the history of the Christian Democratic Party (Die Adenauer CDU, 2001), the changing influence of media (Mass Media and Historical Change, 2015), and global turning points in the late 1970s (Zeitenwende 1979, 2019). He is currently writing a book on Jewish migration from the Soviet Union to Germany between 1970 and 2005, tentatively titled The New Jews in Germany. The Gerda Henkel Lecture Tours were established in 2018 by the Pacific Office of the German Historical Institute Washington in cooperation with the Gerda Henkel Foundation. Each year, the series brings leading German historians to the West Coast to present their latest research and to engage in conversations with diverse academic and public audiences across North America.

events.title: Josette Melchor // Newtemporary: Designing in the Space Between New and Next
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Josette Melchor, founder and cultural strategist working across art, technology, cities, and responsible AI. As the founder of Gray Area and now Newtemporary — and a board member of the Burning Man Project — Josette has spent her career shaping experiences that connect emerging technologies with civic life, cultural infrastructure, and public imagination. Her work moves fluidly across spatial strategy, immersive media, curation, and systems thinking, always with an eye toward how culture and technology evolve together. ​In this talk, Josette will explore the idea behind Newtemporary, the notion that everything from culture to place to technology is always in transition. She will share how this perspective informs her work with cities, developers, and cultural organizations, from designing immersive experiences and public spaces to prototyping ethical and creative uses of AI. Drawing on projects that have ranged from large-scale festivals and artist exhibitions to global placemaking programs for Google, she will reflect on how design can respond to impermanence, support community meaning-making, and help shape the cultural infrastructure of the future. ​This event is free and open to the public. ……���……….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.description: Event description The Central American Research Group (CARG) will host a reception and organizational meeting to kick off Fall 2026. This semester, CARG will meet to discuss drafts of five scholarly works related to Central America.Group description The mission of the Central American Research Group is to advance research and scholarship on the region through a multidisciplinary approach. The group seeks to deepen understanding of Central American history, culture, migration, politics, and contemporary issues through an open, collaborative, and intellectually rigorous environment that is attentive to the experiences of the Central American diaspora while engaging with leading scholarship. Employing a multidisciplinary understanding of Central America illuminates pathways toward improving social, political, and economic conditions, while also empowering members of its diaspora, many of whom reside in the United States, particularly in California. The group also seeks to engage scholarship and intellectual traditions produced beyond the United States, thereby broadening, challenging, and enriching prevailing understandings of Central Americanness. The Central American Research Group meets twice each month to discuss unpublished works by undergraduate and graduate students, visiting scholars, independent researchers, and faculty. Through constructive feedback and interdisciplinary dialogue, the group aims to foster a vibrant intellectual community dedicated to advancing Central American studies. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Debarati Sanyal
events.description: Arts of the Border (Fordham, 2025) investigates the consequences of unfolding catastrophes across the world and the displacement they continue to produce. Through recent narratives and media representations of the refugee "crisis" at Europe's edges, it tells a new story about those on the move, the technologies unleashed on them at borders, the racialized and colonial histories that inform these technologies, and the artistry with which migrants and allies bear witness to displacement. The book reorients us toward the creativity and movement of migrants themselves — their "arts of the border" — as well as toward the political force of the arts that represent them, whether in literature, documentary film, or art installations.Debarati Sanyal (French) proposes kino-aesthetics as a framework for capture and fugitivity at borders. From kino (to set in motion) and aesthetics (relating to sensory perception), kino-aesthetics conveys the force of bodies in motion and the image in its circulation. Sanyal examines the simultaneity of capture and escape at thresholds of illegalization, from airport detention zones to Calais's "jungle" and the Euro-African border at Ceuta and Melilla. What emerges throughout these case studies is a portrayal of border violence in its racial and colonial forms as well as an archive of refusal, fugitivity, and un-bordered imagining. Sanyal is joined by Damon Young (Film & Media and French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Single Cells in Context: A Dyad View that Bridges Single-Cell and Spatial Biology
events.description: Abstract: Single-cell sequencing has revolutionized cell atlases, but it is inherently context-poor: it catalogs cell states after dissociation, while many of the most important biological programs are relational: triggered by contact, proximity, or short-range signaling between specific partners. In this talk, I will present a dyad-centered framework and enabling technologies that treat cell–cell interactions as a measurable layer between single-cell and spatial biology. The central idea is simple: a cell's induced transcriptomic change in response to a partner cell is itself a quantitative readout of the partner's function. If one cell activates, suppresses, kills, rescues, or instructs another, the responder's state encodes information about what the first cell did, often more directly than measuring the first cell's basal transcriptome alone. I will describe our Lab-on-a-Particle platform, which creates millions of standardized microscale assay environments compatible with conventional workflows and downstream sequencing. Using Nanovials, cavity-containing hydrogel microparticles with selectively functionalized interiors, we can capture secreted proteins and binding events while keeping cells viable—enabling secretion-encoded functional screening followed by recovery for single-cell RNA-seq and targeted sequence identification. Building on this, I will introduce Cell-Cell-seq, which uses nanovials to co-compartmentalize defined cell pairs and couple dyad-specific functional measurements with transcriptomic profiling of a composite induced dyad-level transcriptome. By comparing paired interactions to matched single-cell controls, we can isolate interaction-induced programs, infer directionality, and map how heterogeneous immune and tumor populations engage. Together, these approaches provide a scalable route to connect function, interaction context, and molecular identity, offering a practical bridge from dissociated single-cell genomics toward the contextual logic needed for predictive multicellular biology and therapeutic discovery.

events.title: Charting Your Path in a Changing World: Using Creativity & Innovation to Shape What's Next (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a time of ongoing change across higher education and public service, the ability to anticipate, adapt, and move forward with intention has become essential. This highly engaging 75-minute virtual session invites UC Berkeley staff to explore how their creative and innovative capacities can help them chart a meaningful, resilient path - regardless of role, function, or career stage. Participants will explore how to shift from prediction to anticipation, using future-forward thinking to expand possibilities while remaining grounded in UC's mission. The session emphasizes change agility in practice: recognizing signals that it may be time to pivot, letting go of perfection in favor of progress, and using learning, not failure, as feedback. Through real-world examples, guided reflection, and practical application, participants will identify small, intentional actions that build readiness and momentum, even amid uncertainty.Learning Outcomes: –Differentiate between prediction and anticipation and use anticipation as a practical, future-forward approach for navigating complexity and uncertainty in their work. –Recognize signals that indicate when to adapt or pivot, reframing change and learning as sources of insight that strengthen change agility rather than as disruption or failure. –Apply creative and innovative thinking to take one meaningful next action, making progress without waiting for perfect conditions while remaining aligned with UC's mission.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Demography Brown Bag Seminar with Joshua Goldstein and Niklas van der Wagt: "Population Momentum of Replacement-level Migration"
events.description: Joshua R. Goldstein is Maxine J. Elliott Professor of Demography in the Department of Demography at the University of California, Berkeley. He is currently director of the Berkeley Population Center and the Berkeley Formal Demography Workshops and Graduate Advisor in the Department. At Berkeley, he has served as chair of the Department of Demography and the Graduate Group in Sociology and Demography from 2013-2018. He was previously director of the Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research in Rostock, Germany (2006-2013) and a Professor of Sociology and Public Affairs and and Faculty Associate of the Office of Population Research at Princeton University (1996-2006). Niklas van der Wagt is a second-year PhD student in the sociology and demography program. He double-majored in physics and sociology at UCLA, and afterward worked on agent-based models of cellular populations at the Biodynamics Lab at UCSD. He is currently working on incorporating immigration into mathematical models for population momentum, as well as describing uncertainty in fertility decisions. Niklas is also interested in population ethics and the biopolitics of quantification.

events.description: This presentation will discuss the use of wearable sensor technologies to provide quantitative assessment and feedback during healthcare training and clinical simulation. Drawing from research in neonatal and anesthesia care environments, we will explore how wearable sensing can objectively characterize clinical performance in high-risk healthcare settings. events.title: IPSR Colloquium: Ariana Castro, Matthew Elliott, and Nathalia Carvalho
events.location: Room 1102 Berkeley Way West, 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley, CA 94704, USA
events.description: Matthew V. ElliottPostdoctoral ScholarDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyExperiential and Physiological Measures of Emotion Distancing in Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors.Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs) are often motivated by efforts to alleviate distressing emotions, yet the distinct roles of emotion reactivity and regulation are difficult to disentangle. We examined these processes during an emotion distancing task using multimodal measures of subjective emotional experience, autonomic physiology (pupillometry and skin conductance), and functional MRI, and tested their associations with suicidal ideation, nonsuicidal self-injury, and suicide attempts. Emotion reactivity showed limited associations with SITBs across subjective, peripheral physiological, and neural measures. In contrast, regulation-related pupillary and posterior cingulate cortex responses were associated with suicidal ideation, recurrent nonsuicidal self-injury, and lifetime suicide attempt burden, although patterns varied across clinical outcomes. Overall, findings more consistently implicated difficulties with emotion regulation than heightened reactivity and highlighted sensitive physiological measures that may point to specific neural systems for further study.Dr. Matthew Elliott is a postdoctoral scholar in Clinical Science at the University of California, Berkeley, working under the mentorship of Prof. Sheri Johnson. Prior to his postdoc, he completed his PhD in Clinical Science at UC Berkeley and his predoctoral clinical internship through the UC San Diego/VA San Diego Psychology Internship Training Program. His research investigates how challenges to emotional and circadian regulation contribute to vulnerability for mania, impulsivity, and self-injury. Dr. Elliott's work integrates careful clinical characterization, experimental methods, and peripheral and central physiological measures to better understand mechanisms of clinical risk.Ariana Andrea Castro LeonPostdoctoral Research FellowDepartment of PsychologyUniversity of California, BerkeleyEmotion and Reasoning in Mania: Effects of Internal and External Emotion on Analogical ReasoningEmotion changes how people process information, including during analogical reasoning, a process involved in learning across domains and, ultimately, meaning making. Previous research indicates that external emotional information enhances analogical reasoning when it is task-relevant and impairs it when it is task-irrelevant. Internal emotional states amplify some of these effects. The present research examined whether the effects of external and internal emotion on analogical reasoning vary as a function of hypomanic traits. Results may inform our understanding of how emotion influences thinking processes relevant to bipolar disorder.Dr. Castro is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow in the UC Berkeley CALM Program. The goal of her research is to inform models of how and why psychopathology emerges, with a focus on the role of emotional processes. Her work has developed along two interconnected lines of research. First, she examines how emotion influences analogical reasoning, a process through which people identify patterns and form beliefs about themselves, the world, and the future. Second, she studies broader emotion-cognition dynamics across different forms of psychopathology (e.g., how contentment may differentiate internalizing symptoms). She is currently examining the role of analogical reasoning in mania within the CALM Program. She is also expanding the scope of her research by studying motivation, emotion related impulsivity, and suicidality.Nathalia CarvalhoPostdoctoral ScholarDepartment of PsychologyUC Berkeley;Assistant Professor at Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, Psychology DepartmentThe Effects of Individual and Shared Awe on Romantic Relationship QualityAwe is a complex emotional response characterized by feelings of wonder, perceived vastness, and a need for cognitive accommodation. It is often accompanied by a diminished sense of self and a heightened sense of connection to something larger than oneself. Previous research suggests that awe can promote prosocial behavior, in part by reducing self-focus and increasing orientation toward others. Despite these interpersonal consequences, relatively little research has examined awe's role within close relationships. The primary goal of the present study was therefore to examine whether experiencing awe individually or with a romantic partner is associated with romantic relationship quality, and whether shared awe is associated with greater relationship quality than individual awe. We also examined whether these associations vary as a function of theoretically relevant relationship processes, particularly self-expansion and inclusion of the other in the self.Nathalia Carvalho earned her PhD in Psychology from Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, in 2024. She is currently an assistant professor at the same university and earned an unpaid leave in 2026 to work as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, Berkeley.

events.title: Argyris Kriezis: The Invisible Threat: GNSS Jamming and Spoofing in Today’s World
events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) are critical infrastructure for civilian and military navigation and timing, but their weak signal strength at the Earth’s surface makes them highly vulnerable to radio frequency interference (RFI) including jamming, which blocks signals outright, and spoofing, which feeds receivers false position and timing data. GNSS interference has been recorded for years, but since the outbreak of conflicts in Ukraine, Israel, and Iran, such events have grown in number, strength, and duration. Because GNSS signals serve both civilian and military users, disruptions intended for military targets often spill over, disrupting civilian infrastructure hundreds of kilometers from active conflict zones. This seminar presents research from a collaboration between the Stanford GPS Lab and other universities to detect, characterize, and geolocate sources of GNSS interference affecting civilian infrastructure worldwide. By examining these events, Argyris Kriezis assesses the sophistication, impact, and scope of such attacks. Because interference often originates across borders or in regions where direct mitigation is difficult, the work focuses on developing early-warning technologies that can alert authorities in time to eliminate the source or mitigate its effects on critical civilian and military systems.

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten: Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Daniela Witten Testing hypothesis via orthogonalization Abstract Classical hypothesis testing frameworks break down in contemporary settings in which null hypotheses are increasingly abstract, the same data are used to both generate and test hypotheses, and minimal assumptions about the underlying data are made. In this work, we propose a new framework for conducting valid hypothesis tests in broad contexts. We propose to add and subtract external noise generated from a symmetric shift-family to our data, X, to partition it into two pieces, X1 and X2. We provide a generic strategy for orthogonalizing X2 against X1 under the null hypothesis H0, then show that testing whether the orthogonalization was successful provides a valid test of H0 under mild assumptions. Remarkably, this framework extends naturally to the post-selection inference setting with minimal modifications: we simply select a hypothesis on X1, then perform orthogonalization under the selected null. As our approach neither requires pre-specification of the selection mechanism, nor is restricted to a small class of data-generating distributions, it dramatically expands the settings for which valid post-selection inference can be conducted. We showcase the flexibility of our proposal in a number of case studies. This is joint work with Ameer Dharamshi (McGill University) and Runjia Zou (University of Washington). Bio Daniela Witten is a professor of Statistics and Biostatistics at University of Washington, and the Dorothy Gilford Endowed Chair in Mathematical Statistics. She develops statistical machine learning methods for high-dimensional data, with a focus on unsupervised learning. She has received a number of awards for her research in statistical machine learning: most notably the Spiegelman Award from the American Public Health Association for a (bio)statistician under age 40, and the Presidents' Award from the Committee of Presidents of Statistical Societies for a statistician under age 41. Daniela is a co-author of the textbook "Introduction to Statistical Learning", and has served as Joint Editor of Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB (https://climb.berkeley.edu/)), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Heather Christofk: Metabolic Regulation of Cell State
events.description: Our research focuses on the relationship between metabolism and cell state. We began by studying how metabolism changes during different cell state transitions – during malignant transformation, stem cell differentiation, and virus infection. However, our work has suggested a more bidirectional relationship between metabolism and cell state, whereby metabolism is not only altered during cell state transitions, but metabolic changes can also drive them. Here, I will present examples of our recent and ongoing work in three different areas of study: tissue stem cell metabolism, developmental metabolism, and cancer metabolism. I will highlight efforts to translate our findings to the clinic, new tools and methodologies we are developing to better study cell type-specific metabolism in vivo, and new questions we are answering focused on the impact of metabolism on cell state transitions in varied biological contexts.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: REI Colloquium: Banished Citizens: A History of the Mexican American Women Who Endured Repatriation
events.description: From 1921 to 1944, approximately one million ethnic Mexicans living in the United States were removed across the border to Mexico. What officials called "repatriation" was in fact banishment: 60 percent of those expelled were US citizens, mainly working-class women and children whose husbands and fathers were Mexican immigrants. Drawing on transnational archival sources, oral histories, and private collections, Banished Citizens illuminates the lasting effects of coerced mass removal on three generations of ethnic Mexicans. Ramírez argues that banishment served interests on both sides of the border. In the United States, the government accused ethnic Mexicans of dependence on social services to justify removal, thereby scapegoating them for post-World War I and Depression-era economic woes. In Mexico, meanwhile, officials welcomed returnees for their potential to bolster the labor force. In the process, all Mexicans in the United States—citizens and undocumented immigrants alike—were cast as financially burdensome and culturally foreign. Shedding particular light on the experiences of banished women expelled under claims of their likelihood to become a public charge and links to the outdated coverture doctrine, Ramírez demonstrates that US-citizen women and children were targeted as a strategy to banish entire mixed-status families. Nonetheless, banished women courageously and resiliently fought for decades to reclaim their US citizenship and return to their native country. Nevertheless, banishment often interrupted their ability to pass on US citizenship to their children, robbed their families of generational wealth, and drastically slowed upward mobility. Today, their descendants continue to confront and resist the impact of these injustices-and are breaking the silence to ensure that this history is not forgotten. This is an accessible event. If you have accessibility needs and need reasonable accommodations to participate they will be provided. For more information, and to make a request, please contact Ezra Bristow at ezrabristow@berkeley.edu

events.title: A pelagic paradox: the rise and fall of large animals with shells in the pelagic realm
events.description: In contrast to the benthos, where mineralized exoskeletons have proliferated and become increasing well protected over time, the pelagic realm shows first an increase, then a post-Cretaceous decline in large animals with shells. The pelagic realm therefore diverged from the benthos after the Cretaceous, and also shows a divergence within the realm between large and small organisms with respect to mineralization. This example illustrates a widespread phenomenon of phenotypic obsolescence through time.

events.title: The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West
events.description: The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West Thursday, September 17, 2026 12:30 ��� 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/k1UvS6pJUuwKDPXR7) The Institute of International Studies (http://iis.berkeley.edu/) & the Goldman School of Public Policy (http://gspp.berkeley.edu/) are pleased to welcome Prof. Amitav Acharya (https://www.american.edu/sis/faculty/aacharya.cfm) for a public talk at IIS. Since the dawn of the twenty-first century, the West has been in crisis. Social unrest, political polarization, and the rise of other great powers—especially China—threaten to unravel today's Western-led world order. Many fear this would lead to global chaos. But the West has never had a monopoly on order. Surveying five thousand years of global history, political scientist Amitav Acharya reveals that world order—the political architecture enabling cooperation and peace among nations—existed long before the rise of the West. Moving from ancient Sumer, India, Greece, and Mesoamerica, through medieval caliphates and Eurasian empires into the present, Acharya shows that humanitarian values, economic interdependence, and rules of inter-state conduct emerged across the globe over millennia. History suggests order will endure even as the West retreats. In fact, the end of Western dominance offers us the opportunity to build a better world, where non-Western nations find more voice, power, and prosperity. Instead of fearing the future, the West should learn from history and cooperate with the Rest to forge a more equitable order.

How glia accomplish this molecularly is just starting to be decoded. We helped establish C. elegans as a powerful model to study glia in vivo at scale, from single-cell to whole-brain resolution, genes to behavior. I will summarize our prior work in developing the complete molecular atlas of C. elegans glia (first for a metazoan), finding novel regulators of glia-neuron aging, and discovering glial pruning in C. elegans. I will then focus on recent molecular insights into glial roles in Parkinson's disease, and our translational validation of these in human and murine cell-culture models and by human epidemiology studies.

events.description: Join us for a screening of GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/), a film that marks a significant moment in Sikh history. This film captures breathtaking cinematography, soul-stirring soundscapes, while exploring how these women serve as vital carriers of wisdom, faith and strength - bringing 556 years of legacy into a sharp, contemporary and lived focus. The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker Navpreet Kaur. The event will be moderated by Puninder Singh (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/people/puninder-singh), the Sabharwal Lecturer in Sikh Studies at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, September 17, 2026 TIME: 5-7 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall REGISTRATION: The event is FREE but a reservation is required. Please reserve your seat HERE (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/gaavani-film-california-premiere-rsvp-berkeley-tickets-1994097467204?aff=oddtdtcreator) —————-SYNOPSIS:GAAVANI: Her Journey Home (https://www.gaavani.com/) follows a diverse group of 31 women—teachers, students, mothers, and community members—as they journey across northern India to perform Kirtan in the 31 primary raags of the Guru Granth Sahib. From the busy streets of Delhi to historic shrines in Amritsar and beyond, the film captures both the challenges and triumphs of this groundbreaking effort. The film explores the relationship between practice, music, gender, and lived spiritual experience. Featuring insights from scholars and speakers such as Dr. Gurnam Singh and Jessi Kaur, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) reflects on the "female orientation" of the soul in Sikh philosophy and highlights the deep spiritual significance of sung devotion. The film also honors the role of male mentors and allies who supported this movement, presenting a vision of a community in which women and men are empowered to participate fully in the Guru's Shabad. As a legacy project, GAAVANI (https://www.gaavani.com/) seeks to inspire Sikh children and adults to discover their own musical connection to Gurbani Kirtan and to help ensure that this sacred art form continues to thrive for future generations. events.title: A Roundtable on the History of the Far-Right in the US
events.description: Over the past decade, the far right has moved from the margins of American politics to its center. In turn, the topic now transcends the margins of historical scholarship to become a thriving field of inquiry. This roundtable brings together contributors to the Journal of Right-Wing Studies' two-part special issue, "The Far Right in US History (https://jrws.berkeley.edu/issues)," to discuss recent discoveries in the field. Drawing on work that spans conservative Catholic political thought, maternal activism on the right, the transnational circulation of white supremacist violence, Klan electoral politics, American monarchism, and the deep roots of Christian nationalism, panelists will consider what is gained by treating the far right as a subject of history rather than a contemporary aberration, and what remains stubbornly hard to study. How do historians define the "far right?" When does the radical become ordinary? And what do the archives allow us to see about movements with few formal records? Please join Professors Olivier Burtin (Université de Picardie Jules Verne) and Kathryn Olmsted (UC Davis), our distinguished guest editors, as they moderate a discussion on topics in the special issue. Authors and Discussants: -Mary Byrne (Rutgers) - "Moms for Liberty and the Legacy of White Maternalist Activism: Gendered Power and Cultural Organizing in Far-Right Movements" -Faith Lazar (Yale) - "If a Bomb Goes Off in the Woods: Preemptive Counterterrorism and the FBI Sting that Triggered Ruby Ridge" -Kyle Burke (University of South Florida) - "'A Planet-Wide Race War': The Global Circulation of White Supremacist Violence in the Late Twentieth Century" -Chelsea Ebin (Drew) - "Mapping the Influence of Conservative Catholic Political Thought on the American Right" Part 1 of the special issue is available and open access; Look for Part 2, out soon!
