events.title: Irregular Labor Supply and Coordination in the Workplace: Experimental Evidence from India | Shreya Chandra
events.description: Job Market PresentationAbstract This paper studies how irregular labor supply affects the organization of production in the context of a large apparel manufacturing cluster in India. Production is organized as batch processing lines, where tasks are performed sequentially to produce the finished product. In the status quo, workers choose their own work timings, resulting in significant dispersion in arrival times at the firm. I conduct an experiment with 96 small factories comprising 600 workers, where all workers in treatment firms are incentivized to arrive at work by the owner's preferred start time for a period of 4-weeks. Workers are paid a daily bonus equivalent to 20% of average earnings if they arrive on or before the start time. Incentives increase timely arrival in treatment firms by 43% relative to control firms. These changes are driven by workers who were consistently late to arrive at the firm at baseline. As a result, there is meaningful improvement in coordination of worker arrival times – dispersion in arrival times decreases by 17%. Individual worker output increase for all workers in treatment firms, not only those who changed their arrival times as a result of the incentive. I show that these positive spillovers are generated through gains along the production line from improved coordination. Weekly firm output increases by 29% and delays in order-completion fall by 13 percentage points.

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Cesar Favila (UCLA)
events.description: The Franciscan Missionary Voice in Late-Colonial New SpainCesar Favila (UCLA) Throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the Franciscan Order in New Spain published small books containing missionary songs for convincing nominal Catholics to confess their sins and amend their lives. While musicologists and historians have focused on the effectiveness of missionary music in the conversion of Indigenous people with no prior knowledge of Christianity, the musical implications of the Franciscan missions of spiritual renewal to the "faithful" in the centuries that followed the conquest of New Spain remain understudied. This talk explores the contents of these songbooks and the broader missionary context, revealing a Franciscan awareness of the effectiveness of song, aurality, orality, and voice to understand divine presence and to convey the Church's post-Tridentine sacramental and reconciliatory messages that aimed at maintaining a faithful citizenry in Spanish territories. This talk also demonstrates how this missionary process provided for the Franciscans to imitate Christ through voice and reveals the voice as a medium for sacramental expression. A reception will follow.

events.title: GIANTS RISING Film Screening in the Redwood Grove
events.description: A very special outdoor film screening amongst the redwoods! Experience the award-winning documentary film GIANTS RISING (https://www.giantsrising.com/) under towering redwood trees, with featured redwood researcher Dr. Todd Dawson.Movie-goers can enjoy special pre-movie after-hours in the UC Botanical Garden (5:00-6:30pm), exploring our collections of plants from around the world, including all three of the world's redwoods–California's giant sequoias, coast redwoods, and the dawn redwoods of Asia. Bring a picnic dinner to enjoy before the movie!Then head to our historic Redwood Grove outdoor amphitheater for an inspiring talk about these iconic trees with UC Berkeley professor of Integrative Biology Dr. Todd Dawson. Redwood Grove Gate opens just before 6:30pm. Film projection begins at sundown, approx. 7:00pm.Don't miss this perfect film experience celebrating redwoods on screen and in person! ABOUT THE MOVIEGIANTS RISING (https://www.giantsrising.com/)The secrets and superpowers of the redwoods Lisa Landers | USA, 2024 | 82 minutes Language: English (minimal Yurok)GIANTS RISING takes you on an unparalleled adventure through the towering majesty of California's redwood forests, crafting a narrative that's rich and as deep as the woods it explores. The film stands out in the documentary genre, breaking the mold with its heartfelt homage to these ancient sentinels […] The blend of scientific exploration and emotional, artistic depth paints a vivid picture of the redwoods, positioning them as natural marvels and central figures in our environmental dialogue." A journey into the heart of America's most iconic forests, GIANTS RISING explores the secrets, superpowers and saga of the redwoods— the tallest and some of the oldest living beings on Earth. It's an epic tale that reveals the wonders of these majestic trees and our dramatic, ever-evolving relationship with them. Living links to the past, redwoods also hold powers that may play a role in our future, including their ability to withstand fire and capture carbon, to offer clues about resilience, and even to enhance our own well-being. Through the voices of biologists, artists, Native communities and others, we discover the redwoods' scientific marvels and our deep cultural ties to them. It's a story that offers insights about the value of our interconnections, and the promise of solutions that will help us ALL rise up to face the challenges that lay ahead. "GIANTS RISINGis a powerful educational tool—stunningly filmed, deeply rooted in science, and highly engaging. I've witnessed firsthand how this expertly woven tapestry of stories captivates both students and lifelong learners, while sparking critical conversations about our relationship to redwoods, to all forests, and to the natural world." - Dr. Todd Dawson, Professor of Environmental Science at the University of California, Berkeley

events.title: Reading the City: Language and Poetry in Dutch Public Spaces
events.description: In this lecture, we explore the linguistic landscape of the Netherlands by walking through its streets, alleys, and squares and examining the languages that surround us. Which languages do we encounter, where do we find them, in what forms do they appear, and what meanings do they convey? We will see how written language in public spaces can inform us, warn us, instruct us, and even seduce us. A special part of this linguistic landscape is poetry in public places. We will look at several poems in public spaces and discover how they can transform a city from a neutral space into a familiar friend.2026 Snapper Lecture on Dutch Studies (https://dutch.berkeley.edu/prof-johan-snapper-lecture)

events.title: Film Screening: Contempt
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director.

events.title: Film Screening: The Hole
events.description: In Taipei there are only seven days in the year 2000, the rain just keeps pouring, a mysterious plague makes people act like roaches, quarantine zones are everywhere, and even the most alienated urbanite dreams dance numbers from 1950s Hong Kong films. Such is the end of the millennium as pictured by Tsai Ming-liang in this part-musical, part-sci-fi exploration of modern isolation, environmental catastrophe, and the failure of communication. The film's apocalyptic Blade Runneratmosphere fits surprisingly well with Tsai's auteurist vision of societal and emotional collapse, as does its pathetically realistic musical numbers, inspired by the films of popular 1950s songstress Grace Chang.

events.title: Film Screening: Bellissima
events.description: "What is acting after all?" Maddalena (Anna Magnani) rhetorically asks before the mirror in Luchino Visconti's melodrama of mother love and misplaced ambition. Magnani's extraordinary performance is its own answer. As a working-class mother desperate to get her young daughter a shot at stardom through a Cinecittà casting call, Magnani turns what might have been a simplistic caricature of a domineering stage mother into a fully rendered character, both hilarious and tragically human. Visconti's direction similarly refuses to distinguish between satire and sincerity; even while it mocks the business of moviemaking, Bellissima is an exquisite example of the filmmaker's craft.

events.title: Film Screening: The Last Waltz
events.description: Martin Scorsese grew up listening to seminal rock DJ Alan Freed, and from Mean Streets onward, his movies have been driven by the power of rock and roll. His love of music is innate and instinctual, so when The Band decided to hang it up after seventeen years on the road, they chose Scorsese to film their farewell concert at Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving 1976. The film intercuts the glorious music from one of the all-time great concert lineups with interviews with members of The Band as they talk about their lives and music. The Last Waltz is an elegiac masterpiece that captures a special moment in music history.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Fermionic optimal transport
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (daj@math.ku.dk) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Paola Zurlo, Universita degli Studi Aldo Moro, Bari, ItalyWe consider optimal transport between quantum dynamical systems on $Z _2 $- graded von Neumann algebras. In the usual, non-graded setting, Wasserstein distances between quantum systems can be defined in terms of transport plans on tensor products involving the commutant of one of the algebras. We briefly recall this construction and describe its extension to the graded setting, where the usual commutant and tensor product are replaced by the twisted commutant and the Fermi tensor product. The main point of the construction is a correspondence between fermionic and usual transport plans. More precisely, using cyclic representations associated with transport plans and the Klein isomorphisms induced by the gradings, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between fermionic transport plans and graded transport plans in the usual tensor product. This correspondence allows the Wasserstein distances in the fermionic setting to be related to the corresponding distances in the non-graded setting, and in particular yields their metric properties.

events.title: Vivien Schmidt | The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis—and its applications to Europe
events.description: Vivien Schmidt's new book, The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) provides a sweeping appraisal of how ideas and discourse are used by policymakers and everyday citizens to understand the world, communicate with one another, and mobilize for collective action. It illustrates using examples of scholarly work on capitalism and democracy, international diplomacy and human rights, environmental, economic, and social policy, conservativism, neoliberalism, socialism, and populism. In so doing, the book also provides a discursive institutionalist perspective on the (constructivist) nature of meaning, the dynamics of change and the exercise of power. At a time of major political upheaval, with populism and authoritarianism on the rise, understanding agents' ideas and discourse is even more essential today than ever. The talk will illustrate with examples from the European Union and Europe more generally, both in terms of substantive issues and methodological approaches.Vivien A. Schmidt is Jean Monnet Professor of European Integration, Professor Emerita of International Relations and Political Science, and Founding Director of the Center for the Study of Europe at Boston University. She is Visiting Fellow at the European University Institute and Honorary Professor at LUISS University. Recent books include The Power of Ideas and Discourse in Political Analysis: A Discursive Institutionalist Perspective (Oxford 2026) and the award-winning Europe's Crisis of Legitimacy: Governing by Rules and Ruling by Numbers in the Eurozone (Oxford 2020). Schmidt is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Chevalier in the French Legion of Honor, and a recipient of the Lifetime Achievement Award of the European Union Studies Association, an Honorary Doctorate from the Free University of Brussels, and a Guggenheim Foundation Fellowship. If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: The 2nd Workshop on Governance and Policy in East Asia
events.location: IEAS Conference Room (2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor)
events.description: This workshop brings together scholars in public administration, political science, and public policy to examine governance and policy in Japan and East Asia from a variety of perspectives. The presentations cover a wide range of contemporary issues, including responses to declining birthrates, health policy, criminal justice policy, and political reporting, offering insights into how governments, political institutions, and societies respond to changing social and political challenges. A central aim of the workshop is to foster dialogue across different areas of research. Rather than limiting discussion to highly specialized debates within each field, presenters will introduce the broader questions that motivate their research, share their approaches and findings with scholars working on different topics, and discuss their wider implications. English and Japanese will be used flexibly throughout the workshop, allowing participants to exchange ideas in either language and encouraging open and accessible discussion across disciplinary and linguistic boundaries. By bringing different research areas and perspectives into conversation with one another, the workshop seeks to create opportunities for participants to discover new perspectives, make connections across fields, and develop a broader understanding of governance and policy in Japan and East Asia.Speakers:Ito, Masatsugu (Tokyo Metropolitan University) Matsubara, Hideyo (Konan University) Naito, Horoko (Institute of Developing Economies) Maeda, Takahiro (University of the Ryukyus) Mitani, Soichiro (Konan University)

events.title: Polly Fordyce: "Using microfluidics for high-throughput and quantitative biophysics and biochemistry"
events.description: Macromolecular interactions drive all biological processes: proteins bind DNA and RNA to regulate transcription and translation, dense networks of protein-protein interactions convey cellular signals, and enzyme-substrate interactions allow all of the chemical transformations essential for metabolism and signaling. The strength of these interactions predicts the timing and identity of downstream responses; therefore, quantitative biophysical and biochemical measurements are critical to decipher these networks, predict how they are disrupted in disease, and manipulate them for therapeutic purposes. Here, I will discuss the development of and results from several new microfluidic platforms that make it possible to acquire quantitative biochemical and biophysical data in vitro for thousands to millions of sequence variants in parallel.

events.title: Provincializing National Literatures: Soviet Literary Universalism and Georgian Alternatives
events.description: How can a literary system celebrate cultural diversity while quietly organizing it into a hierarchy? This talk explores that contradiction through the Soviet project of "multinational literature." At its center is the six-volume History of Multinational Soviet Literature (1970��1974), which presented the literatures of the USSR as equal parts of a common whole while positioning Russian literature as the privileged route to universality. Georgia reveals both the power and the limits of this model. Through Georgii Lomidze, Akaki Bakradze, and Guram Dochanashvili, the talk traces three competing visions of literary belonging: imperial integration, national self-assertion, and a transnational republic of readers. At stake is a larger question: Who gets to define the universal—and what happens to literatures forced to reach it through an imperial center?Zaal Andronikashvili is Professor of Cultural Studies at Ilia State University in Tbilisi and a Research Fellow at the Leibniz Center for Literary and Cultural Research (ZfL) in Berlin. A literary scholar and cultural historian, he works on empire, modernity and the cultural histories of the Soviet and post-Soviet worlds, with a particular focus on Georgia and the South Caucasus. His research rethinks European and global cultural history from the perspective of regions conventionally treated as peripheral, asking how imperial and national frameworks shape literary and cultural fomations. He has published widely in German, English, and Georgian.

events.description: Mike Bollong, Associate Professor, Scripps ResearchChemical approaches to regenerative organ repair Despite perceived organismal complexity, mammals possess relatively poor regenerative potential compared to certain lesser species of Animalia (e.g., amphibians). Indeed, there are many human disease states where an insufficient regenerative response limits organ repair and is determining of disease etiology (e.g., heart failure, T1D, IPF). To overcome these limitations, we have ongoing programs aimed at identifying novel small molecules, drug targets, and repurposed drugs which control the context-specific cell growth and differentiation pathways limiting regenerative potential in a given tissue or cell type. events.title: Lara Fabian (UCLA), "The Caspian Corridor and the Making of a Connected Eurasia"
events.description: In this talk, I explore what happened when expanding empires from Iran and the Mediterranean world met the "circumcaspian system"—a constellation of patterns of mobility, exchange, and interaction that played out around the Caspian Sea over millennia. This framework helps us to see the processes that brought supra-regional powers into ever deeper contact with the diverse communities of the Caspian Sea territories. Moreover, it calls our attention to the network standards that developed as a result of imperial expansion. These norms made sociopolitical actors in the space increasingly legible to one another, facilitating increased cooperation as well as competition. To illustrate this process, I draw on multi-scalar archaeological and historical evidence concerning the eastern Caucasus beginning with the expansion of the Achaemenid Empire into this space and continuing through periods of intense Roman and Parthian interest in the space. The vectors of contact and exchange explored help us understand the shape of regional networks operating in the Caspian zone at different scales and within different social strata, and in doing so allow us to re-integrate the eastern Caucasus into broader patterns that crosscut the Iranian, Steppe, and Mediterranean worlds. But I moreover argue for the importance of the Caspian Sea as a corridor—an oft-overlooked north-south axis of connectivity—in the development of Eurasia in the second half of the first millennium BCE.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "House Prices and Quantities Around the World"
events.description: Abstract: We establish several first-order facts using house price and quantity data for middle- and high-income countries. First, housing units and rooms per person rise with per capita income and then asymptote so that additional increases in income are uncorrelated with housing quantities. Second, growth in housing units is strongly correlated with population growth at all income levels. Third, real house prices and housing expenditure shares rise in near-constant proportion with per capita income. A model with non-homothetic demand for home space, homothetic demand for housing quality, and upward-sloping supply of the unit-quality housing bundle can explain these relationships. A standard model where unit-supply is increasingly inelastic does not match the facts.

events.title: Black Critical Theory Initiative: Cecilio M. Cooper
events.location: 820 Social Sciences Building, the Social Sciences Matrix
events.description: "'Seeing Hints of a Trans Fella': Holotypic Black Feminisms, Stereoscopic Transantagonisms" Impelled by Hortense Spillers' and Sylvia Wynter's interventions, the 'black female', 'black woman', 'black femme', 'black feminine,' 'black girl', 'black mother', 'bulldagger', and so on have become valorized topics of gender analysis while also being intermittently leveraged to camouflage collusion with negrophobic antitrans retrenchment. Suffering deemed intrinsic to both structural emplotment beneath these specific racial headings and the sex-gender binary writ large has long been narrated as stemming from black experiences with coercive masculinization. This talk not only critically appraises black transmasculinity's aporetic function for cis-aspirant parsings of black female/woman from black male/man. Via psychosexual questions about aesthetics, taxonomy, and visuality, it likewise contends with the ways black transmasculinity and black trans manhood have been deployed as foils to ideal trans(gender) subjectivity.Cecilio M. Cooper's first monograph examines the occulted roles blackness and darkness play throughout the visual cultures of alchemy and demonology while the second contends with depictions of black transmasculinity across art and media. They have held postdoctoral fellowships in History of Science at the Science History Institute's Beckman Center for the History of Chemistry and in History of Art at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor. Their research has also been previously supported by Long-Term fellowships from the Folger Shakespeare Library, National Endowment for the Humanities, and American Antiquarian Society. Alongside their scholarship and criticism, Cooper's creative practice draws from performance, moving image, and sculpture. They completed a PhD with distinction in Black Studies and a Graduate Certificate in Critical Theory from Northwestern University as well as an MA in Performance Studies with a Designated Emphasis in Feminist Theory & Research from the University of California-Davis.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jin Qian, Staff Scientist, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory,Development and Application of Digital Twin & Real-Space KS-DFTThe concept of a Digital Twin originated in industry as a "digital copy of a physical asset." We aim to build a virtual laboratory infrastructure to address challenges in data acquisition, control, analysis, and model-driven interpretation, with a focus on X-ray Photon Science and its potential applications in chemical conversions. This approach enables a bidirectional feedback loop between theory and experiment. I will outline our key challenges and milestones, including: 1) developing quantum chemistry methods to improve XPS binding energy (BE) accuracy, 2) recognizing the universality of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) across systems like heterogeneous catalysis, and 3) introducing our user-friendly Digital Twin for Chemical Sciences (DTCS) v.01 software package, which we welcome collaboration and feedback on. The second part of my talk addresses a major bottleneck in developing and applying Digital Twin, which is the computational limits of conventional KS-DFT with a maximum cell size of a couple hundred atoms. We employed a combination of the real space finite-difference formulation and Chebyshev filtering (CheFSI) technique to solve the Kohn–Sham equation and implemented this approach in a multi-processor, parallel environment. We derived, implemented, and achieved a ~0.15 eV desirable accuracy of ab-initio X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy binding energy predictions within the theoretical framework of real-space Kohn–Sham Density Functional Theory (real-space KS-DFT). Our work provides key advantages for calculating accurate core–electron binding energies of exascale systems with 10,000 atoms, hence bridging the knowledge gap between molecules to nanosystems of energy priorities.

events.title: A Book is Born: The Pleasure of Texting
events.description: Lynne Huffer (Emory) and Mario Telò (Berkeley) had long admired one another's work, but always at a distance. The two met in person for the first time in fall 2025, when Huffer visited the Bay Area. A Saturday trip to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art sparked the first of what would become thousands of texting exchanges, ranging from reflections on the banalities of daily life to sustained philosophical conversations. This text chain eventually became the basis for their coauthored book, The Pleasure of Texting: Sapphic Writing and Reading at the Edge of the World, forthcoming from Duke University Press.The Pleasure of Texting explores what it means to think across different intellectual, academic, and personal experiences. The authors' collaboration takes the form of a poetic riffing in which intellectual difference becomes generative. The rhythms of digital communication — with its waiting, gaps, and moments of connection — become part of the writing itself. The result is not a fusion of two voices but a juxtapositional form in which the authors play off of one another. In conversation with their editor, Ryan Kendall (Duke UP), Huffer and Telò explore the capacity of texting as a new model of collaborative writing, in which quotidian, obsessive texting is shaped into paragraphs, chapters, and eventually a book.

events.title: Ariel Tang | Scripting Silence: Animals Political and Unpolitical in Charlotte Beradt's Dreamscape
events.description: This talk features the implicit dialogue between the German-Jewish journalist Charlotte Beradt (1907-1986) and her fellow émigré, Hannah Arendt, regarding the boundaries between humans and animals, as well as the ethical limits of anthropocentrism during political crises. Beradt's Third Reich of Dreams, a catalogue of dreams compiled between 1933 and 1939 on the basis of dreams retold by more than fifty Germans living under totalitarian rule, prompts her readers to re-evaluate the unique traits of physiological activities such as dreaming—as opposed to discursive reasoning—in safeguarding the humane promise of politics. While conventional pictures of human nature often fall prey to naturalistic or essentialist tendencies, the vital dialogue between Beradt and Arendt helps to resuscitate the unmistakable normative value of anthropological evidence, the substance of which often escapes the immediate capture of language and yet preserves the hope for political renewal lost in effable experience. Ariel Tang is a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Political Science at Stanford University. Her research focuses on Enlightenment political thought and its legacies, with special attention to questions related to knowledge institutions, education, and the interactions between culture and nature. Her current book manuscript traces an entangled history of the idea of Bildung and the rise of the modern research university. She received her bachelor's degree in Philosophy from Barnard College, Columbia University, and her PhD in Political Science from Yale University. events.title: PMB Seminar with Lila Fishman | The genomics of multi-trait adaptation to Yellowstone's geothermal soil mosaic in monkeyflowers
events.description: Environmental mosaics can generate strong divergent selection on plant traits even in the face of cross- habitat gene flow, leading to microgeographic local adaptation and (perhaps) incipient speciation. Here, we use yellow monkeyflower adaptation to the fine-scaled yet physically-extreme mosaic of soil conditions in the geyser basins of Yellowstone National Park to explore fundamental questions about the genomic and molecular mechanisms of adaptation to extreme conditions. For two traits with simple genetic bases (trichome density and minimum critical photoperiod for flowering), candidate variants in predictable molecular pathways underlie dramatic phenotypic divergence over a 100m scale gradient. In contrast, a novel multi-gene locus (out6 supergene) co-ordinates plant architecture and phenological traits underlying a unique-to-Yellowstone thermal annual strategy. The out6 locus draws on both old (but novel relative to known life-history polymorphisms) standing variation and recent introgression to confer adaptation to extreme thermal soils, and contains several strong functional candidates. Finally, although Yellowstone thermal annuals are highly specialized to the unique niche created by winter snowmelt on hot soils, thus escaping summer's deadly heat and drought, they have also evolved remarkable xylem drought/heat resistance. Together, these instances of extreme local adaptation provide a composite picture of how different plant traits and pathways evolve in response to novel environments.

events.title: Sappho and Critical Theory
events.description: Taking inspiration from the Sapphic collages of Lynne Huffer on display at the Townsend Center through May 2027, this symposium gathers together scholars working at the intersection of philosophy, literature, and creative practice. Speakers reflect on the ways in which Sappho and the Sapphic tradition have contributed in subterranean ways to counterintuitive modes of thinking — and thus to the radical work of critical theory, broadly defined. Because so little of her work survives intact, Sappho has long been particularly available for reinterpretation. Engaging with this rich field of possibility, panelists ask: can we see Sappho as a philosopher or critical theorist who preemptively contests the all-male tradition that brackets her in the domain of ancient poetry? Can we approach her oeuvre as a practice of feminist and transfeminist production that problematizes the very distinction between poetry and philosophy? How does an approach that emphasizes the discontinuous and fragmentary state of the archive change our perceptions of Sappho — such as her traditional association with Victorian and post-Victorian models of white lesbianism? How can a fresh return to Sappho help us navigate a moment in which gender is increasingly entangled with fear, anxiety, and political contestation? Following the symposium, audience members are invited to the Townsend Center for a reception to celebrate the opening of the exhibition, Thinking with Sappho: Lynne Huffer and the Art of Collage. Participants:Judith Butler, UC BerkeleyPenelope Deutscher, Northwestern UniversityLynne Huffer, Emory UniversityRanjana Khanna, Duke UniversitySalar Mamemi, UC BerkeleyVictoria Rimell, University of WarwickMario Telò, UC Berkeley

events.title: The Futures of Black Internationalism and Global South Solidarity
events.description: This project examines the international dimensions of Black radicalism and the prospects and complications of multilateral solidarity in the 21st century. 2025 and 2026 have seen the acceleration of draconian immigration policies and the reinforced legitimacy and expansion of police and prison institutions in the U.S. These developments have demonstrated how the carceral state and western imperialism operate as collaborative forces. The fates of racialized communities in the U.S. and oppressed communities throughout the Global South are therefore deeply interconnected. This project engages participant-observer methods that involve delegations of Los Angeles youth activists in immersive traveling experiences to critical locations of Black radical developments. These delegations endeavored to connect and build community with local activists, artists, and farmers and to engage the Black radical tradition as a precondition for effective and meaningful solidarity in advancing movements for sovereignty, self-determination, reparations, and economic justice. These locations include Cuba, Puerto Rico, and South Africa.Gabriel is the UC Chancellor's Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of African American and African Studies at UC Davis and he studies Pan Africanism, the Black radical tradition, Marxist theory, abolition theory, and Caribbean and African decolonization. He earned his Ph.D. in African Diaspora Studies and Critical Theory at UC Berkeley.

events.title: CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy: Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting
events.description: Please join us for a joint CLIMB + Neyman Seminar with Susan Murphy Online Reinforcement Learning for Digital Health Interventions in the Dyadic Setting Abstract We present our ongoing work on the development of an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that personalizes delivery of interventions sequentially, over time, to members of a dyad. The RL algorithm is one component in the design of the digital health intervention. Different RL components target different elements of the dyad; these elements are a target individual, a carepartner and their relationship. The RL algorithm is a multi-agent RL algorithm in which the 3 agents make decisions on the 3 elements of the dyad. We incorporate domain knowledge in the form of approximal causal directed acyclic graphs to speed up online learning in this sparse data setting. This work is motivated by our development of the ADAPTS-HCT multi-agent RL algorithm, designed to improve medication adherence by young adults who have undergone a blood and bone marrow transplant. The RL algorithm will be deployed in a clinical trial in late summer 2026. BioSusan A. Murphy is Mallinckrodt Professor of Statistics and of Computer Science and Associate Faculty at the Kempner Institute, Harvard University. Her research focuses on improving sequential decision making via the development of online, real-time reinforcement learning algorithms. Her lab is involved in multiple deployments of these algorithms in digital health. She is a member of the US National Academy of Sciences and of the US National Academy of Medicine. In 2013 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her work on experimental designs to inform sequential decision making. She is a Fellow of the College on Problems in Drug Dependence, Past-President of Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Past-President of the Bernoulli Society and a former editor of the Annals of Statistics. CLIMB Voleon Seminars are organized by the Center for the Theoretical Foundations of Learning, Inference, Information, Intelligence, Mathematics, and Microeconomics at Berkeley (CLIMB), and are generously supported by the Voleon Group. CLIMB addresses new conceptual and mathematical challenges arising at the interface between technology, science, and society.If you require an accommodation for effective communication or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Naomi Yamasaki at climb-support@eecs.berkeley.edu (mailto:naomiy@berkeley.edu) or 510-710-8488 with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Creating a political community of fate in care and caregiving
events.description: With Margaret Levi, Emerita Professor of Political Science, Stanford University Caregiving is essential to the health and well-being of society. It shapes how we raise our children and how we tend to the ill, elderly, and disabled in our families and communities. We rely on paid caregivers in health care, education, and government services to support those who need care beyond what families can provide. Caregiving is also a fundamental human experience: Almost all of us will both care for others and be cared for during our lives. But despite the importance of care work in all its forms — paid and unpaid, in our families, in health care, in education and public services — and despite the demographic changes speeding us toward a care crisis, this work has been largely invisible in the social and human sciences. The solution, argues political scientist Margaret Levi, is to understand care as a widely shared interest and lived experience that can become the basis of an expanded and inclusive community of fate in which people come to recognize a societal responsibility for those in need, even if they are strangers or unlikely to be able to reciprocate. In this talk, Levi will explore the conditions for creating such an expanded and inclusive community of fate in care and the political economic implications of such a strategy.Register Now (https://forms.gle/GJcUtGC8AxirUZiu7) About the speaker Margaret Levi is emerita professor of political science at Stanford University and a senior at the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law and the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies. She is the former Sara Miller McCune Director of the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS), where she remains a faculty fellow, and is a senior fellow at the Woods Institute. Levi's research explores how organizations and governments provoke member willingness to act beyond material interest. She is the author or coauthor of numerous articles and six books, including most recently, A Moral Political Economy (Cambridge, 2021). Levi is the winner of the 2019 Johan Skytte Prize and 2020 Falling Walls Prize for Breakthrough of the Year in Social Sciences and Humanities. She became a fellow of the National Academy of Sciences in 2015, the British Academy in 2022, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2001, the American Academy of Political and Social Science in 2017, and the American Philosophical Society in 2018. She was a John Simon Guggenheim Fellow in 2002. She served as president of the American Political Science Association from 2004 to 2005. Levi was the general editor of Cambridge Studies in Comparative Politics. She is co-general editor of the Annual Review of Political Science and on the editorial board of PNAS. She serves on the boards of the Berggruen Institute, the Center for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (CEACS), the Research Council of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR), and CORE Economics.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Identification of Novel Targets to Reverse Hepatic Fibrogenesis
events.description: Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, UC San Francisco Dr. Jennifer Y. Chen is a physician-scientist and hepatologist at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). She completed her medical training at Harvard, where she also pursued postdoctoral research in hepatic stellate cell biology and the molecular mechanisms of liver fibrogenesis. Her research program integrates basic, translational, and clinical investigation to advance precision medicine for patients with chronic liver disease. Focusing on the cellular and molecular pathways that drive hepatic fibrosis, her laboratory is developing novel antifibrotic therapies through collaborations with medicinal chemists to design and optimize small-molecule inhibitors that target key fibrogenic pathways. In parallel, her team is discovering and validating biomarkers that improve the diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring of patients with liver fibrosis. Her work aims to accelerate the translation of mechanistic discoveries into innovative, personalized treatments that improve outcomes for patients with chronic liver disease.

events.description: Please join the UC Berkeley Department of English at 5 pm in Wheeler Hall, Room 300, for "Living Literature: Roland Barthes, Citation, and the Reading of Everyday Life," a talk with Professor John Lurz (Tufts). John Lurz's lecture, drawn from his recent book The Barthes Fantastic: Literature, Criticism, and the Practice of Language (Chicago, 2025), revisits the writings of Roland Barthes to examine citation as an intellectual practice that mobilizes fragments of particular texts to galvanize our conventional or mythologized sense of the world. events.description: Join us for a film screening of Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life is Here, followed by a talk-back with artists, filmmakers, curators and faculty.Register Here (https://forms.gle/45335qFWQb5YQ62C8)Event Timeline: 5:15 PM - Reception 6 PM - Film Screening 7:15 - 8 PM Talk BackKõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life is Here (2025) documents the 2023 journey that brought together Marshallese elders and youth with an international team of artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers to consider the intertwined legacies of nuclear testing and a changing climate across the Marshall Islands. events.title: Maayan Levy: Toward the development of metabotherapy
events.description: Diet can be a powerful, low-cost lever for treating disease. We previously showed that a ketogenic diet suppresses intestinal tumorigenesis in mouse models of colorectal cancer, mediated by the metabolite beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) acting through HCAR2 to induce the differentiation factor HOPX (Dmitrieva-Posocco et al., Nature, 2022). A follow-up trial in Lynch syndrome patients confirmed that BHB supplementation reduces colonic epithelial proliferation, and a clinical trial for colorectal cancer prevention is now underway (NCT05338307). We asked whether the same metabolite could address a different problem: CAR T cell therapy fails in roughly half of patients and rarely works in solid tumors. Screening diets in mouse lymphoma models, we found that a ketogenic diet- again acting through BHB- potentiates CAR T cell function, fueling the TCA cycle and reprogramming T cells away from exhaustion toward a more cytotoxic state. BHB supplementation alone dramatically improved tumor clearance and survival in lymphoma and solid tumor models, and enhanced T cell metabolic fitness in healthy human volunteers, motivating an ongoing Phase I trial combining BHB with CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma patients. Together, this work suggests that a single, inexpensive dietary metabolite can be repurposed across cancer prevention and immunotherapy to meaningfully improve patient outcomes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Lecture | Taking God Seriously in Modern Islamic Politics: Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), Science, and Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt
events.description: Abstract: In his new book, Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt, Arthur Zárate argues that although God stands at the center of contemporary Muslim moral and political visions, the deity's presence is often neglected in scholarship. This talk explores why that neglect persists and what comes into focus when theological claims are taken seriously in the study of modern Islamic politics. Focusing on the Egyptian theologian Muhammad al-Ghazali (1917–1996), it examines his engagements with modern scientific discourses to show how science became one avenue through which divine presence was encountered and affirmed. Debates over science, it argues, were simultaneously debates about God, and competing understandings of the natural world underwrote competing visions of political and social reform. Ultimately, the talk proposes "activist theology" as a more adequate framework than "Islamism" for understanding al-Ghazali's politics.Bio: Arthur Zárate is a historian of the modern Middle East whose research explores the intersections of politics, science, and theology in modern Islam. He is the author of Mediating God: Muhammad al-Ghazali and the Politics of Divine Presence in Twentieth-Century Egypt (Oxford University Press, 2025). His work has appeared in Comparative Studies in Society and History and the Journal of the American Academy of Religion, and is forthcoming in the International Journal of Middle East Studies. He is Assistant Professor of Global Humanities at San José State University, where he teaches in the Honors Humanities Program. He is currently writing a second book on Sufism, spiritual experimentation, and Muslim and Coptic saintly mediation in modern Egypt.

events.title: Life ascending: mechanisms of environmental adaptation in extreme high-elevation Andean mice
events.description: A fundamental goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how the realized niche of a given species has been shaped by local adaptation to extreme environmental conditions, such as those that prevail at range margins. Investigation of local adaptation of montane species at their upper elevational range limits may be especially informative in this effort. Andean leaf-eared mice, Phyllotis vaccarum, live on the summits of 6700 m volcanoes in the Puna de Atacama, far surpassing the known elevational range limits of all other terrestrial vertebrates. Such elevations were previously thought to be uninhabitable by mammals due to severe hypoxia and frigid temperatures. In addition to holding the record as the highest-dwelling mammal, P. vaccarum also has the broadest elevational range, as it is distributed from sea level along the desert coast of northern Chile up to the crest of the Andean Cordillera. Here I report results of physiological and genomic analyses that provided new insights into mechanisms of physiological adaptation to extreme elevations in P. vaccarum. Our genomic analysis also revealed unanticipated dimensions of environmental adaptation related to feeding ecology.

events.description: This panel will discuss the recent rise of sovereigntist and independentist politics in Quebec and Alberta. However, they also share a sense of alienation from "Canadian" culture and national identity. What factors are causing this resurgence of sovereignist feeling in Canada? How are proponents of Canadian federalism responding to their grievances? And how are international developments, including heightened Canada-US tensions, shaping the trajectory of these movements?About the PanelistsMartha Hall Findlay is the Director and Palmer Chair in Public Policy, School of Public Policy, University of Calgary; a member of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations. A former two-term Member of Parliament, she served on the Official Opposition shadow cabinet as well as on committees concerned with trade, finance, and public works. Before politics, she worked as an international corporate lawyer and senior executive for Suncor Energy and the Canada West Foundation. She is currently overseeing the official Alberta government report on the economic impact to the province of leaving Canada.Philippe Gervais is a seasoned leader in communications and public affairs with more than 30 years of experience across the public and private sectors. He currently serves as the Vice-President, Communications and Institutional Relations, for McGill University. Before joining McGill, Mr. Gervais was a Managing Principal for Navigator Ltd, a Canadian crisis management, government relations and public opinion company. He has worked for both the Federal and Quebec provincial governments, and he has advised political campaigns at all levels of government across Canada.Kristina Michaud was elected to Canada's House of Commons at age 26, becoming one of the youngest federal representatives ever elected. events.title: Arash Afraz - How Does the Activity of Visually Responsive Neurons Generate Visual Perception?
events.description: We typically study the mechanistic underpinnings of vision by observing how "visually responsive" neurons in the brain respond to and encode visual stimuli. While highly informative, this approach is indirect and correlational and does not reveal the causal contribution of these neurons to visual perception. In this talk, I will introduce a new methodology, Perceptography, that quantitatively and graphically determines the causal role of cortical neurons in perception. I will then propose a new roadmap and theoretical framework for understanding visual perception.

events.title: Ned Wingreen: Collective dynamics in B cell affinity maturation
events.description: In the humoral immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called affinity maturation. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GC), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust "homeostatic" regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of GC lymphocytes. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to "backsliding" of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.Division(s): INFORMAL SEMINAR

events.title: Stone Center for Environmental Stewardship Lecture: Kevin Washburn (Chickasaw), "Tribal Co-Management, Landback, and Indigenous Cosmology"
events.description: Kevin K. Washburn is a Professor of Law at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law. He is part of the advisory group for the UC Berkeley Stone Center for Environmental Stewardship. Professor Washburn's research explores the way federal law and policy works, and sometimes fails, for tribal nations in the United States. In this talk, he will explore the complicated relationships between tribes, conservation advocates, and land conservation policies. He will discuss how, on the one hand, tribes sometimes resent conservation groups because their actions can infringe on tribal sovereignty. On the other hand, conservation groups are sometimes concerned that tribes won't exercise their sovereignty in ways consistent with the goals of the conservation movement. Washburn will describe the dramatic improvement in these relationships in recent years, and the reasons such trust is well-placed and should continue to grow. events.description: Speaker: Yongwook Paik (KAIST) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: Drawing on insights from the co-authored book The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future, this lecture offers an insider's perspective on Korea's evolving innovation landscape. It traces the nation's transition from a conglomerate-driven growth model to an innovation-led economy, highlighting the critical interplay between venture capital, government policy, conglomerates, and entrepreneurial culture. The talk demonstrates how Korea's global cultural powerhouses—including K-pop, K-dramas, and K-beauty—are strategic outcomes of this systematically built ecosystem. Through a comparative lens, the lecture examines the institutional features that distinguish the Korean and U.S. markets across key dimensions like financing, risk tolerance, and policy intervention. It concludes by outlining strategic implications for global founders, investors, and policymakers, followed by an interactive Q&A session. The English edition of The Korean Startup Ecosystem: Past, Present, and Future is available for download for free at the following link for those who are interested: https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ (https://bit.ly/4tNQSAJ) Speaker Bio: Professor Paik is a tenured professor at the KAIST College of Business and an affiliated professor at the KAIST College of AI. His research explores the intersection of entrepreneurship, innovation, strategy, institutions, and public policy. He serves as an editorial review board member and referee for numerous top-tier academic journals in his field, and his research has appeared in premier publications such as the Strategic Management Journal, Organization Science, Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal, and the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy. Before joining KAIST in 2018, Professor Paik served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California's Marshall School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis's Olin Business School. He holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to his academic career, he was a patent attorney at the leading South Korean law firm Kim & Chang, advising both multinational corporations and entrepreneurial ventures. A seasoned advisor in the innovation ecosystem, Professor Paik cofounded the venture capital firm TBW Investment, which was later acquired via M&A. He is a Board Member of Hanyang Eng Co., a major KOSDAQ-listed semiconductor and high-tech facility engineering firm, and currently serves as a policy advisor to South Korea's National Economic Advisory Council.

events.title: Julia Nelsen | Translation as Rediscovery: Introducing Fausta Cialente
events.description: Fausta Cialente (1898-1994) was one of Italy's most significant twentieth-century authors. Though she won critical acclaim—albeit late in her career—Cialente remained overlooked for decades until the recent rerelease of her literary works in Italian. A Very Cold Winter (Transit Books, 2026) is the first of Cialente's novels to be rediscovered in translation by Julia Nelsen. In conversation with Professor Mairi McLaughlin, Nelsen will discuss her translation of A Very Cold Winter, situate Cialente within the broader landscape of modern Italian and international literature, and explore the role translators play in recovering unsung voices.Julia Nelsen translates between English and Italian. In addition to her work on Fausta Cialente, her essays and translations have appeared in journals including Circumference, Two Lines,Firmament, and the Chicago Review. Alongside translation, she currently serves as policy analyst for the UCLA Academic Senate, and previously taught writing and literature courses and managed international partnerships between Europe and the West Coast. She holds a PhD in Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley and a Masters in European languages from the University of Milan.Mairi McLaughlin is Professor and Chair in the Department of French and an Affiliated Member of the Departments of Linguistics and Italian Studies at UC Berkeley. She specializes in French/Romance Linguistics and in Translation Studies and has published extensively on language contact, the language of the media, and journalistic and literary translation. Her books have been published by Garnier, Legenda, and Oxford University Press, and she has published articles in journals such as French Studies, The Italianist, Langages, META, Perspectives, and Target.If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: This Death is Not One
events.description: In conversation with Salar Mameni, Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at UC Berkeley The publication of The Right to Maim by Jasbir K. Puar in 2017 was critical to advancing studies on disability and to further articulating how the body figures in the nexus of capacity and debility across racializing and extractive neoliberal lines. It offered a complex and rigorous anti-capitalist account of disability that is useful to both scholarly work and political and social organizing. However, despite its paramount contribution to scholarship on Palestine, delivered by its scathing analysis of the Israeli biopolitical policy—its right to maim—in how the injured Palestinian body is produced and reproduced, its reception was difficult, and hard to stomach. It cohered a political logic in writing before it was visibly evident on the ground. In the moment and aftermath of the Great March of Return (2018-19), Puar's offerings became much harder to ignore, as the event crystallized a mass maiming campaign of Palestinian protesters inside the edges of the militarized borders of Gaza.This Death is Not One (Bilnaes 2026) is the first translation into Arabic of the chapter "Will Not Let Die": Debilitation and Inhuman Biopolitics in Palestine, alongside the postscript of The Right to Maim. Not simply a reissue of previously published work or a translation, This Death is Not One includes a new preface from Jasbir K. Puar revisiting the right to maim from within this moment of genocide in Gaza that interrogates the new vectors of living and dying under settler-colonialism, and how maiming, in fact, speaks of extermination; an introduction by Nasser Abourahme reflecting on the book's stakes in the present and its reception in the past, alongside searing analysis of genocide in excess of the law, and what this reveals and forecloses in how we understand the juridical body and militancy in the wake of Zionism; and original drawings by Xaytun Ennasr that inscribe a relation between land and body mapped through cosmological patterns tracing the relation between martyrs, who are referred to as moons, and the moon, a symbol for martyrdom in Palestine.

events.title: Architecting Human Power in the Age of AI (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) In a workplace increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, many professional development sessions focus on what tools to learn next. This session takes a different approach. It focuses on what AI cannot replace: the distinctly human ability to decide what matters, what you stand for, and how you choose to show up. This is not an AI skills workshop. It is an invitation to become more intentional about your human advantage. As AI expands what is possible, our opportunity is not to compete with technology, but to become clearer about what makes us uniquely valuable and then use AI to amplify it. By knowing what deserves your attention, what guides your decisions, and how you want to show up, you can engage AI with greater clarity and intention rather than simply using it to do more, faster. Led by Executive Coach and former Fortune 500 Marketing Leader Sarah Peterson, this interactive 90-minute session combines provocative ideas, personal reflection, and practical application. Drawing on her own journey from high-achieving executive through burnout and realignment, Sarah introduces her Leadership DNA Pyramid, a framework inspired by the strategy used to build iconic brands and adapted to help individuals navigate change, complexity, and an increasingly AI-enabled workplace. Participants will work with three dimensions of the broader Leadership DNA framework that become increasingly important as AI accelerates how we work: Priority, Value, and Presence. They will make three intentional choices: one priority to focus their energy, one value to guide their decisions, and one quality of presence to embody in how they work and lead. They will then move from insight to implementation by identifying the behaviors and actions that will bring those choices to life over the next 90 days. Together, these choices create a personal compass for working and leading with greater clarity and intention in an AI-enabled world.Learning Outcomes: –Recognize their distinctly human contribution as a source of advantage in an AI-enabled workplace. –Define one priority that deserves their focus and energy over the next 90 days. –Identify one value to intentionally guide their choices and decisions. –Choose one quality ofpresence they want to embody in how they lead, collaborate, and contribute. –Turn Priority, Value, and Presence into Practice by defining concrete behaviors and actions they can begin applying immediately.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as this virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: A Conversation with Senator Lisa Murkowski
events.location: Hertz Hall, 101 Cross-Sproul Path, Berkeley, CA 94704
events.description: Join the Goldman School of Public Policy for an in-person conversation with U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski, one of the Senate's most independent voices and a leading voice on political leadership and bipartisan governance in an era of deep political polarization. Over more than two decades in the U.S. Senate, Murkowski has helped shape some of the nation's most consequential policy debates while earning a reputation for independence, institutional stewardship, and a willingness to challenge presidents and party leaders alike. Drawing on her memoir, Far From Home: An Alaskan Senator Faces the Extreme Climate of Washington, D.C., she will reflect on the defining moments of her career, the evolution of American politics, and what it means to govern with conviction in a divided democracy. The discussion will explore Murkowski's journey from Alaska to the U.S. Senate, her historic 2010 write-in reelection campaign, and the transformation of American politics from the Tea Party era to today. As institutions face growing public scrutiny and political divisions continue to deepen, she will offer a candid perspective on the challenges confronting American democracy, the future of bipartisan governance, and the role of political leadership and public service in sustaining democratic institutions.This event is part of the Goldman School of Public Policy's Democracy Book Club series, which features authors whose work enriches our understanding of democracy by examining the institutions, policies, and civic traditions that shape democratic life. —Lisa Murkowski is a third-generation Alaskan proudly serving as the state's senior senator. Since joining the U.S. Senate in 2002, she has earned a reputation for her collaborative approach and her ability to work across the aisle to reach commonsense solutions. She and her husband live in Anchorage, Alaska, where they raised their two sons.David C. Wilson is the dean of the Goldman School of Public Policy and a Professor of Public Policy at the University of California, Berkeley. A leading scholar of political psychology and public opinion, his research explores race, democracy, and political behavior. Before joining Berkeley, he held senior academic leadership roles at the University of Delaware and worked with the Gallup Polling Organization. Wilson is also a U.S. Army veteran who served 19 years in the Army Reserves, including tours during Operations Desert Storm and Iraqi Freedom.

events.title: Karen Van Dyck | The Greek Alphabet in America
events.description: Thehistory of Greek assimilationin America can be traced in the slow erasure of Greek as a symbol of difference and indecipherability, the most recognizably unrecognizable alphabet– "It'sallGreek to me!"By the 1930s and 1940s,looking and sounding differentled to thesubstitutionnot only of different faces and races, butoftypefaces. If, during the mid-century, nations were intent on keeping things as separate as possible and popular fiction and film made sure Greeks and Greek in America were erased and monoalphabeticism won out, in the 1970s and 1980s, a more cosmopolitan moment, Greek's indecipherability became the grounds for literary experimentation and, particularly for women writers, a "politics of transliteration."Karen Van Dyck, Kimon A. Doukas Professor of Modern Greek Literature in the Classics Department at Columbia University, works on questions of translation, migration, gender and classical reception. She is the founding director of Hellenic Studies and an active member of the Institute of Comparative Literature and Society and the Istanbul and Athens Global Centers. Her translations includeThe Greek Poets: Homer to the Present (Norton, 2010), Austerity Measures: The New Greek Poetry(2016, Penguin) and Margarita Liberaki's Three Summers (NYRB, 2019)If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.description: The stationmaster in Zvare, a remote valley town in Georgia, is bracing himself for change. Soon the high-speed trains of the New Silk Road will race through the old train station built in 1890, during the period of Tsar Nicholas II. The Chinese-led construction project is blasting through the mountains to construct the world's third-longest tunnel, and this brings the opposition of the local residents, who do not want their land to be spoiled. events.title: The Smart Curb: How Cities Can Control Their Most Valuable Asset
events.description: Gene Oh, CEO of Tranzito, will present The Smart Curb: How Cities Can Control Their Most Valuable Asset at the ITS Berkeley Transportation Seminar on Sept. 25, 2026. Join us for cookie hour at 2:30 in the ITS Library, hosted by TRANSOC.Bio: Gene Oh is the founder and CEO of Tranzito, with over 20 years in new mobility. He leads the company's strategy to help cities actively manage the curb, the most contested space on the street, positioning Tranzito as the property manager of the public right-of-way. Gene's view is that as ride-hailing, shared micromobility, delivery, and autonomy drive up demand for curbspace, agencies need to manage private operators rather than compete with them, keeping public transit as the backbone of the system. Under his leadership, Tranzito grew from secure bike parking into citywide smart infrastructure, including the $500M+ LA STAP program (3,000+ smart bus shelters and 200 urban panels) and the 97-hub LADOT Integrated Mobility Hubs program, where he serves as Executive Director. Gene treats this infrastructure as a connected network of smart-city nodes, tied together by Tranzito's open CurbOS platform, and designed the public-private partnership models that let agencies partner with private operators at the LADOT and Caltrain SF mobility hubs. His next focus is smart loading zones and dynamic curb management, which combine sensing, digital signage, policy, enforcement, and field operations into a single managed program launching through the IMH network. Gene specializes in strategic design, stakeholder management, and business development, and keeps Tranzito self-funded to stay focused on public benefit.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Phillip Milner, Associate Professor, Cornell UniversityTaming the Halogens using Metal-Organic Frameworks Fluorinated molecules represent a double-edged sword: they are present in 30% of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, but are also persistent organic pollutants of growing concern due to their long environmental lifetimes and high global warming potentials. Herein, we will discuss how porous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) present a unique opportunity to capture and utilize fluorinated (and other halogenated) building blocks to design new catalysts and reagents for applications in the synthesis of complex molecules. We will first focus on catalytic strategies that leverage MOFs bearing metal-halogen bonds as recyclable catalysts for challenging reactions such as halogen exchange, C-H functionalization, and contra-thermodynamic alkene isomerization. Then, we will discuss how MOFs can be used to directly capture fluorinated gases to allow for their safe handling as solid reagents, enabling a diverse range of thermal, photochemical, and electrochemical reactions. Last, we will show how ozone-depleting and greenhouse gases can be captured from realistic mixtures and employed directly as building blocks for fluorochemical synthesis.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Establishing Chronology in Tibetan art: a Study of Taklung Paintings
events.description: This lecture addresses chronology in early Tibetan art. Dr. Casey highlights over a decade of research on a group of approximately 100 paintings from Taklung and Riwoche monasteries in Tibet. The main purpose of the study has been to establish a reliable foundation for assigning dates to Taklung paintings. The Taklung painting corpus particularly lends itself to the task of building a chronology. Almost three-quarters of the paintings bear inscriptions with chronological implications. Using visual lineages (the succession of teachers represented in the top, side, and, occasionally, the bottom registers of paintings), inscriptions, narrative scenes (in which principal structures in the Taklung Monastery compound may be linked to specific dates), and style analysis, the speaker identifies fundamental parameters that help to create firm chronological designations for these c. twelfth to mid-sixteenth century paintings. Tibetan textual historians and historians of Tibetan religion will appreciate the evidentiary underpinnings of the chronology put forth. And anyone interested in understanding the history of Tibetan Buddhist culture will appreciate the wealth of information contained in these remarkable, often very well preserved works of art.Jane Casey is an art historian specializing in Himalayan art. Educated in the History of Science (A.B.) and in Fine Arts (A.M. and Ph.D.) at Harvard University, since 1991 she has worked as an independent art historian, curating exhibitions at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and at Casa Asia, Barcelona. She is a Guest Professor at the Zhejiang University Center for Buddhist Art in Hangzhou, and a Research Fellow in Tibetan Art at the Palace Museum in Beijing. She resides in Marlborough, New Zealand.

events.title: Rethinking the Republican Interregnum in South Vietnam (1964-1967)
events.description: Speaker: Y Thien Nguyen (Assistant Professor of Asian Pacific Studies, California State University, Dominguez Hills) This talk reframes the widely disparaged interregnum period in South Vietnam (1963-1967) as a critical juncture in which civil society and non-state actors actively shaped the political realm, contributing to the rise and fall of governments and eventually to the emergence of the Second Republic of Vietnam (1967-1975). In addition to exploring the routinization of oppositional politics, it charts the development of a dominant discourse of "true democracy and freedom" which conditioned the actions and political language of state and non-state actors as well as popular apprehensions of political legitimacy.This talk is funded byThe Republic of Vietnam Endowment for Vietnamese Studies,made possible by the generous donation fromMr. and Mrs. Nguyễn Đức Cường.Speaker bio: Y Thien Nguyen specializes in the study of modern Vietnam and Vietnamese refugee experiences. His work examines the ideological, political, and institutional connectivity between the Republic of Vietnam and Vietnamese America. He received his PhD in Sociology from Northwestern University and previously served as a Teaching Fellow in South East Asian History at the University of Leeds, UK and a Research Associate for the US-Vietnam Research Center at the University of Oregon. He is currently completing his book manuscript entitled Diasporic Legacies: The Making and Remaking of Vietnamese Anticommunism. He has published multiple academic works on the Republic of Vietnam, the Vietnamese diaspora, and various sociopolitical issues related to the Vietnamese American community. Beyond his immediate academic duties, Dr. Nguyen also serves on the Board of Director for the US-Vietnam Research Center, the Boat People SOS Center for Community Advancement, and offers consulting and grant writing services to Vietnamese American non-profit organizations.

events.title: Film Screening: Taming the Garden
events.description: With astonishing cinematic style, Taming the Gardentracks the surreal uprooting of ancient trees from their Georgian locales. With each removal, tensions flare between workers and villagers. Some see financial incentives—new roads, handsome fees—while others angrily mourn the loss of what was assumed to be an immovable monolith of their town's collective history and memory. With a steady and shrewdly observant eye, Salomé Jashi documents a single man's power over Earth's natural gardens: how majestic living artifacts of a country's identity can so effortlessly become uprooted by individuals with no connection to the nature they claim as their own.

events.title: Georgian Cinema Now Symposium—Activism in Authoritarian Times: The Republic of Georgia as a Case Study
events.description: Free and open to the public, this symposium offers an invaluable introduction to the current political and cultural context in the Republic of Georgia. Guest speakers will offer a range of perspectives, from analyzing the political situation under the current Georgian Dream government to sharing experiences from the field as activists on the frontlines fighting for civil liberties, especially freedom of speech and LGBTQ+ rights. We will hear from journalists, media commentators, cultural historians, teachers, and independent filmmakers on the challenges and threats they face as a result of the Georgian government's introduction of the Foreign Agent Law—censorship, arrests, trials, and imprisonment—and parallels with broader global threats to democracy. The symposium will feature two panels, "Modern Georgia's Political History" and "Reports from the Field by Georgian Independent Filmmakers." In between, we will screen two recent documentaries on the impact of the current authoritarian government.

events.title: [UC Berkeley campus premiere] A Job in the Shade: The Emily Vasquez Story
events.location: Chevron Auditorium, International House (2299 Piedmont Avenue, Berkeley, CA)
events.description: About the Film This inspiring documentary chronicles the extraordinary life of Judge Emily Vasquez, the first Latina appointed in 2001 to the Sacramento County Superior Court in its history. Through intimate interviews with family members, friends, colleagues, and mentees, A Job in the Shade explores Judge Vasquez's remarkable journey from the agricultural fields of California to the courtroom. The film highlights a lifetime of service, leadership, and mentorship while demonstrating how education can transform lives and expand opportunities for future generations. Through her strength of character, hard work, and keen intellect, Judge Vasquez defied the odds. Judge Vasquez has made it look easy with her many accomplishments but her many achievements did not come easy (not when you one of the first and come from humble beginnings). Her parents were poor, immigrant farmworkers from Mexico. As a child, she lived in labor camps and worked in the fields when school was not in session to help supplement the family income. She spent her early years living in tents and one-bedroom shacks with everyone, including her parents sleeping in the same room as her siblings. The bathroom was an outhouse. From her childhood in California's Central Valley, working alongside her poor farmworker parents, to her groundbreaking legal career, Judge Vasquez's story is one of resilience, determination, and the transformative power of education.Presented by:UC Berkeley Division of Equity & Inclusion Latinx Thriving Initiatives The Spencer Group In partnership with:University Development and Alumni Relations (UDAR) UC Berkeley College of Letters & Science Cal Alumni Association

events.title: Film Screening: English Teacher and Bakhmaro 2050
events.description: Georgia's movement to teach English to schoolchildren is the backdrop for this beautifully observed documentary about an English teacher, Bradley Nelson from South Africa, and his experiences in a remote Georgian village, Sajijao. There he encounters both the warmth of the local community, and some resistance to the "linguistic revolution" as a national initiative. A finely drawn portrait of a critical moment in Georgia's development as an independent nation in the post-Soviet era. Before construction begins on a major housing complex in Bakhmaro, a resort town in western Georgia that travelers visit for the special healing properties of the air, filmmaker Anka Gujabidze observes life as it is. Employing superimpositions and dissolves, this documentary portrait ruminates on the changes that will come with construction and what will be lost.

events.description: Derived solely from video recordings of Georgian parliamentary proceedings on June 10, 1993, when Eduard Shevardnadze was the head of state, An Incomplete Day in the History of Georgia presents the debate surrounding the introduction of Georgia's national currency coupon to replace the Russian ruble. Members of parliament voice their concerns from the floor, questioning the resolutions presented by the vice prime minister and president of the National Bank. How should the country's leaders proceed in light of domestic challenges such as starvation, fuel shortages, budget shortfalls, and rapid inflation? Viewed with hindsight, this document from the early days of Georgian independence reminds us how fragile the democratic process can be.
