events.title: Pariroo Rattan | Technologies of Populism: The Moral Politics of Digitization in India's Informal Economy
events.description: A talk by Pariroo Rattan (https://sociology.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/visiting/pariroo-rattan.html), Postdoctoral Fellow in Science in Human Culture in the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University, that examines why marginalized street vendors in India continue to embrace Aadhaar and digital payments despite their shortcomings, arguing that these technologies foster a powerful sense of political belonging and direct connection to the nation-state. Event moderated by Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, September 28, 2026 TIME: 12-1:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: On FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) —————-About the talk: Why do marginalized citizens in India continue to embrace biometric identification and digital payment technologies even when these systems routinely fail to deliver their promised economic inclusion? Digital India is a flagship policy of the Government of India to foster "economic growth combined with social inclusion." Central to Digital India is the Aadhaar card, a biometric identification now distributed to over 1.3 billion Indians, and a real time mobile payment technology, Unified Payments Interface (UPI), that has significantly replaced cash transactions. Technological promises to improve governance and economic opportunities are often not fully realized and create new sources of friction, especially for citizens in the informal economy such as street vendors. Nevertheless, many street vendors regard digital identification and payments as signs of economic and national progress. Why does there continue to be faith in techno-utopia even when its promises fall short, and what can this tell us about the nature of contemporary populist politics? Through interviews, archival work, discourse analysis and ethnographic research with street vendors in Delhi from 2020–2024, I argue that digital technologies acquire political force for marginalized citizens not simply through coercion or what they enable materially, but through the political relationships they establish between marginalized citizens and the nation-state. While the bureaucratic state was historically built as an instrument for advancing national development and extending citizenship rights, contemporary populist politics increasingly represents bureaucratic mediation itself as an impediment to democratic responsiveness and national progress. I use technology to illuminate some of the core tensions in the moral relations, state obligations, and forms of political belonging that constitute the foundations of citizenship in contemporary India.About the Speaker:Pariroo Rattan (https://sociology.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/visiting/pariroo-rattan.html) is a Weinberg College Postdoctoral Fellow in Science in Human Culture and the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University. She will also be teaching at the Department of Anthropology at Northwestern. Pariroo is a recent PhD graduate from Harvard University, where she was a long-standing Fellow at the HKS Science, Technology and Society (STS) program and received a secondary field in Music. Her doctoral dissertation is titled "A Marketplace for Populism: The Moral Politics of Digitization in India's Informal Economy" and studies the relationship of the digital economy with mediating state institutions and nation-building in India, through an ethnography of street vendors in New Delhi using digital biometric ID Aadhaar and payment system Unified Payments Interface. She also works comparatively on citizen resistance to legal data regulation regimes across the US, EU and China. Apart from digitization, Pariroo is writing about topics relating to the law such as the politics of evidence in the Harvard affirmative action lawsuit, and on the acoustic and sound politics of the urban economy. events.title: AI & Disability: A Roundtable Discussion feat. Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes
events.description: A History & Theory of New Media event with Jeff Nagy, Assistant Professor, Communication and Media Studies, York University; Renée Cummings, Professor of Practice, School of Data Science, University of Virginia, and Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director, AI Equity Lab, Brookings Institution; and Os Keyes, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Massachusetts, Lowell - Monday, September 28, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (http://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdsmOw4XW_mhfHzcHEg012STGGi9YE_lwF5AYv-7wTx4xVmJg/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=NzBtNDI4MWUzNzcwOXZucDA1N3R2M2MyZ2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - What does AI have to do with disability, and what is it doing to disability? This question undergirds a roundtable discussion featuring Jeff Nagy, Renée Cummings, and Os Keyes. In brief individual presentations, followed by a moderated discussion, these three experts in the field will tackle the question of AI and disability from a range of distinct and overlapping perspectives. Professor Nagy will examine the remaking of psychiatric disability in an AI era through the case of algorithmic depression diagnostics. Tracing a deep history of attempts to bring computing to bear on depression, he argues that the shift from clinic to program and platform, and the substitution of machine learning features for diagnostic criteria, are rewiring the political economy of diagnosis and overwriting disability identities. Through close reading of contemporary systems and the datasets they depend on, he reveals an emergent technopolitics of disability in action, one that operates at cross-purposes with disability community and activism. Professor Renée Cummings wil discuss what happens when automated systems become gatekeepers of opportunity for individuals with disabilities. Focusing on the data infrastructures governing healthcare, education, employment and public services, she exposes how incomplete datasets, inaccessible design, and reductive classifications can convert ableism into computational logic. Through the lens of data justice, she will confront the ethics of algorithmic exclusion: whose needs are recognized, whose experiences are misread, and who is excluded altogether. Centering accessibility, disability justice, and community expertise, Professor Cummings argues that disabled people must possess meaningful power to design, govern, challenge and—when necessary—refuse the systems shaping their lives. Finally, Dr. Keyes will ask what the history of computational psychiatry teaches us about the political economy of diagnostics.The role of AI in psychiatry is often framed as novel, and focused on improving efficiency and patient access to care. But neither is the case. AI has a long history in the upper echelons of psychiatry, as a field and a practice, and that history has consistently been entangled with broader political conflicts over who plays a role in shaping diagnosis and treatment., and under what conditions. Beginning with the start of computational diagnostics in the 1960s, he will trace out the history of how (and why) computational approaches to psychiatry have come in and out of vogue, arguing that the ultimate purpose of these diagnostic tools is to reshape the political economy of diagnosis and disability. About Jeff Nagy Jeff Nagy is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication and Media Studies at York University. He is a historian of computing and AI, currently focused on the intersection of AI development, the behavioral sciences, and disability. He holds a PhD in Communication from Stanford University. With the DISCO Network, he is a co-author of Technoskepticism: Between Possibility and Refusal (Stanford University Press, 2025). His research and writing have appeared in Parapraxis, n+1, New Media and Society, Technology and Culture, and elsewhere. About Renée Cummings Professor Renée Cummings is an internationally recognized AI governance leader, criminologist, public interest technologist, and public sector intelligence futurist whose work is helping shape how governments, institutions, and organizations prepare for the intelligence age. She is widely recognized as one of the leading global voices advancing responsible AI, trustworthy public sector AI, innovation governance, algorithmic accountability, and the governance frameworks required to strengthen public trust, democratic resilience, and institutional integrity. An award-winning AI innovator and internationally sought-after keynote speaker, Professor Cummings serves as Professor of Practice at the University of Virginia School of Data Science, where she teaches future leaders how to excel with AI and deliver AI excellence. She is also a Nonresident Senior Fellow and Co-Director of the AI Equity Lab at the Brookings Institution and serves as Co-Chair of the Global Academic Network at the Centre for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), one of the world's leading organizations dedicated to AI governance, policy, and digital rights. About Os Keyes Dr. Os A. Keyes is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell. A widely published and award-winning scholar of everything from the history of medicine to critical approaches to Artificial Intelligence, their first book, Trans Science, is under contract with University of Washington Press. About History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series The History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series brings to campus leading humanities scholars working on issues of media transition and technological emergence. The series promotes new, interdisciplinary approaches to questions about the uses, meanings, causes, and effects of rapid or dramatic shifts in techno-infrastructure, information management, and forms of mediated expression. Presented by BCNM, these events are free and open to the public.

events.title: Five Years after the Youth Protests: The Thai Monarchy Strikes Back
events.description: Speaker: Pavin Chachavalpongpun (Professor, Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto University) This talk discusses the Thai monarchy's strategic response to the 2020 youth-led protests, which called for reforms to the royal family's place in national life. The speaker argues that King Vajiralongkorn did not merely seek to restore the status quo but executed a profound transformation which he terms 'overt power codification and defensive hyper- personalisation.' This shift converted informal influence into visible, legally codified, and personally commanded authority, entrenching absolute power within the constitutional framework to neutralize reformist momentum. Speaker bio: Pavin Chachavalpongpun is a professor at the Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto University. He is the chief editor of the online journal Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia, in which all articles are translated from English into Japanese, Thai, Bahasa Indonesia, Filipino, Vietnamese, Burmese and Khmer. Earning his PhD from the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London, Pavin is the author and editor of several books, including the upcoming Kings in the American Mirror: Two Centuries of U.S.-Thai Monarchy Relations (University of Hawai'i Press).

events.title: Synchro and SimTraffic for Signal Coordination
events.description: Description This four-session online course (4 hours per session) provides beginning-to-intermediate training in Synchro and SimTraffic software and the recently published Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7th Edition: A Guide for Multimodal Mobility Analysis (TRB 2022 and HCS7). Using a combination of interactive lecture, question and answer, and virtual computer lab, you will become proficient in the network coding and use of Synchro and SimTraffic for signal optimization and coordination projects. Working on a real-world multi-modal project, students will use Synchro to incorporate a Bing aerial background, add/modify roadways, input intersection geometrics, enter multi-modal traffic volumes (cars, trucks, pedestrians, and bicycles), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. Students will also use Synchro to evaluate and develop optimal signal timing plans that reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. The seamless integration of Synchro with SimTraffic, a microsimulation software, will be used to evaluate intersection operations and compare the differences between "isolated - macro-level" Synchro and "network-wide - micro-level" SimTraffic analysis that is recommended for multi-modal, closely spaced intersections and congested corridors. Lastly, this course will teach you how to review and understand the potential differences in delay, level of service, and queuing analysis when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis. Topics IncludeDetailed review of Synchro input requirements Developing a Synchro network for a real-world multi-modal project Analysis of signalized, unsignalized and roundabout intersections using Synchro Multi-modal vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle LOS using HCM 7th Edition Optimizing signal timings for a single intersection that is added to an existing corridor Optimizing signal timings for a group of intersections Seemless Integration of SYNCHRO with SimTraffic SimTraffic Model Calibration and Application What You Will Learn Using a real-world project in a virtual computer lab class setting, students will be able to interact with the instructor as they learn how to develop a network and use the Synchro and SimTraffic software. This includes incorporating a Bing aerial background, add/modify straight and curved roadways, inputting intersection geometrics and pocket lengths, entering multi-modal volumes (cars, trucks, peds, and bicyclists), and signal timings to replicate / validate existing operations analysis for signalized and unsignalized intersections and roundabouts. You will learn the steps used to optimize and coordinate a group of intersections to reduce delays, stops, congestion, fuel consumption, and greenhouse gas emissions. Lastly, you will learn how to review and understand the analysis results and the potential differences when using the empirical (Synchro) analysis or the micro-simulation (SimTraffic) analysis for signal coordination projects. The materials in this course are based on the following references:Transportation Research Board. Highway Capacity Manual, 7th Edition, 2022 CUBIC Transportation Systems. Synchro Studio 12 Traffic Signal Software -User Guide, 2024 Who Should Attend No prior experience using Synchro and SimTraffic is necessary. This course is designed for traffic engineers, planners, and technicians in both public agencies and private firms who engage in improving signal system optimization and coordination projects using the integrated Optimization Module in the Synchro software.

events.title: Lecture | Towards a Transnational Disability Justice: Wounded Bodyminds and the Politics of Survival
events.description: In her new book, Disabling Relations (https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Ftupress.temple.edu%2Fbooks%2Fdisabling-relations&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1788721620000000&usg=AOvVaw2AEfvc0GMN5Yf3xDPscb0e), Dr. Kazemi draws on thirteen years of ethnographic research, hundreds of interviews, and her own lived experience to invite readers to bear witness to the lives of disabled dissidents, veterans, and civilians in the aftermath of Iran's 1979 Revolution. Her analysis spans multiple sites of disablement and survival, including dissidents incarcerated and tortured by the Islamic Republic, veterans and civilians wounded in and by the Iran-Iraq War, survivors of state-sanctioned punitive limb amputation, and survivors of gender-based violence. Through the concepts of "wounding" and "disability consciousness," Kazemi theorizes disability as a historical process of becoming and remaining disabled through unequal social relations of power, while also examining how survivors make meaning of, negotiate, and resist the conditions of their disablement.

events.title: Robert G. Strand | Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism
events.description: Why do the Nordics consistently rank among the world's happiest, most prosperous, and most trusted societies? What lessons might the Nordics offer the United States at a moment when many people feel growing frustration and anxiety about the direction of American capitalism?Nordic Capitalism: Lessons for Realizing Sustainable Capitalism (2026, Cambridge University Press; open access:https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp (https://bit.ly/3MSvrOp)) by Robert G. Strand explores a simple but urgent idea: capitalism must be rooted in democracy if it is to support freedom, shared prosperity, and sustainability. Drawing on research, lived experience, and comparative analysis between the Nordics and the United States, Strand argues that the Nordic countries offer practical inspiration for reimagining capitalism in the twenty-first century. "Where democracy is in charge of capitalism, the people win. When capitalism is in charge of democracy, the oligarchs win. In this important book, Robert G. Strand shows how democracies can stay in charge. Nordic Capitalism explains that the Nordic nations can be a model for the US, and how democratic capitalism serves the many, not the few." — Robert B. Reich, Former U.S. Secretary of Labor and Professor Emeritus of Public Policy, UC Berkeley Dr. Robert G. Strand is the founding Executive Director of the Nordic Center at UC Berkeley and Executive Director of the Center for Responsible Business at Berkeley Haas, where he serves on the faculty. He is also Associate Professor at Copenhagen Business School. His research examines how Nordic societies have organized capitalism and how companies pursue responsible and sustainable business, with attention to applications for reimagining American capitalism. Before joining UC Berkeley in 2014, he served as Assistant Professor at Copenhagen Business School following a decade in corporate America with IBM and Boston Scientific. He received a Ph.D. in Corporate Social Responsibility from Copenhagen Business School, an MBA in International Business from the University of Minnesota, and a B.S. in Industrial Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. He was a U.S. Fulbright Scholar to Norway at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold"
events.description: Abstract: We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and its impact on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure of proteins. Researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold can predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of these AI-predicted structures virtually overnight. Yet, to date, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination has remained almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to facilitate and complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find that basic research on proteins that had no structural information prior to AlphaFold increases by 23 to 32% relative to proteins that already had a structure, with the effects increasing dramatically over time. This represents a significant shift in the direction of research toward less-studied proteins. By contrast, the response of applied R&D, as measured by patents referencing those proteins, has been far more muted.

events.title: Seminar 221, Industrial Organization: Lucio Wasserman "Shrinkflation: What Happens When Package Sizes Change?"
events.description: JMC PracticeAbstract: Package sizes are one of the main features of consumer goods and one of the determinants of unit prices. However, they have received little research attention. This paper develops a method to identify size changes at scale, opening the door to systematic studies of this issue. We apply it to retail scanner data and show that size reductions are considerably more common than increases. Next, we estimate the size elasticities of demand over time using an event study approach. We find different dynamics in response to size increases and decreases. The demand response to size increases is immediate and stable over time. On the contrary, after size decreases, demand has a sluggish response: the size elasticity is smaller in the short term than in the medium term. An incentivized shopping experiment shows that individuals deviate from optimal behavior by responding less to size than to price, and provides evidence of attention as a mechanism. With the experiment, we test policy interventions, showing that the display of unit prices and of sizes more prominently can reduce welfare losses. On the other hand, size change labels can generate the opposite bias, with individuals responding to sizes more than what is optimal. We explain the empirical results with a dynamic demand that allows for inattention, paired with a supply model in which firms strategically advertise size increases but not reductions. Finally, using model-derived sufficient statistics, we evaluate the effect of inattention and of related policies on consumer surplus.Draft of the paper (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_dmfFkjdc4QwcMT6gSoWWerCMXLU5spC/view)

events.description: Allan C. Wilson Memorial LecturesMitochondria are central to cellular energy metabolism and arose through a singularendosymbiotic event ~2 billion years ago. Human mitochondria retain a vestige of theirbacterial ancestry – a compact mtDNA encoding just 13 proteins – while the remaining~1,100 proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported. Both genomes operate in concert toensure normal physiology, and defects in either can underlie human disease.In Lecture I, I will present our lab's recent work leveraging biobank-scale genomicsacross more than 750,000 humans to resolve co-variation between nuclear and mtDNAgenomes in health, aging, and disease. events.description: A talk by David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/), President of the Ethnic Art Foundation (EAF) and Former Executive Director of International and Area Studies, UC Berkeley, drawing on his newly edited volume, India's Mithila Painting (https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295753225/indias-mithila-painting/), co-edited with Paula Richman. The presentation will examine the long-term transformation of Mithila painting from a domestic ritual practice into a distinctive indigenous art form characterized by an expanding repertoire of themes, styles, and subjects. Through an illustrated discussion, Szanton will consider the work of contemporary practitioners, focusing on the ways in which established visual forms and stylistic conventions are adapted to address immediate social, cultural, and political concerns. He will also discuss a significant turning point in the late 1960s, when paper became an important medium for Mithila artists, facilitating new modes of production, circulation, and artistic experimentation. The talk will further explore the diversity of artists and stylistic approaches that have emerged over subsequent decades, while highlighting the important role of the Ethnic Art Foundation in supporting artists and advancing the recognition and wider appreciation of Mithila painting.Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Sept 29, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ——��—–About the Book: Since at least the fifteenth century, Hindu women in the Mithila region of northern India have been painting images of deities, flora and fauna symbolizing fertility and prosperity, and floor designs that sacralize sites for ritual within their homes. Their artwork remained ephemeral since its plant-based colors faded over time. In response to an extended drought that led to widespread crop failure in the 1960s, the Indian government's All India Handicraft Board provided high-quality paper to the women of Mithila to test the income-generating possibilities of transferring wall and floor artwork to a new medium. The unique Mithila aesthetic, novel compositions, and precise linework won enthusiastic buyers in New Delhi and abroad. The small number of women painters expanded across the ranks of the social hierarchy and even included a few men. They developed individual styles and depicted novel subjects such as village history, their own life stories, the tsunami in Sri Lanka, social justice, protecting trees, and changing social norms. Major international museums now house Mithila collections, and individuals around the world own paintings. This volume, the first to present an up-to-date analysis of the history and practitioners of Mithila painting, includes contributions from Mithila artists, anthropologists, art historians, historians of Indian religions and specialists of visual culture, gender studies, and translation studies.About the Speaker:David Szanton (https://ethnicartsfoundation.com/about/) is an American anthropologist renowned for his extensive work in South Asian studies and education policy. Beyond his roles at the Social Science Research Council (SSRC) and the University of California, Berkeley, Szanton has collaborated with several esteemed institutions. He has authoredMithila Painting: The Evolution of an Art Form(2007) andMany Visions, Many Versions: Art from Indigenous Communities in India(2017). In 1971, he served as an assistant to Howard G. Schaller in the Ford Foundation's Southeast Asia office, contributing to the foundation's initiatives in the region. In 1980, Szanton co-founded the Ethnic Arts Foundation (EAF), a nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting and supporting Mithila art—a traditional women's art form from the Mithila region of India and Nepal. As president of the EAF, he has been instrumental in fostering cross-cultural understanding and appreciation through the arts. David's enduring commitment to anthropology, education, and the preservation of indigenous art forms underscores his significant contributions to these fields. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Thomas Farber
events.description: Describing America's deeply unsettling current politics, at age eighty-one Thomas Farber (English) explores personal accountability, impending second childhoods, mortality, and the hunger for immortality. Weighing the functions of satire and the meaning of art, his short takes illuminate, debunk, commiserate, and celebrate by rejoinder.Reckonings (El León Literary Arts/Manoa Books, 2026) is framed by two insights: no one chooses to be born, and no one can help being what they are. Reckoning with democracy in crisis, aging and mortality, his career, the role of the writer, and the fate of books, Farber reflects on endings with curiosity, honesty, wit, and compassion. Reckonings is the latest in a series of remarkable creative memoirs he has written over the past decade, coming to terms with life and its limits. Farber is joined by Sam Otter (English). events.title: (Vamsi Mootha) Mapping the Powerhouse: From Human Disease to Evolutionary Origins - Charting the Mitochondrial Proteome Across the Tree of Life
events.description: Allan C. Wilson Memorial LecturesMitochondria are central to cellular energy metabolism and arose through a singularendosymbiotic event ~2 billion years ago. Human mitochondria retain a vestige of theirbacterial ancestry – a compact mtDNA encoding just 13 proteins – while the remaining~1,100 proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported. Both genomes operate in concert toensure normal physiology, and defects in either can underlie human disease.In Lecture II, I will widen our lens to explore mitochondrial diversity across theeukaryotic tree of life. I will present integrated experimental and computationalstrategies to map the mitochondrial proteomes of highly diverged eukaryotes. Usingthese data, we reconstruct the lineage-specific gain-and-loss events that shape extantmitochondria and infer the ancestral mitoproteome of the Last Eukaryotic CommonAncestor (LECA). We envision this work laying the foundation for an emerging field ofcomparative mitochondrial biology.Division(s): Department of Molecular & Cell Biology

events.title: California Agriculture and the Seeding of Silicon Valley
events.description: In the years immediately following World War II, California's Santa Clara Valley was an agricultural breadbasket to the world. A mere 30 years later, the Santa Clara Valley would be known as 'Silicon Valley', and would be the most technologically productive region on the planet. This transition from an agricultural economy to an urbanized, technological economy came to be seen as aberrational, or even an object of nostalgia. But in fact, the midcentury period of rapid suburban development out of an agricultural landscape laid the foundation for the housing and labour markets that came to characterize the contemporary Silicon Valley. This talk will discuss how the years following the Second World War set the stage for what Silicon Valley would become today. It argues that the roots of Silicon Valley's current housing and labor system were based in the agricultural regime of the immediate post-World War II period and the subsequent Cold War economy. Jeannette Estruth is an Assistant Professor of History at Santa Clara University and a Faculty Associate at the Harvard Berkman- Klein Center for Internet and Society. Estruth's writing has appeared in the Washington Post, The Drift, Urban History, IEEE Annals of the History of Computing, the Business History Review, and Enterprise and Society, among others. She is currently completing her book manuscript, "Think Different: Silicon Valley Activism and the Making of Modern American Politics," which explores the history of social movements, the technology industry, and ideological formation in the United States.

events.title: Michael Maltzan: Scales of the City | Architecture Lecture Series
events.description: Michael Maltzan founded Michael Maltzan Architecture, Inc. in 1995. His projects cross a wide range of typologies, from cultural institutions to city infrastructure. His notable projects include the Moody Center for the Arts at Rice University, MoMA QNS, Star Apartments, the Pittman Dowell Residence, the new Sixth Street Viaduct, MIT Vassar Street Residential Hall, the UCLA Hammer Museum, and the Winnipeg Art Gallery Inuit Art Centre. Maltzan received an MArch from the Graduate School of Design at Harvard University, as well as BFA and BArch degrees from the Rhode Island School of Design. He is a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects and received the 2016 AIA Los Angeles Gold Medal. He is a recipient of a 2012 American Academy of Arts and Letters Architecture Award and was inducted as a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters in 2023. He was elected to the National Academy of Design in 2020 and to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2026, and he currently serves on the Dean's leadership council at the Harvard Graduate School of Design and the Visiting Committee to the GSD. He was featured in the Canadian Centre for Architecture's 2019 film, What It Takes to Make a Home, delivered the 20th Annual John T. Dunlop Lecture for the Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, and his work was named one of the 25 Best Inventions of 2015 by Time magazine. Maltzan's work has gained international acclaim for innovation in both design and construction. It has been recognized with five Progressive Architecture awards, 52 citations from local, state, and national chapters of the American Institute of Architects, the Rudy Bruner Foundation's Gold Medal for Urban Excellence, the Zumtobel Group Award for Innovations for Sustainability & Humanity in the Built Environment, a 2020 Best of the Millennium AIA LA Honor Award, the 2025 AIA California Maybeck Award, and the 2025 Cooper Hewitt National Design Award in Architecture. The firm and its projects have been widely featured in national and international publications and have been exhibited in museums worldwide, including the Museum of Contemporary Art Los Angeles, the Museum of Modern Art, New York, the Heinz Architectural Center, the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the Carnegie Museum of Art. The firm's work was selected for the 2006, 2018, and 2020 La Biennale di Venezia and is included in the permanent collections of the Carnegie Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the Art Institute of Chicago.

This situation had a profound effect on her childhood and identity, caught in the middle of two warring countries. In Self-Portrait Along the Borderline, the filmmaker returns to the Abkhazian family home built by her grandfather, located in a country that is off-limits to Georgian citizens and still not recognized by Georgia.

events.title: Erin Schuman: Carla & Corey Lectureship Series
events.description: The Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute (HWNI) are delighted to announce the 2026 Carla & Corey Lectureship Series. This event, created through the generosity of co-founding directors of the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, Dr. Carla Shatz and Dr. Corey Goodman, will bring outstanding neuroscientists to our campus to share their research and engage with our vibrant, interdisciplinary scientific community, spanning the full breadth of mind and brain science. This year's guest speaker will be Dr. Erin M. Schuman (https://brain.mpg.de/schuman), former Professor and Director of the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt, Germany, and now Director of University College London Queen Square Institute of Neurology. The Schuman lab's long-standing research interest is the study of cellular mechanisms and neural circuits that underlie information processing and storage. The lab focuses on the molecular and cell biological processes that control protein synthesis and degradation in neurons and their synapses. The complex morphology of neurons, with most synapses located hundreds of microns from the cell body, presents a logistical challenge for the establishment, maintenance and modification of local synaptic proteomes. For her groundbreaking work on local protein translation in neurons and the establishment of its importance for brain development and plasticity, Dr. Schuman has been awarded the 2026 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience (https://www.kavliprize.org/bio/erin-schuman). The event will take place October 1 from 4-6pm at the Brower Center (https://events.berkeley.edu/hwni/event/310822-carla-shatz-corey-goodman-lectureship-series-with-dr-), with a reception to follow. Join us for an inspiring afternoon of conversation and meaningful connections as we delve into the latest advances in neuroscience.

events.title: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West
events.description: Are We Living in a 1938 Moment? How Autocracies Threaten the West Thursday, October 1, 12:30 – 2 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://forms.gle/aJvKjMEtZbCn3H1JA)The warning signs of the 1930s feel alarmingly familiar today: nationalist rhetoric, revisionism, military rearmament, political polarization. The liberal order is eroding, autocracies are rearming, and the West appears weaker than at any point in decades. In this book talk, historian and security expert Dr. Moritz Pöllath argues that these patterns function as an early warning system for the present: a new authoritarian axis — Russia, China, North Korea, Iran — is forming, exploiting a strategic power vacuum to impose a world order beyond freedom and democracy. The years ahead may prove decisive: between 2027 and 2030, the world may decide whether it descends into a new global systemic conflict, with a possible attack on Taiwan as its most dangerous flashpoint. Moritz Pöllath is an Assistant Professor of Public History at Ludwig Maximilian University Munich, where he teaches courses on the History of Democracy, US History, the Cold War, and history teaching methods for secondary schools. He studied Diplomatic and Military History at Hawaiʻi Pacific University and American History at the University of Cologne. His first book, Out-of-Area? NATO and Decolonization in Africa and Asia 1949–1961 (2017), explores the roots of NATO's global security policy during the early Cold War; his second book (habilitation), Narrating Freedom: Challenges to American and German Master Narratives in the 21st Century, was completed in 2023. He has held visiting professorships at the University of Leipzig and was previously a visiting scholar at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a fellow of the Cold War Studies Program at Harvard University and the University of Udine.

events.title: Black Feminism & The Issue of Practice
events.location: Maude Fife Room, 315 Wheeler Hall, UC Berkeley
events.description: Please RSVP to attend (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScBDQrjMuo76n6pZySYpqe58aLn5PGOzcfC-UsmeoIXwLOYeg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). Join the Banned Scholars Project in African American and African Diaspora Studies at UC Berkeley for a conversation with scholars Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor and Sarah Haley. Responding to the move to reduce Black feminism to an analytic, Taylor and Haley will trace its genealogies and practices as a guide for political struggle. How can the tools of Black feminism and the legacy of radical Black left feminists inform resistance in our current moment and authoritarian times?Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor writes and speaks on Black politics, social movements, and racial inequality in the United States. ​She is author Race for Profit: How Banks and the Real Estate Industry Undermined Black Homeownership, published in 2019 by University of North Carolina Press. Race for Profit was a semi-finalist for the 2019 National Book Award and a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize in History in 2020. She is a 2021 MacArthur Foundation Fellow. Her earlier book From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation won the Lannan Cultural Freedom Award for an Especially Notable Book in 2016. She is also editor of How We Get Free: Black Feminism and the Combahee River Collective, which won the Lambda Literary Award for LGBQT nonfiction in 2018, and co-editor with Colin Kaepernick and Robin D.G. Kelley of Our History Has Always Been Contraband: In Defense of Black Studies.Sarah Haley's research areas include African American and queer history, feminist historical methods, carceral history, and prison abolition. She is the author of No Mercy Here: Gender, Punishment, and the Making of Jim Crow Modernity. She organizes with Scholars for Social Justice and is director of the Institute for the Study of Sexuality and Gender at Columbia University.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Markus Covert - The E. coli Whole-Cell Modeling Project: Accelerating Discovery via Comprehensive Biological Simulation
events.description: Abstract: Francis Crick first called for a coordinated worldwide scientific effort to determine a "complete solution" of the bacterium Escherichia coli. We have been working for some years now to complete a model of E. coli that takes into account all of the known functions of every well-annotated gene, in order to better understand and predict the behavior of this scientifically-relevant and industrially-significant model organism. Now that a majority of the annotated gene functions have been added to the model, our simulations have generated biological insights that change our perspectives about cellular biology and physiology. As examples, I will present our new findings regarding how metals are utilized in E. coli, as well as the effect of gene organization into operons, and the impact of engineering new gene content into the chromosome.Bio: Markus Covert is the Ram Shriram Chair and Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. Over the course of his career, his lab has generated several new exciting technologies to measure, analyze, and mathematically model the behaviors of individual cells. The lab is probably best known for constructing the first "whole-cell" computational model, which explicitly represents all known gene functions and molecules in a bacterial cell - an advance which was highlighted by the journal Cell as a highlight publication of the 40-year history of that journal. Markus is the author of the textbook Fundamentals of Systems Biology: from Synthetic Circuits to Whole-Cell Models. He has received several awards for his efforts to develop new technologies, in particular the NIH Director's Pioneer Award, and the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation Distinguished Investigator and Discovery Center awards. He has also consulted in industry, including on the scientific advisory board of Emerald Cloud Labs, and as an inaugural Ambassador at X Labs, (previously Google [X]). Finally, Markus has taught one of the most popular courses at Stanford for several years, an integrated "lecture, lab and lunch" course entitled Bon Appétit, Marie Curie! The Science of Haute Cuisine.

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Demos: How the People Ruled Athens"
events.description: REGISTER (https://forms.gle/KddCT6ubaNBAkJXY8) Join us on October 1 for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, by Daniela Cammack, Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, with a courtesy appointment in the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies (formerly Classics). Professor Cammack will be joined in conversation by James Porter, Distinguished Professor and Irving Stone Chair in Literature in the Department of Rhetoric at UC Berkeley, and Kinch Hoekstra, Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Departments of Political Science and Ancient Greek & Roman Studies. The Social Science Matrix Authors Meet Critics (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/authors-meet-critics/) book series features lively discussions about recently published books authored by social scientists at UC Berkeley. For each event, the author discusses the key arguments of their book with fellow scholars. These events are free and open to the public.About the Book In ancient Greece, demokratia meant "rule by the people"—but what people, and how did they rule? Scholars have long argued that demokratia signified the rule of all adult male citizens over themselves. In Demos, Daniela Cammack counters this view by arguing that demokratia meant rule by the crowd that assembled when a public meeting was held. This crowd was the demos, which the Greeks distinguished from orators, generals, councilors, public benefactors, and other civic leaders. Drawing on literary and epigraphical evidence as well as the key theoretical insights of Aristotle and Hobbes, Cammack explains how constantly changing masses of ordinary ancient Greek men ruled while their leaders were ruled over. This political system relied on kratos, the power to prevail militarily, epitomized by the victories of the Athenian demos in civil conflicts around 508 and 404 BC. In peacetime, the superior strength of the demos revealed itself in large, frequently summoned crowds of ordinary citizens acting as policymakers, legislators, and (crucially) judges, who wielded great power over politicians. Aristotle characterized the years 403 to 322 as the era of "ultimate democracy," and it was during this period that the Athenians pulled off a feat unmatched by modern democrats: making use of talented and ambitious leaders without being ruled by them. By contrast, the Greeks called rule by elected office-holders "oligarchy." As people today lose faith in democratic institutions, Cammack's account prompts us to ask if we've been doing democracy all wrong—or even at all.PanelistsDaniela Cammack (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/daniela-cammack) is Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Berkeley, with a courtesy appointment in the Department of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies (formerly Classics). She holds a B.A. in Modern History and English Literature (2002) from Oxford, an M.Phil. in Political Theory and Intellectual History (2005) from Cambridge, and a Ph.D. in Political Theory (2013) from Harvard, where her dissertation, Rethinking Athenian Democracy, won Harvard's Noxon Toppan Prize for the best dissertation in Political Science. Before moving to Berkeley in 2019, she was a Junior Fellow in Harvard's Society of Fellows and an Assistant Professor at Yale. Over the past decade, she has published in numerous edited volumes and journals including Political Theory, History of Political Thought, The Journal of Political Philosophy, Polis, The Journal of Politics, Classical Quarterly, Classical Philology, and The Journal of Sortition. Cammack studies the differences and similarities between ancient and modern democratic ideas and practices, focusing on the themes of crowd power, deliberation, representation, and sovereignty. Authors of special interest are Aristotle, Hobbes, and Rousseau. Her first book, Demos: How the People Ruled Athens, will be published in May 2026 by Princeton University Press. A sequel, entitled What was Democracy? A Short History, is in progress and also under contract with Princeton.Kinch Hoestra (https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/kinch-hoekstra) is Chancellor's Professor of Political Science and Law at UC Berkeley. He works on the history of political, moral, and legal thought, especially ancient, renaissance, and early modern political philosophy. Recent contributions to ancient political thought include "Athenian Democracy and Popular Tyranny," "Thucydides and the Politics of Necessity" (with Mark Fisher), and "The Liberties of the Ancients" (with Quentin Skinner). Another focus of Hoestra's research has been the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes (including studies of his theory of equality, obligation, democracy, tyranny, mixed government, natural law, and the rationality of justice); he co-edited The Oxford Handbook of Hobbes. Work that bridges these two areas includes "Hobbes and Aristotle on the Foundation of Political Science" (with Nicholas Gooding), "Hobbes's Thucydides", "Thucydides in the Renaissance and Reformation", and "The Melian Dilemma". From 1996 to 2007, he was a member of the Faculty of Philosophy at the University of Oxford, where he regularly taught graduate students in the Faculty of Classics and the Department of Politics and International Relations.James Porter (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/james-porter) is Irving Stone Professor in Literature and Distinguished Professor in Rhetoric. His teaching and research has followed a few different trajectories. One is a study of Nietzsche's thought, early and late (Nietzsche and the Philology of the Future and The Invention of Dionysus: An Essay on 'The Birth of Tragedy' (both Stanford University Press, 2000). Another is a study of models of aesthetic sensation, perception, and experience in ancient Greece and Rome, which he explored in The Origins of Aesthetic Thought in Ancient Greece: Matter, Sensation, and Experience (Cambridge University Press, 2010; pbk. 2016). A continuation of this inquiry is The Sublime in Antiquity (Cambridge University Press, 2016; pbk. 2020), which received the C. J. Goodwin Award of Merit from The Society for Classical Studies (2017). A further strand is Jewish literary and critical thought in authors from Spinoza to Freud, Adorno, and Arendt. His most recent book is Homer: The Very Idea (University of Chicago Press, 2021; pbk. 2023), which captures some of his interest in classical reception studies. Current projects include Existence, Crisis, and Faith: Selected Essays and Letters by Rachel Bespaloff, a Cambridge Critical Guide to The Birth of Tragedy (co-edited with Michael Forster), and The Cynics: A Very Short Introduction. Dylan Riley (https://sociology.berkeley.edu/faculty/dylan-john-riley) studies capitalism, socialism, democracy, authoritarianism, and knowledge regimes in a broad comparative and historical perspective. His first book, The Civic Foundations of Fascism in Europe: Italy, Spain, and Romania 1870-1945 (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010), argues that fascist regimes arose paradoxically on the basis of strong civil societies in the pre-fascist period. Reviewers have called this book "the most original and provocative new analysis of the preconditions of Fascism that has appeared in years", and "brilliant and courageous". A second book, How Societies and States Count: A Comparative Genealogy of Censuses (with Rebecca Jean Emigh and Patricia Ahmed in preparation for Palgrave), argues, against state centered accounts of official information that censuses work best where there is intense interaction between state and society. He has started a new project investigating the connection between the meaning and substance of democracy in interwar and post-war Europe. Riley has also published articles in the American Journal of Sociology, American Sociological Review, Catalyst, Comparative Studies in Society and History, Comparative Sociology, Social Science History, The Socio-Economic Review, and the New Left Review. He is a member of the editorial committee of the New Left Review.

events.title: Film Screening: Italianamerican and American Boy: A Profile of Steven Prince
events.description: Martin Scorsese's documentaries are like portals to his sources of inspiration, and Italianamerican takes us to the heart of the matter via a conversation with his parents. As his mother prepares meatballs, she and her husband tell the stories of their families' journeys from Sicily to Elizabeth Street, which speak volumes about the immigrant experience. American Boy is the realization of Scorsese's idea for a film in which "a man sits down, tells his story, and little by little you see an era emerge, a way of life, a way of surviving." He found the perfect subject in Steven Prince, a great storyteller, who played the gun dealer in Taxi Driver, a role for which he provided his own guns.

events.title: Vaṭivam: The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures | A Conference in Tamil Studies
events.description: The Berkeley Tamil Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/berkeley-tamil-initiative) is pleased to present The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies), a Tamil Studies conference exploring vaṭivam—form, shape, style, arrangement, and embodiment—as a way to understand how Tamil narratives are created, circulated, and transformed across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media. More than a neutral vessel for narrative, vaṭivam offers a way to understand form as an aesthetic practice, a material structure, and a response to changing social worlds. Bringing together scholars working across literature, performance, visual culture, cinema, and digital media, the conference will examine how Tamil narrative forms have been made and remade across time. By placing premodern and modern materials in conversation, The Work of Form in Tamil Narrative Cultures (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/language/tamilberkeley/uc-berkeley-conference-tamil-studies) asks how Tamil traditions can contribute to broader debates on form, media, and circulation, while remaining attentive to the histories, languages, and material contexts that shape Tamil cultural production. Conference led by Vasugi Kailasam (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/vasugi-kailasam), Assistant Professor of Tamil Studies in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. Welcome remarks by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Associate Professor, South & South East Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. events.title: Composition Colloquium: Nicholas Isherwood
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: Oct 2: Nicholas Isherwood (MORRISON)TITLE: TESSITURA: VOCAL REGISTERSCONCERT: 8pm CNMATBIO: The Franco-American bass Nicholas Isherwood did musical, literary and theatrical studies at Oberlin College (B.A. in French Literature, B.M. in voice with Richard Miller), The Actors Centre in London and the Ecole des Hautes Etudes (D.E.A. in Musicology). An eclectic artist, Isherwood has sung medieval music with Joel Cohen, baroque music with William Christie, the Magic Flute at the Salle Pleyel, Wagner's Meistersinger with Zubin Mehta, several world premieres by Karlheinz Stockhausen and an evening at the Knitting Factory with Steve Lacy. His interest for contemporary music has led him to work with composers such as Sylvano Bussotti, Elliot Carter, George Crumb, Mauricio Kagel, György Kurtág, Olivier Messiaen, Giacinto Scelsi, Karlheinz Stockhausen and Iannis Xenakis as well as the leading composers of younger generations. He has performed both the Bach and Gubaidulina St. John Passions with Helmuth Rilling and improvised with Joëlle Léandre, Steve Lacy, David Moss and Sainkho Namtchilak. Isherwood has sung on five continents, including the greatest theaters in Europe and the United States (Ravinia, Tanglewood, the Disney Hall, La Scala, the Teatro dell'Opera in Rome, Covent Garden, the Châtelet, the Théatre des Champs Elysées, the Philharmonie, the Royal Festival Hall, the Concertgebouw, the Biennale in Munich, all three Berlin opera houses, the Moscow Conservatory, the Konzerthaus in Vienna, the Salzburg Festival, the Aix Festival, etc.) and with world class orchestras and ensembles (London Philharmonic, RAI Orchestra, the Philharmonic Orchestra in Paris, the London Sinfonietta, the SWR Orchestra, the Ensemble Intercontemporain, the Ensemble Modern, the Arditti and Diotima Quartets, etc.) Isherwood has recorded 70 CDs for labels such as Erato, Naxos, NEOS, Stockhausen Verlag and Harmonia Mundi. He has participated in films with Stockhausen, Aperghis and Frize for Arte, the WDR and the INA. In addition to his work as a singer, he has directed contemporary music theatre (SMIO in Orléans, Sons d'Hiver, Parvis St. Jean in Dijon, Teatro Regio in Torino, Stuttgart Opera, Tadashi Suzuki's theatre in Togamura, Deutsche Oper Berlin, etc.) and taught master classes in 5 languages on the French Art Song (USC, UdK), Olivier Messiaen (cnsmd in Paris), baroque singing (Cal State LA) and contemporary singing (Salzburg Mozarteum, ARIAM, UdK in Berlin, Munich Conservatory, Milan Conservatory, etc.), given lectures (Harvard, USC, Penn, Stanford, Berkeley, Freie Universität Berlin, IRCAM, etc.) and composed several pieces for voice (2 commissions from the DRAC and one from Art Zoyd). Nicholas Isherwood has taught at numerous universities in the United States, as well as the Ecole Normale de Musique and the Conservatoire National Supérieur in France, the UdK in Berlin and the Hochschule für Musik in Munich. He has published a book, "The Techniques of Singing" (Bärenreiter, 2013), as well as three peer reviewed articles (LIM, the Journal of Singing, Vox Humana). He is professor of singing at the Conservatoire du Pays de Montbéliard and professor of contemporary singing at the Conservatorio di Santa Cecilia.

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: Losing the Law: How Legal Polarization Threatens American Democracy (Princeton University Press, 2026)
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: Featuring Deborah Pearlstein, Director, Program in Law and Public Policy and Visiting Professor in Law and Public Affairs, Princeton University Abstract: The norms that have separated law from politics in America are eroding, making government by constitutional democracy increasingly hard to sustain. Losing the Law tells the story of how we came to this precarious moment. This powerful, persuasively argued book describes how a decades-long revolution in professional culture and legal thought is fueling the nation’s authoritarian slide. It also offers essential guidance on what we can do to change course, not just by crafting institutional reforms but by resetting professional incentives and popular beliefs about the power and limits of the rule of law in constitutional governance. Looking behind the well-recognized politics of red and blue, Deborah Pearlstein charts the independent rise of “legal polarization”—a growing divide between lawyers and judges who believe there should be a difference between law and politics and those who no longer do. Drawing on original interviews and archival research, a close reading of American law and legal thought, and a sobering accounting of recent events, she unearths the conservative legal movement’s foundation-shifting secondary effects as it established a new career pipeline from law school to judgeship, promoted partisan loyalty above professional responsibility, and popularized legal theories in irreconcilable conflict with long-settled understandings of how law worked. From the early role of unitary executive theory in kneecapping major post-Watergate reforms to originalism’s inevitable rejection of precedent, Pearlstein traces how legal polarization has supercharged democratic backsliding under Trump 2.0. An urgent call to action by one of today’s foremost legal minds, Losing the Law lays out the complex task ahead for those committed both to understanding the depth of the current crisis and to reestablishing sustainable constitutional governance in the years ahead. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diego Pirillo
events.description: The Atlantic Republic of Letters (Pennsylvania, 2026) offers an alternative intellectual history of early America. Focusing on Benjamin Franklin's Philadelphia, the book frames Euro-American colonialism as an intellectual enterprise, established not only through military and economic means but also through books, ideas, and cultural institutions. Through extensive archival research, Diego Pirillo (Italian) brings together two interconnected histories. First, he recovers the place of British America in the cosmopolitan world of the Republic of Letters, studying the communication system that facilitated the transatlantic circulation of knowledge. Second, he shows that knowledge was weaponized in the effort to survey and control North America. While fashioning themselves as independent and cosmopolitan scholars, Franklin and his associates were in fact deeply tied to political power and tailored their ideas to the needs of their patrons. They served as agents of empire and helped to devise and put into practice the colonial project. Not only were books, libraries, and cultural institutions funded by the wealth created by the slave trade and the expropriation of Indigenous land, but, as Pirillo argues, the very taxonomies and classification systems that Euro-American scholars devised directly shaped the colonial enterprise. The Atlantic Republic of Letters illuminates the relationship among books, intellectuals, and colonial governance, and explores the ways in which knowledge circulated and shaped conquest. Pirillo is joined by Brian DeLay (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: California Spotlight: Wealth & Poverty
events.description: REGISTER California is one of the wealthiest states in the country, yet it also faces persistent poverty, stark economic inequality, and some of the highest costs of living in the nation. These tensions raise fundamental questions about who benefits from California's economic growth and why so many residents struggle to achieve economic security. This panel brings together leading scholars to examine the forces shaping wealth and poverty across the state. Drawing on research spanning inequality, affordability, economic mobility, and social policy, the discussion will explore the roots of California's economic divides, how they are reproduced across generations, and what is at stake for families, communities, and the future of the state. This panel will feature David Grusky, Edward Ames Edmonds Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, and Professor of Sociology at Stanford; Marianne Page, Professor of Economics and Director of the Center for Poverty Research at UC Davis; and Samuel Trachtman, Senior Researcher at the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative at UC Berkeley. Evan White, Executive Director of the California Policy Lab at UC Berkeley, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Goldman School of Public Policy, the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment, the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative, and the Opportunity Lab.PanelistsDavid Grusky (https://grusky.people.stanford.edu/) is Edward Ames Edmonds Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, Professor of Sociology, Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Faculty Fellow at the Center for Population Health Sciences, Faculty Director of the Stanford Center on Poverty and Inequality, and coeditor of Pathways Magazine. He is a member of the National Academy of Sciences and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, a corecipient of the 2004 Max Weber Award, the founder of the Cornell University Center for the Study of Inequality, and a former Presidential Young Investigator. His recent books are Inequality in the 21st Century (with Jasmine Hill, 2017), Social Stratification (with Kate Weisshaar, 2014), Occupy the Future (with Douglas McAdam, Robert Reich, and Debra Satz, 2012), The New Gilded Age (with Tamar Kricheli-Katz, 2011), and The Great Recession (with Bruce Western and Chris Wimer, 2011).Marianne Page (https://mepage.faculty.ucdavis.edu/) is a Professor of Economics (https://economics.ucdavis.edu/) and a founding director of the Center for Poverty Research at UC Davis (http://poverty.ucdavis.edu/). She is a Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research and member of the Institute for Labor Economics. She currently serves as a Co-Editor of the Journal of Human Resources, and recently completed a term serving on Governor Newsom's Council of Economic Advisors. She is an expert on policies promoting intergenerational mobility and equality of opportunity for children in the United States. Her research has appeared in economics journals including the Quarterly Journal of Economics, the American Economic Review. and the Journal of Labor Economics, and has been funded by the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.Sam Trachtman (https://besi.berkeley.edu/people/samuel-trachtman/) is a senior researcher at the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI), where he leads the research program on the political economy of California. Sam completed his Ph.D. in political science in 2021 at UC Berkeley, where he honed skills in quantitative methods and policy-engaged empirical research. He has published widely in academic journals including American Political Science Review, Climatic Change, Governance, Legislative Studies Quarterly, Nature Energy, Public Opinion Quarterly, and Perspectives on Politics.Evan White (https://capolicylab.org/staff/evan-white/) co-founded the California Policy Lab, which generates research insights for government impact. Through hands-on partnerships with government, CPL performs research across issue silos and builds the data infrastructure necessary to improve programs that millions of Californians rely on. Since 2017, CPL has helped conduct 300+ projects with 75+ agency partners. As Executive Director, Evan leads the Lab's Berkeley site and authors reports on household finance, migration, and poverty. Prior to joining CPL, Evan served as Senior Advisor to the first Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Evan also served as Director of Fair Housing for northern California's largest fair housing nonprofit. He holds a joint degree in Law and Public Policy from UC Berkeley.

events.title: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time
events.description: Tang Music in Contemporary China: Sensing Artistry Through Time October 8 Keynote Lecture (125 Morrison Hall) October 9 (125 Morrison Hall) October 10 (Hertz Hall)— Full program will be available later this spring — The resplendent court-entertainment music of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), born from cultural exchange along the early Silk Road, has always loomed large in histories of Chinese music. But in today's China, reconstructive performances of this music have begun to assert its place — as living, breathing performance art — in concert halls and social media feeds, too. This conference brings together scholars and performers from across the world, including leading and emerging experts from China, to present, evaluate, and propel forward global scholarly and artistic discourse on Tang music in the contemporary world. Papers will explore the material culture of the Silk Road, early notations and musical instruments, techniques of historical reconstruction and performance, and the place of historical music and dance in contemporary Chinese society. Three leading ensembles from China and the United States will give live performances of Tang music and dance, followed by a roundtable discussion bringing scholarship and performance into critical dialogue.

events.title: 2026 Gerald D. Feldman Lecture | Reckoning with the Past in Germany and the United States: The Case for Thinking Comparatively about Reparative Justice
events.description: German atonement for the Holocaust has been widely hailed by the international community as a paragon of national reckoning, and over the last decade, African American intellectuals such as Ta-Nehisi Coates have explicitly invoked Germany as a useful model in their calls for Americans to confront the legacy of slavery and other forms of state-sanctioned racism. In this lecture, Rita Chin, will trace the complicated, fraught 80-year process by which Germans have dealt with the Nazi past, focusing on developments and debates in the Federal Republic. She will consider the specific ways in which the German case is instructive for Americans seeking to pursue redress but also explore how Germany's vaunted memory culture has become fossilized such that it has sometimes become a stumbling block for a German society struggling to respond to contemporary challenges. Thinking comparatively about how to reckon with legacies of state-sanctioned racial harm, oppression, and violence not only presents Americans with a concrete template for imagining what reparative justice might look like, Chin suggests, it may also help Germans acknowledge the shape-shifting aspects of racism and perhaps even rethink some of the outdated aspects of their memory culture. Rita Chin, Louise A. Tilly Collegiate Professor of European History and Associate Dean of Social Sciences of the Rackham Graduate School at the University of Michigan, is a historian of modern Europe with particular expertise in immigration and human mobility, race and ethnicity, and colonialism and post-colonialism. Trained in European cultural and intellectual history, she has sought to apply these modes of inquiry to her ongoing interest in how difference and diversity have shaped the very terms of modern Germany and Europe more generally. Her research and writing have been supported by the SSRC, the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, the ACLS Burkhardt Fellowship for Recently Tenured Scholars, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. events.title: Matthew Shutzer | Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis
events.description: A talk by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History, on his new book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691265919/until-the-last-ton?srsltid=AfmBOorxSc-xwrFM8YrmGZbYMJ4vEm3ZcucGahHadYBaRZA9ySGhXWds), a panoramic historical account of India's ascent in the global fossil economy. Event moderated by Sharad Chari (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-sharad-chari), Associate Professor of Geography, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 8, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Book: India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.About the Author:Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is Assistant Professor of History at University of California, Berkeley. He is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching focus on the place of the environment in global history, with particular attention to fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. His work also connects global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. It traces India's rise as a world-leading fossil economy in the twentieth century and examines the processes of empire, capitalism, and agroecological change that shaped this transformation. The book moves beyond the prevailing focus in the environmental history of energy on production and consumption, offering instead a longer-term perspective on land, subsurface property rights, geological knowledge, and mining conflicts. In doing so, it reveals the central role of agrarian development in shaping India's trajectory of fossil fuel dependence. Shutzer is currently working on a second book project examining climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945. Before joining the History Department at UC Berkeley, Shutzer taught as an Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Duke University. He previously served as a Junior Scholar at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies at Harvard University and as an S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup Fellow in Natural Resource Economics and Political Economy in the Department of Geography at UC Berkeley. He has also worked as a researcher on several projects related to the implementation of India's Forest Rights Act in western Odisha. Along with Rebecca Herman, Rebecca McLennan, and Bernadette Perez, Shutzer is one of the faculty conveners of the Berkeley Workshop on Environmental History, based in UC Berkeley's Department of History. events.title: The Significance of Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Sungik Yang (Arizona State University) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The years after Korea's independence from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 were a time of extreme crisis that opened a space for fascist ideologies and discourses to gain ascendancy. In response to national division and political polarization and violence, there arose a heavily nationalist ruling discourse that openly promoted the supremacy of the homogeneous ethnic nation above all competing forms of identity while rejecting core tenets of Western liberalism, containing strong parallels with fascist ideologies in Europe and Japan. Furthermore, this hegemonic discourse pervaded Korean political culture for decades, helping to prop up authoritarian regimes in the country until the 1980s. This discourse, which I call "transcendent nationalism," was a product of the intersection of Korea's postcolonial and Cold War conditions. It sought to overcome Cold War divisions through an embrace of the Korean nation while maintaining colonial-era suspicions of Western capitalist modernity. Ultimately, the fascistic aspects of South Korea's post-1945 political culture reveals the liminal position that Koreans found themselves in during the Cold War, being pulled into the U.S.'s anticommunist orbit but expressing discomfort with American political and cultural hegemony. In addition, postcolonial Korea emerges as an intriguing case study to better understand the nature of fascism as a political discourse promoting an alternative form of modernity that rejected those of capitalist liberalism and communism. By analyzing how fascism took root in a postcolonial nation-state after World War II, we can also gain an understanding of fascism's enduring appeal in global politics even today. Speaker Bio: Sungik Yang is an assistant professor of history at Arizona State University. He is a political and intellectual historian of modern Korea, focusing on political ideology, nationalism, democracy, and historical memory. His forthcoming book is titled Nation Transcendent: Postcolonial Fascism in Cold War Korea.

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSolar Chemical TechnologiesInspired by the blueprint of photosynthesis, creating synthetic systems for the direct conversion of sunlight into sustainable fuels has long been a defining ambition of chemistry. While decades of research have been spent on developing solar water splitting catalysts to produce green hydrogen, recently a new generation of photosynthesis-inspired architectures capable of directly converting sunlight, carbon dioxide and carbon waste streams has emerged. This advance has been made possible by developing and integrating metal complex and biological catalysts with semiconductor materials and electrodes, together with the engineering of bespoke devices. This lecture will first introduce functional mimics of photosynthesis, which couple semiconductor light absorbers with immobilised (bio)catalysts to achieve solar-driven carbon dioxide fixation alongside water oxidation to oxygen. Next, an alternative strategy will be presented that replaces the challenging water oxidation reaction by the oxidation of waste biomass and plastics. This concept, termed solar reforming, simultaneously improves reaction thermodynamics, enhances overall rate of catalysis, and creates economic value through oxidative valorisation while simultaneously generating clean fuel. The ongoing demonstration of outdoor solar plastic reforming at the kilogram and square-metre scale illustrates the growing potential of this approach as a practical route towards circular solar-powered manufacturing. The lecture will close by giving an overview of emerging frontiers in integrated solar chemistry, including atmospheric CO₂ utilisation, advanced light-management strategies, and solar-powered cascade catalysis for selective chemical organic synthesis. Together, this presentation aims to provide a compelling vision for a new generation of solar technologies that combine carbon capture, plastic and biomass waste valorisation, and renewable chemical manufacturing in integrated, scalable systems. More information: https://www-reisner.ch.cam.ac.uk/
