events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies with Selina Makana
events.description: Materialist Nationalism: Challenging the Heroic Masculinist Rendering of the Nation Nation building exists in an uneasy and fraught relationship with women. On the one hand, nations revere women for their social reproductive labor. In twentieth-century Africa, nationalist movements deployed the figure of "Mama Africa" to galvanize the masses for the fight for independence. On the other hand, women and girl women's bodies were used as battlefields in wars and political repression in the colonial and postcolonial period, albeit in different ways. This lecture focuses on Selina Makana's new book, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (https://www.ohioswallow.com/9780821426739/beyond-the-battlefield/), to examine the meanings and complexities of Angolan women's lived experience of war and militarism and reveal the extraordinary means by which they contend with and contest the politics of the nation. Selina Makana is an Assistant Professor of African history at the University of Memphis. Her research and teaching interests focus on African history, gender and militarism, and African diaspora studies. Her first monograph, Beyond the Battlefield: Women and the Nation in Twentieth-Century Angola (Ohio University Press, 2026), probes the relationship between women, war, and nationalist politics in Angola. She is currently working on her second book project Paranoia and Pathology in the Colony: Hygiene, Health, and Colonial Governance in Early Twentieth-Century Angola, that examines the entwined histories of public health and colonial governance in Angola. She has published articles in Meridians: Feminism, Race, Transnationalism; Gender and History; and The Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African Women's History.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Jared Shaw, Professor, UC DavisStereoselective Synthesis with Rhodium Carbenes and NitrenesLow-valent reactive intermediates of carbon and nitrogen—namely, transition-metal complexes of carbenes and nitrenes—display diverse and powerful reactivity in the synthesis of complex organic molecules. Our group has focused on rhodium carbene complexes derived from substrates that lack electron-withdrawing groups. The diminished electrophilicity of these intermediates imparts exceptional functional group tolerance, enabling the construction of architecturally complex organic frameworks. The development of new methods and their application to the synthesis of a variety of heterocycles, including several natural products, will be presented. In parallel, analogous transformations involving rhodium nitrenes have been employed to generate complex heterocycles. The discovery of the first five-membered aromatic heterocycles featuring point chirality within the ring will be described, along with discussion of their distinctive structural characteristics.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. events.description: A talk by Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/), film historian, screenwriter, and author, based on his new book, The Tree Within: Octavio Paz's Years in India (https://0235947a.streak-link.com/C3VGHy6fX8I10Qk1JABJW9Rn/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2FTree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio%2Fdp%2F0143471651%2F%3F_encoding%3DUTF8%26pd_rd_w%3DF95xZ%26content-id%3Damzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%253Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0%26pf_rd_p%3D4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%26pf_rd_r%3DVR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB%26pd_rd_wg%3Dvlupw%26pd_rd_r%3D12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464%26ref_%3Dpd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d), that explores how Octavio Paz's years as Mexico's ambassador to India transformed his personal life, poetry, philosophy, and understanding of cultural exchange.Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor of Global Modern Art and South and Southeast Asian Art, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley.The Tree Within (https://www.amazon.com/Tree-Within-Mexican-Laureate-Octavio/dp/0143471651/?_encoding=UTF8&pd_rd_w=F95xZ&content-id=amzn1.sym.4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631%3Aamzn1.symc.5a16118f-86f0-44cd-8e3e-6c5f82df43d0&pf_rd_p=4efc43db-939e-4a80-abaf-50c6a6b8c631&pf_rd_r=VR6CA1607Z5S9X17FJWB&pd_rd_wg=vlupw&pd_rd_r=12aba704-4be6-41aa-b6f0-8da866b68464&ref_=pd_hp_d_atf_ci_mcx_mr_ca_hp_atf_d) is the enchanting story of Octavio Paz's passionate love-affair with India where he served as Mexico's ambassador in the 1960s. Immersing himself in the country's rich cultural life and contemplative traditions, Paz travelled widely, forged deep friendships with some of India's finest minds, and produced several of his most inspired poetry and essays. It was here that he met the love of his life and experienced what he called his 'second birth'. In this richly textured and erudite work, Chakravarty reconstructs the inner journey of the poet by delving into multilingual archives, declassified diplomatic files, personal letters, and intimate interviews. Blending biography, cultural history, and literary criticism, The Tree Within is a luminous testament to the enduring alchemy between India and the world through one of the greatest writers of the 20th century.Indranil Chakravarty (https://indrachakra.com/) has taught film history and screenwriting over two decades at film institutes in India and abroad, and has made several documentaries. He studied at Presidency College (Calcutta), Escuela Internacional de Cine y TV (EICTV) in Havana, and earned PhD from Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand. He has published extensively in international research journals about biopics, literary biography and cosmopolitanism. His earlier book publications include The New Latin American Cinema, India's Audiovisual Market, and one in Spanish titled Redescubriendo a Tagore. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Diana Martinez
events.description: During US colonial rule in the Philippines, reinforced concrete was used to the near exclusion of all other building materials. In Concrete Colonialism (Duke, 2025), Diana Martinez (Architecture) examines the motivations for and lasting effects of this forgotten colonial policy. Arguing that the pervasive use of reinforced concrete revolutionized techniques of imperial conquest, Martinez shows how concrete reshaped colonialism as a project that sought durable change through the reformation of environments, colonial society, and racialized biologies. Martinez locates the origins of this material revolution in the development of Chicago, highlighting how building this urban center atop exceptionally challenging geology made it possible to transform diverse global ecologies. She details how the material's stability, plasticity, strength, and other qualities served the shifting imperatives of the US colonial regime, playing a central role in defending territory, controlling disease, and constructing monuments to nation and empire. By describing a world irreversibly remade, Martinez urges readers to consider how colonialism persists — in concrete forms — despite claims of its conclusion. Martinez is joined by Matthew Shutzer (History). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Gautam Dantas | Understanding, Predicting, and Remediating Perturbations to Host-Microbe Interactions
events.description: Antibiotics can acutely and persistently compromise microbiome stability and resilience, enabling enhanced colonization of pathogenic microbes, and loss of host-beneficial functions from depleted commensals. We interrogate resistome, taxonomic, and functional dynamics of microbiota of humans, animals, soils, and built-environments via high-throughput functional metagenomic selections, whole metagenome and transcriptome sequencing, and isolate phenotyping and whole genome sequencing. We use these datasets to model and predict the impact of various biotic and abiotic perturbations on the transmission and evolutionary dynamics of diverse microbiomes and their resistomes across time and habitats, through application of generalized linear mixed models and machine learning algorithms. By integrating community-level analyses of microbiome perturbation and response, with mechanistic analyses of novel microbial resilience functions, we are improving the accuracy and sensitivity of genomics-based methods for diagnosing and treating pathogens and their resistance properties in the clinic and maintaining or rescuing healthy microbiome states.

events.title: Aaron Gitler: Granulin loss and TMEM106B risk converge on lysosomal C-terminal fragment pathology in frontotemporal dementia
events.description: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer disease. Mutations in GRN, which encodes progranulin, are a major cause of FTD. Common genetic variants in the TMEM106B gene modify risk of FTD and the effect is especially strong in GRN mutation carriers. Intriguingly, in GRN mutation carriers, being homozygous for the protective TMEM106B haplotype seems to confer near lifetime protection against FTD. Despite the strong genetic link between GRN and TMEM106B, how these two genes interact mechanistically has remained unresolved. Recent studies have revealed that a C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B forms amyloid fibrils and accumulates in the brains of older individuals and patients with neurodegenerative disorders, including FTD. How the production of this fragment connects to granulin deficiency is also unknown. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation, we show that granulin deficiency drives the accumulation of the TMEM106B C-terminal fragment within lysosomes in Grn-knockout mice and GRN-null human iPSC-derived neurons. Recombinant progranulin supplementation reduced TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation. Isogenic neurons carrying the TMEM106B risk allele displayed allele-dose-dependent fragment accumulation that was reversible by progranulin. Structural and genetic analyses demonstrated that TMEM106B dimerization stabilizes the protein and limits C-terminal fragment formation. These findings define a lysosomal pathway linking granulin deficiency to TMEM106B C-terminal fragment accumulation and explain how protective TMEM106B alleles can confer resistance to FTD, even for GRN mutation carriers.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Munis D. Faruqui | Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold
events.description: Please join us for a special book launch celebrating Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/aurangzeb-alamgir-and-the-mughal-empire/A6421F92BBEEBA78238E75F4D636E7C0), the new work by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director of the Institute for South Asia Studies and Professor of South and Southeast Asian Studies at UC Berkeley. In this compelling reassessment, Professor Faruqui offers a fresh and nuanced account of Aurangzeb's reign, illuminating the ambitions, conflicts, and political pressures that shaped the Mughal Empire at a pivotal moment in its history. The conversation will be moderated by Abhishek Kaicker (https://history.berkeley.edu/abhishek-kaicker), Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, Oct 15, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ————– ABOUT THE BOOKAurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658–1707) was the last of the so-called 'great' Mughal emperors. He remains a controversial historical figure: castigated for religious intolerance and placed at the centre of a narrative of Mughal decline by some; considered a great Muslim hero by others. In this richly researched exploration of Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's life and times, Munis D. Faruqui contests such simplistic understandings to unearth a more nuanced picture of the emperor and his reign. Drawing on a large and varied archive, Faruqui provides new insights into the emperor's rise to power, his administrative and religious policies, and the role of the imperial eunuchate and harem. By unpicking the complex dynamics of a long reign, from Aurangzeb 'Alamgir's accession to the last weeks of his life and his eighteenth-century memorialisation, this remarkable new history cuts through the many myths that have obscured the extraordinary life story of Emperor Aurangzeb 'Alamgir. SPEAKER BIOMunis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/) is a historian and the holder of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies. His focus is on the Muslim experience in South Asia, especially during the Mughal period. His books include Princes of the Mughal Empire, 1504-1719 (Cambridge University Press, 2012), Expanding Frontiers in South Asian and World History, co-edited with Richard Eaton, David Gilmartin and Sunil Kumar (Cambridge University Press, 2013), and Religious Interactions in Mughal India, co-edited with Vasudha Dalmia (Oxford University Press, 2014). His most recent book is titled Aurangzeb 'Alamgir and the Mughal Empire: A History Retold (Cambridge University Press and Juggernaut Press, 2026). He is co-editor-in-chief, along with Ali Anooshahr, of the Journal of Mughal Studies. In 2014, Dr. Faruqui was one of three faculty recipients of UC-Berkeley's Distinguished Teaching Award. The award recognizes teaching that "incites intellectual curiosity in students, engages them thoroughly in the enterprise of learning, and has a lifelong impact." Dr. Faruqui is the current Director of both the Institute for South Asia Studies and the Global, International & Area Studies unit. In addition to the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, Dr. Faruqui is affiliated with the Department of History and the Department of Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures. events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSemi-artificial Photosynthesis using Formate Dehydrogenase Semi-artificial photosynthesis interfaces biological catalysts with synthetic light absorbers to overcome the inherent limitations of both artificial and natural photosynthesis. Furthermore, this emerging approach can also unlock novel reaction pathways and chemistries with significant technological potential and thus provides new opportunities that are currently not available in solar fuels or algae research. This presentation will summarise our progress in integrating the redox enzyme formate dehydrogenase into bespoke hierarchical 3D electrode scaffolds, photoelectrodes and semiconductor powders. Specifically, formate dehydrogenase immobilised on electrodes enables catalytic CO₂ reduction to formate with electrochemical reversibility and can thus operate at very low overpotential with high selectivity. The design principles for the integration of formate dehydrogenase in bespoke synthetic 3D electrode scaffolds and a detailed analysis of the biocatalyst-material interface will be presented. The understanding of the biotic-abiotic interface ultimately allows for the rational wiring of the biocatalyst into photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems for the solar synthesis of fuels and chemicals. Overall, the lecture aims to demonstrate that formate dehydrogenase should be considered as unique model electrocatalyst for CO₂-to-formate conversion in solar catalysis as it enables performance currently not achievable by synthetic catalysts. A recent review on this topic is available: Liu et al., Chem. Rev., 2026, 126, 8034–8088 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.6c00095).

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Castrato Phantoms Book Chat w/ Martha Feldman (University of Chicago)
events.description: Castrato PhantomsBook ChatMartha Feldman (University of Chicago) Held in the Townsend Center's Geballe RoomMartha Feldman (Ferdinand Schevill Distinguished Service Professor, Music & Theater and Performance Studies, University of Chicago) discusses her sweeping account of the castrato dilemma in its end stages as an index of modern consciousness. How can we write the histories of a complex multigenerational past when it is mired in obfuscations that stretch from the most intimate of family events to the doings of the Roman church to the machinery of the Italian state? This was the challenge Feldman faced when she crossed paths with descendants of the last castrato to star in Roman chapels, whose uncle turned out to be the iconic film director Federico Fellini. Some years after their first encounter, she offers a book that unravels the entanglements of family traumas with the secret suppressions of the Vatican and fascist state. Her Castrato Phantoms: Moreschi, Fellini, and the Sacred Vernacular in Rome (Zone Books, 2026) provides compelling answers that follow up on her Berkeley Bloch Lectures (published as The Castrato: Reflections on Natures and Kinds, University of California Press, 2015). Her novel concept of the sacred vernacular makes sense of the profanations of everyday sacred rituals and objects, traced here through sound recordings, literary texts, photographs, films, and letters. Drawing on Roman archives, a previously unknown family archive, and a wealth of Roman historical documentation, she deploys the sacred vernacular to rewrite the history of old-world hauntings in a modern key. Feldman will deliver a half-hour lecture before conversing with Prof. James Q. Davies. A Q & A with the audience will follow. Prof. Ramona Naddaff will moderate.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Risk Appetite and Monetary Transmission"
events.description: Abstract: We construct a new high-frequency measure of changes in risk appetite around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings. Fed policy actions and communication have substantial effects on risk appetite, consistent with the literature on the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Most of the variation in asset prices and risk appetite is unexplained by conventional interest-rate surprises, which points to an important role of risk appetite in monetary transmission. Proxy SVARs with two separately-instrumented monetary policy shocks—a risk-free rate shock and a risk appetite shock—show the empirical importance of this channel. Risk appetite shocks have large, significant, and theory-consistent effects on inflation, output and employment. By contrast, the effects of risk-free rate shocks become insignificant or switch signs as soon as a risk-appetite shock is included in the VAR setup. Our evidence suggests that monetary transmission works primarily through risk asset prices and risk appetite. Standard estimation of monetary transmission based solely on interest-rate surprises misses most of these effects for two main reasons: First, the impact of interest-rate policy on asset prices is time-varying and state-dependent. Second, central bank communication can affect risk appetite and asset prices in ways that go beyond changes in the expected policy path.

events.description: Over the next 25 years, Americans will inherit more than $100 trillion. Economists anticipate a "great wealth transfer" from the Baby Boomer generation to their children and grandchildren. At the same time, this enormous wealth will be distributed extremely unevenly throughout society. While a select few will inherit vast fortunes, many will inherit little, nothing at all, or even debt. This raises questions with renewed urgency—questions that have been debated in the transatlantic world since the American and French Revolutions: Who should receive a deceased person's estate? Who counts as family? Who should decide how an estate is distributed? How can the unequal distribution of inherited wealth be justified, and how can the rights to private property and equal opportunities be reconciled? In his lecture, Jürgen Dinkel traces the history of inheritance in the US and Europe since 1800. He demonstrates how governments, families, and individuals repeatedly negotiated the transfer and distribution of estates, thereby also renegotiating kinship relations, the bonds between the individual, the family, and the state, as well as the legitimization of wealth inequalities within their societies. Ultimately, this lecture contributes to the new histories of capitalism, the family, and the state, arguing that Euro-American societies from the 19th to the 21st century are fundamentally structured around inheritance and the family. Jürgen Dinkel is Professor of Modern and Global History at the University of Leipzig. His research focuses on the history of colonialism and decolonization, the Global South in World Politics, and European social history. His most recent publications include: Acknowledgments: The History of Academic Gratitude, in Bulletin of the German Historical Institute, Washington D.C. 76 (Fall 2025); "'The Rich Uncle from America': Transnational Inheritance Transfers between the United States, Germany, and Russia, 1840s–1980s," Law and History Review (2025); and "The Non-Aligned Movement: The Role of Diplomacy in Third-worldism and the Global South," in Oxford Handbook on the History of the Global South (Oxford UP, 2025). events.title: PMB Seminar with Adam Steinbrenner | Seeing like a plant: immune recognition and signaling by cell surface receptors
events.description: Plants sense extracellular cues through several hundred cell surface receptors. The most rapidly evolving group of receptors is the leucine-rich repeat receptor-like proteins (RLPs), which transduce immune signals as a bipartite receptor complex with the adapter SOBIR1. In recent years many new examples of immunogenic patterns detected by specific RLPs have been described, highlighting their versatility as immune sensing modules. I will discuss unique features of the RLP family that mediate recognition and signaling functions. For recognition, RLPs encode an extracellular island domain, which allosterically couples ligand binding to co-receptor recruitment. For signaling, RLPs lack a kinase domain typical of most receptors, but the short cytoplasmic tail domain can encode signaling through different defense pathways. For both recognition and signaling functions, I will describe new insights from our study of Inceptin Receptor (INR), which detects caterpillar-derived peptide elicitors and evolved 28 mya in a single subtribe of legumes. Since both island and tail domains are small (~10-60 aa) shared features of all RLPs, they may represent modular, editable handles to engineer plant immune systems.

events.title: Indispensable but Invisible: Legal Expertise and Juridical Capital in the Governance of Late Imperial China | Lecture by Li Chen
events.description: During the Qing period (1644–1912), late imperial China was in theory governed by approximately two thousand local administrators who were appointed for their mastery of the Confucian classics rather than for their administrative or legal expertise. How did these scholar-officials actually carry out the daily tasks of local governance, including judicial administration? Based on a forthcoming monograph, this talk analyzes the training and roles of the thousands of legal specialists who advised local officials behind the scenes and handled most of the judicial and other substantive administrative work on their behalf. Despite their important functions in local governance, these legal specialists were ideologically marginalized. This talk, as well as the larger study from which it is drawn, provides new insights into why they became so indispensable to Qing law and governance and why they remained obscure to outsiders and modern researchers. Speaker BioLi Chen, J.D. (UIUC) and Ph.D. (Columbia), is Professor of History at the University of Toronto, with a cross-appointment at the Faculty of Law. Among his extensive publications on the intersection of law, culture, and politics in Chinese and international history since the 1500s is his monograph,Chinese Law in Imperial Eyes: Sovereignty, Justice, and Transcultural Politics(Columbia University Press, 2016), which received the 2018 Joseph Levenson Book Prize from the Association for Asian Studies and an Honorable Mention for the 2017 Peter Gonville Stein Book Award from the American Society for Legal History. He has recently completed another monograph,Invisible Power in China: Legal Expertise, Statecraft Traditions, and Cultural Politics, 1651–1911. He was the founding president (2014–2017) of the International Society for Chinese Law and History and currently serves on the boards of that organization and the American Society for Legal History. He also serves on the editorial boards ofLaw and History Review,Law & Social Inquiry, and theJournal of World History. He is currently working on book projects on the Qing system of Autumn Assizes for major criminal cases and on the remarkable but little-known history of Qing legal lineages.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Brandon Barnett, Assistant Professor, University of RochesterNon-Heme Iron Enzyme Mimicry Through Confinement Biological enzymes have evolved over billions of years to mediate kinetically challenging transformations under mild conditions and with excellent selectivities. Inspired by nature, our group works at the interface of bioinorganic chemistry and materials science toward the precise engineering of void spaces that can kinetically stabilize high-valent, bio-inspired complexes. This talk will focus principally on the chemistry of bio-inspired high-valent iron-oxo and iron-nitrosyl species that have been kinetically stabilized through confinement within a rigid macrocycle. The unique thermal stabilities of these species enable novel investigations of their photochemical behaviors both in solution and in the solid state. Most notably, photocrystallographic studies have illuminated novel C–C cleavage reactions mediated by "oxyl"-type excited states of a confined high-spin iron(IV)-oxo. Mechanistic studies of reactions arising from direct photoexcitation of this complex will be discussed. At the end of the talk, I will briefly highlight our work using dynamic porous solids for separation science and energy storage.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Rachana Vajjhala (University of California, Davis)
events.description: Thinking Through NautchworkRachana Vajjhala (University of California, Davis) In this talk, I share two threads of my current book project. The first considers Indianist danced works at the turn of the twentieth century, with a focus on Le Dieu bleu (1912). Rather than characteristic Russian locales or reimagined Hellenic ones, this ballet was set in a mythologized version of the subcontinent. In the words of a critic for Revue hebdomadaire, there was a chasm between "the strongly colored gestural aspect of Le Dieu bleu and the lightly shaded musical one." Registral discordances were nothing new for such productions of course, but I dwell here on the coloristic language, which was both literal and metaphorical. Nijinska shaded her body with makeup and darkly hued tights, but Nijinsky blued his skin from head to toe. In this way, Le Dieu bleu anticipates a more complexly tinted approach to Indianist markers of performed authenticity to come. The rest of my talk picks up another strand of Nautchwork, specifically the way earlier danced productions (including Le Dieu bleu) contributed to the aestheticization of a contiguous embodied practice—postural yoga—as well as the shift of those Indianist markers from a visual dimension to the sonic register of the teacher's voice. Rachana Vajjhala is an Assistant Professor of Musicology at UC Davis. Her first book, Kinetic Cultures, was published by UC Press in 2024. A reception will follow.

events.title: (Julia Mahamid) Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: "In-cell structural biology at a systems level"
events.description: Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: (https://thevalleefoundation.org/programs/kdl) Recent technological breakthroughs in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) open the disruptive possibility to image macromolecular complexes in their native cellular or multicellular context at close to atomic resolution, and can directly reveal how their different conformational states and interaction networks are linked to biological functions. We advance sample preparation techniques for in-cell cryo-ET, including cryo-focused ion beam thinning and 3D correlative (super resolution) fluorescence microscopy. Preparations of such site-specific 'electron-transparent windows' enable the assignment of macromolecular structures directly from the high-resolution three-dimensional stills captured by cryo-ET when aided by an array of methods, including computational patter recognition and novel developments of genetically-encoded molecular tags. Furthermore, integration of multiple data sources is key to the interpretation of the mined structural signatures. For example, using the genome-reduced human pathogen Mycoplasma pneumoniae as a minimal cell model, we established the synergistic application of whole-cell crosslinking mass spectrometry and cellular cryo-ET to determine an in-cell integrative structural model of actively transcribing RNA polymerases coupled to translating ribosomes. Our contributions to computational methods now allow resolving these molecular machines to high resolution, reveal small molecule antibiotics bound to their active site in ribosomes within the intact pathogen, provide snapshots of their structural dynamics, and illuminate functions of previously unknown macromolecular complexes. Such integration of cutting-edge methods unlocks an enormous potential for mechanistic understanding at a system-spanning level by in-cell structural biology.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with David Henkin
events.description: In Out of the Ballpark (Oxford, 2026), David Henkin (History) reconsiders the character, meaning, and delights of baseball by exploring the game's unusual features and the sport's many resonances with other aspects of modern life. To this end, he abandons several assumptions and mythologies that underlie most approaches to histories of baseball: that it is unique among sports and fundamentally different from other kinds of entertainment; that it is specific to the United States; that it has changed fundamentally in recent years; and that the keys to understanding it lie primarily in examining what happens on the field of play. Instead, Henkin moves across time and space to examine baseball's history since the nineteenth century and beyond US borders. He takes readers inside the structures of clubs and leagues, interprets the sacred scripture of rulebooks, and illuminates some of baseball's rites and rituals that are often associated with honor and manhood. He charts baseball's significance along the routes of American and Japanese imperial expansion and the shifting maps of race and ethnicity in the US. Baseball is found at negotiating tables that pit capital against labor and in pivotal moments in the history of mass media. He shows us how baseball might offer a complex and capacious space for thinking about such things as spectatorship, success, community, order, and contingency in the modern world. Henkin is joined by Alva Noë (Philosophy). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.organizer: Thelton E. Henderson Center for Social Justice
events.description: Join us for a conversation with Professor Osagie Obasogie and Savala Nolan about critical race theory. They’ll discuss its basic tenets, its uses (and misuses) across the law, politics, and culture, and how students can engage the analytical tools of CRT to advance their social justice work in and beyond law school. Osagie K. Obasogie is the Haas Distinguished Chair and Professor of Law at UC Berkeley, with joint appointments in the Joint Medical Program and the School of Public Health. He holds a B.A. from Yale University, a J.D. from Columbia Law School, and a Ph.D. in Sociology from UC Berkeley. His extensive scholarly work focuses on the intersection of law, race, and medicine, covering topics like policing, bioethics, and reproductive technologies. He has written for prestigious academic journals and major public outlets, and his book Blinded By Sight won the Herbert Jacob Book Prize. Lunch will be served inside of Room 170 starting at 12:50 PM. RSVPs will be prioritized.

events.title: Matrix on Point: The State of U.S. Immigration Enforcement and Surveillance
events.description: REGISTER Federal immigration enforcement in the United States is increasingly shaped by the convergence of surveillance technologies, data systems, and on-the-ground policing practices. From AI-assisted identification tools to information-sharing across agencies, these developments are transforming how enforcement operates, and raising urgent questions about civil liberties and democratic oversight. This panel will bring together scholars to examine the social and political consequences, and the stakes for rights in an era of technological governance. The panel will feature David Hausman, Assistant Professor at UC Berkeley Law School, Caitlin Patler, Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and Jennifer Urban, Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law School. Deirdre Mulligan, Professor in the UC Berkeley School of Information, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Asian American Research Center, the Center for Race and Gender, the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative, the Goldman School of Public Policy, and the UC Berkeley School of Information.Matrix On Point (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/matrix-on-point/) is a discussion series promoting focused, cross-disciplinary conversations on today's most pressing issues. Offering opportunities for scholarly exchange and interaction, each Matrix On Point features the perspectives of leading scholars and specialists from different disciplines, followed by an open conversation. These thought-provoking events are free and open to the public. Panelists David Hausman (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/david-hausman/#tab_profile) is an Assistant Professor at Berkeley Law School. He does empirical work on U.S. immigration enforcement, mostly using government data disclosed in response to Freedom of Information Act requests. He also co-directs the Deportation Data Project (https://deportationdata.org/). Before joining Berkeley, he practiced law at the ACLU Immigrants' Rights Project in New York City.Caitlin Patler (https://gspp.berkeley.edu/research-and-impact/faculty/caitlin-patler) is Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and faculty affiliate of the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative (BIMI), Berkeley Population Center, and the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment. Dr. Patler's research examines US immigration and criminal laws, legal statuses, and law enforcement institutions as drivers of socioeconomic and health disparities.Jennifer M. Urban (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/jennifer-urban/#tab_profile) is a Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law, where she is Director of Policy Initiatives at the Samuelson Law, Technology & Public Policy Clinic (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/experiential/clinics/samuelson-law-technology-public-policy-clinic/). Her research focuses on information policy: intellectual property, privacy and data protection, and security. She regularly collaborates with technologists and academics in disciplines other than law to develop empirically grounded understandings of how new technologies and the regulatory structures around them interact with civil liberties, innovation, and creative expression. In March 2021, Urban was appointed by California Governor Gavin Newsom to be the inaugural Chair of the California Privacy Protection Agency Board.Deirdre K. Mulligan (https://www.ischool.berkeley.edu/people/deirdre-mulligan) (moderator) is a Professor in the School of Information at UC Berkeley, a faculty Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/bclt/), and a co-organizer of the Algorithmic Fairness & Opacity Working Group (http://afog.berkeley.edu/). Mulligan's research explores legal and technical means of protecting values such as privacy, freedom of expression, and fairness in socio-technical systems. Her book Privacy on the Ground: Driving Corporate Behavior in the United States and Europe (https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/privacy-ground), a study of privacy practices in large corporations in five countries, with UC Berkeley Law Prof. Kenneth Bamberger was published in 2015 by MIT Press. Mulligan served as Principal Deputy U.S. Chief Technology Officer at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, (https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/) and Director of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office (NAIIO), in the Biden-Harris Administration. In November 2025, Mulligan was appointed to Governor Newsom's California Innovation Council. REGISTER

events.title: Laura Sánchez Carrasco & Íñigo Cobeta: What Space Builds | Architecture Lecture Series
events.description: Laura Sánchez Carrasco is an architect and associate professor at the Escuela Técnica Superior de Arquitectura, UPM, where she has taught since 2018. She holds a degree in architecture (2007), a master's in analysis, theory, and history of architecture (2014), and a PhD cum laude (2017), all from UPM. Her research addresses postwar North American architecture and its connections with Spanish architecture, combining architectural history with digital methods of historiographic analysis. She is currently part of the research project "Conexiones de la arquitectura española con las Américas (1976–2006)" and has previously collaborated with MIT on the project "Mapping Global Architectural Histories on Modernism". Alongside her academic career, she practiced architecture professionally for nearly 20 years, both running her own studio and working within established firms, where she led competition-winning projects from design through construction. Íñigo Cobeta is a researcher and associate professor in the Department of Architectural Composition at the Escuela Técnica Superior de Arquitectura de Madrid (ETSAM), where he has taught since 2006. He has collaborated with specialized international publications such as ArquitecturaCOAM or RITA. He has also acted as an independent national curator (Bienal Iberoamericana de Arquitectura y Urbanismo 2006). For 20 years he worked as an architect, collaborating with MoneoBrockStudio on the Termas de Tiberio in the Panticosa Spa and developing his own practice. In 2019, the bicentennial of the Museo Nacional del Prado, he was invited to lecture on some of the conclusions of his thesis, The Prado, from Territory to Stage, directed by Rafael Moneo. He is currently part of the research project "Conexiones de la arquitectura española con las Américas (1976–2006)". Since 2020, he has focused on teaching, research, and developing experimental projects on public schools.

events.title: Marius Wernig: Human iPS cell-derived microtissues to study neurodegenerative disease
events.description: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and embryonic stem cells (ESCs) havebecome valuable tools to investigate disease mechanisms because they can bedifferentiated into various somatic cell types, including those of the central nervoussystem (CNS), which are difficult to obtain from primary sources. Microglia are theimmune cells of the central nervous system and are thought to be key players inboth physiological and disease conditions. Several microglial features are poorlyconserved between mice and human, such as the function of the neurodegeneration-associated immune receptor Trem2. iPSC-derived microglia offer a powerfulopportunity to generate and study human microglia. However, human iPSC-derivedmicroglia often exhibit activated phenotypes in vitro, and assessing their impact onother brain cell types remains challenging due to limitations in current co-culturesystems. We developed fully defined brain microtissues, composed of human iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, co-cultured in 2D or 3D formats. Ourmicrotissues are stable and self-sufficient over time, requiring no exogenouscytokines or growth factors. All three cell types exhibit morphologies characteristicof their in vivo environment and show functional properties. Co-cultured microgliadevelop more homeostatic phenotypes compared to microglia exposed toexogenous cytokines. Hence, these tri-cultures provide a unique approach toinvestigate cell-cell interactions between brain cell types. We found that astrocytesand not neurons are sufficient for microglial survival and maturation, and thatastrocyte-derived M-CSF is essential for microglial survival. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing analyses nominated a network of reciprocalcommunication between cell types. Brain microtissues faithfully recapitulatedpathogenic α-synuclein seeding and aggregation, suggesting their usefulness ashuman cell models to study not only normal but also pathological cell biologicalprocesses.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

Talk Summary: COMING SOON Speaker Bio: Janet Poole teaches in the fields of Korean literature and literary translation at the University of Toronto. Her most recent book Patterns of the Heart and Other Stories (Columbia University Press, 2024) presents an introduction to the little known modernist writer Ch'oe Myŏngik (1903-?). Born and based in Pyongyang throughout his career, Ch'oe's work lovingly details life in that city and chronicles the hopes and dreams for a new society in the age of decolonization. A dedicated literary translator, Poole has also translated works by mid-twentieth century writer Yi T'aejun (1904-?), publishing a collection of his anecdotal essays (Eastern Sentiments) and a selection of his short stories (Dust and Other Stories). A new book project, "Decolonizing Style: Going North and the History of Korean Modernism," looks at the writings of Korea's modernist writers and artists who crossed the 38th parallel into what was to become the Democratic People's Republic in the late 1940s. The project follows upon an earlier study of modernist responses to the fascist regime of the late colonial era, When the Future Disappears: The Modernist Imagination in Late Colonial Korea (Columbia University Press, 2014).

events.title: Naeem Mohaiemen | Celluloid Frontiers: A Missing Can of Film and Stop Genocide
events.description: In conjunction with the exhibition Private Frontiers (https://bampfa.org/program/campus-collaborations-private-frontiers-media-legacies-cold-war), BAMPFA presents A Missing Can of Film (2025), a 44-minute essay film by artist and filmmaker Naeem Mohaiemen. Commissioned by the EVA International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, the project explores the legacy of slain Bangladeshi filmmaker Zahir Raihan and the unresolved complexities of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War The screening will include a conversation between Naeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) and Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator at BAMPFA. Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATE: Thu, Oct 29, 2026 TIME: 7-8 pm PST VENUE: BAMPFA TICKETS: Tickets for BAMPFA members are now on sale.Tickets for the general public go on sale Friday, August 7 at 11 AM. Buy tickets HERE (https://secure.bampfa.org/33280/33347?_gl=1*ev5un9*_ga*NzQxNDczMzYzLjE3ODU5NjA0MTU.*_ga_SDH80YD3Z1*czE3ODU5NjA0MTUkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODU5NjA5OTAkajYwJGwwJGgw) —About the Film Commissioned by EVA Ireland International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, AMissing Can of Film (2025) traces the lost-left politics buried within Zahir Raihan's Stop Genocide (1971)—a film edited in the style of Soviet Realism and Third Cinema during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War. Raihan, a novelist and director, was abducted only forty-five days after the end of the war. A Missing Can of Film combines scenes from Stop Genocide with footage shot at the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation after the nation's 2024 July Student "Monsoon" Uprising, interrogating the film canister as a vessel of contested history.About the Artist/FilmmakerNaeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) imagines rhizomatic families, malleable borders, and socialist utopias– beginning from postcolonial markers and then radiating outward to unlikely transnational alliances. In spite of underscoring a tendency toward misrecognition of allies, the hope of a future global left, against current categories of race, religion and nation, drives the work. He is author of Prisoners of Shothik Itihash (Kunsthalle Basel, 2014); editor of Chittagong Hill Tracts in the Blind Spot of Bangladesh Nationalism (Drishtipat, 2010); and co-editor w/ Lorenzo Fusi of System Error: War is a Force that Gives us Meaning (Sylvana, 2007).About the DiscussantTausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor) is Assistant Curator at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, where he helped organize the exhibition To Exalt the Ephemeral: The (Im)Permanent Collection. He previously worked as the Spiegel-Wilks Curatorial Fellow at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania and at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Noor's writing, for which he has received awards from the Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant and the Robert B. Silvers Foundation, has been published in various periodicals and journals, including the New Yorker, the New York Times, the New York Review of Books, Art History, and Artforum, as well as in various artist catalogues and edited volumes. He holds degrees from Dartmouth College and Goldsmiths, University of London and is a PhD candidate in History of Art at the University of California, Berkeley. ————————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.description: Jim Morken, Professor & Louise and Jim Vanderslice and Family Chair, Boston CollegeCatalytic Stereoselective Synthesis with Boron ReagentsChiral organoboronic esters are versatile intermediates for chemical synthesis. Not only are these compounds stable under a variety of reaction conditions, they are generally non-toxic and can be transformed with minimal generation of hazardous waste. An important feature of aliphatic organoboronic esters is that the boron atom may be replaced with an array of different functional groups through efficient, stereospecific transformations. This seminar will cover new strategies for the construction of alkylboronic esters from simple starting materials in a catalytic enantioselective fashion, and will also discuss ways in which these compounds can functionalized by catalytic stereospecific couplings. In addition, application of organoboronate-based transformations to address compelling problems in chemical synthesis will be discussed. Professor James Morken was born in Concord, California and obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1989 from UC Santa Barbara working with Prof. Bruce Rickborn. He obtained his Ph.D. from Boston College in 1995 with Prof. Amir Hoveyda and was an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with Stuart Schreiber at Harvard University. In 1997, he became an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 2002 and in 2006 joined the faculty of Boston College. In 2014, he was named the Louise and James Vanderslice and Family Chaired Professor of Chemistry at Boston College. Professor Morken's research focuses on the development of transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric processes and their use in complex molecule synthesis. He is particularly interested in the study and development of catalytic enantioselective reactions involving organoboron reagents. Because of the broad array of reactions that available to organoboronates, these types of process can be employed to address a number of compelling problems in the construction of organic frameworks.

events.title: Harold S. Johnston Lecture
events.description: Steven Brown, Deputy Director, NOAA Chemical Sciences LaboratoryPyrogenic Skies: Photochemistry, heterogeneous chemistry and air quality impacts of wildfire smoke As wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity across North America, their emissions have become a driver of regional air quality degradation. Biomass burning is a large source of ozone precursors, nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), as well as particulate matter that impacts air quality directly and also drives heterogeneous chemical processes. Photochemistry within smoke plumes creates pyrogenic ozone over a variety of timescales, leading to short- and long-range transport and widespread increases in the ozone background. Mixing and entrainment of smoke that is rich in pyrogenic VOCs into NOx-rich urban areas alters regional photochemistry and can further enhance ozone production. However, aerosol loads associated with smoke layers may also suppress photochemistry. Heterogeneous chemistry in smoke plumes influences atmospheric composition through a different set of chemical cycles that affect both the lower and upper atmosphere. A series of recent airborne and ground-based field studies has investigated these chemical processes in biomass burning influenced air. These include the 2019 Fire Influence on Regional to Global Environments and Air Quality (FIREX-AQ), the 2022 California Fire Dynamics Experiment (CalFiDE), the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactivity Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaign, the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone study, and others. These studies provide new insights into the biomass burning influence on tropospheric ozone at all scales, from near field plume chemistry to the global remote troposphere, and from the continental background to local urban influence.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Atreyee Gupta
events.description: Atreyee Gupta takes a revelatory look at modernism in India, exploring art's role in decolonization and aesthetic discourse across the Global South. Modernism's peak in the interwar and postwar decades coincided with the eruption of antifascist and decolonization movements globally, including the League against Imperialism, the Bandung Asian-African Conference, and the Non-Aligned Movement. Viewing artistic practices through the lens of the radical intellectual possibilities that these epoch-making events prompted, Atreyee Gupta (History of Art) uncovers a modernist internationalism incongruous with Westernist cultural hegemonies. Modernism, she shows, cannot be separated from concepts of freedom and autonomy generated by Third World political struggles. Gupta mobilizes concepts including liberation, anti-imperialism, development, and modernization as essential analytic categories for art history, reorienting our understanding of both global modernism and Indian art. Intertwining stories of art and liberation, aesthetics and decolonization, and intellectual practices and political revolution in the Third World, or what is now known as the Global South, Non-Aligned (Yale, 2025) follows the far-flung interwar and postwar networks in which Indian artists and intellectuals such as Francis N. Souza, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, and Jagdish Swaminathan participated alongside interlocutors like W. E. B. Du Bois, Richard Wright, Octavio Paz, André Malraux, and Le Corbusier in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

events.title: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas: Diverse Strategies for Transforming Unions, Schools, and Society
events.description: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas explores why teachers' unions in Brazil, Mexico, and the United States, representing similar constituencies and fighting for comparable goals, have embraced radically different strategies. Through an ethnographic comparison of teacher organizing in São Paulo, Oaxaca, and New York, the book focuses on three key strategies in teacher organizing—leftist party politics, autonomist politics, and interest group politics—to demonstrate how the strategic choices teachers make matter for both schools and society. In São Paulo, teachers' leftist party politics helped to elect pro-labor presidents five times, with significant social reforms; yet these same politics failed to influence education policy and led to factionalism within the union. In Oaxaca, teachers' autonomous politics led to robust cultural initiatives, an innovative pedagogical proposal, and the capacity to boycott national education reforms. Finally, in many U.S. cities in the 2000s, teachers rejected interest group politics in favor of rank-and-file caucuses that prioritized union-community coalitions and racial justice, which also created new fault lines within the unions and an ambiguous relationship with electoral politics. Teaching Organizing Across the Americas offers important lessons for both scholars and activists interested in transforming institutions like unions to promote more just schools and societies. Rebecca Tarlau is Associate Professor of Education at Stanford University and former Associate Professor of Labor and Employment Relations at Pennsylvania State University, where she was the co-founder of the Consortium for Social Movements and Education Research and Practice. Her ethnographic research focuses on theories of the state and state-society relations; social movements and popular education; Latin American education and development; and labor movements and teachers' work. She is the author of the award-winning Occupying School, Occupying Land: How the Landless Workers Movement Transformed Brazilian Education (OUP, 2019).

Bridging practice and pedagogy, her research engages contemporary design methods while critically revisiting the past. In 2026, she was the Douglas Gillmor Visiting Co-Lecturer at the University of Calgary, collaborating with Anna Neimark. events.title: Composition Colloquium: Julis Dobos
events.description: TITLE:Spatial Composition: The New Frontier Composers have been using rhythm and melody for thousands of years; harmony for centuries. Musique concrète expanded the use of timbre some 75 years ago. Are we on the verge of another musical disruption? What if, using spatial location and movement as compositional tools, songwriters, composers, and producers not only mixed but composed in and for immersive systems? Can SPACE be considered a new element of music? Do spatial decisions made during the composition phase have an effect on the musical content itself? Do listeners respond differently to spatially composed music than to immersive mixes of non-spatial concepts? How should one approach writing in an immersive environment to yield conceptually novel musical content? Based on his latest research in spatial composition and reflecting the global interest among music professionals in its findings, this presentation and immersive demonstration by composer Julius Dobos explores the use of spatial location and movement in music composition and production.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description: Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information
events.description: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information Abstract: Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms. Biography: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marc Hillmyer, McKnight Presidential Endowed Chair, University of Minnesota Telechelic polymers for sustainable polyolefins Polyolefins are ubiquitous. They are lightweight, strong, and stable. These features render them useful in countless applications. Unfortunately, these attributes also contribute to the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in the environment. While polyolefins can be mechanically recycled, often this results in an inferior product and is in part the reason that only a small percentage of polyolefin products are effectively recycled. We have embarked on an effort to prepare polyolefins with functional groups at their chain ends. These telechelic polyolefins can be stitched together to form high molar mass plastics and thermosets. By virtue of the synthetic pathway used to make these materials, we generate products that include weak links along the backbones of the polymer chains. These links can be chemically cleaved to quantitatively deconstruct the material and allow for efficient chemical recycling back to the starting telechelic polymers that can be subsequently repolymerized. Our approach takes advantage of a tandem catalysis strategy that is perfectly atom economic and readily scalable. In this lecture I will discuss the preparation of the telechelic polyolefins and their use in the preparation of degradable polyolefin-based plastics and thermosets. I will also report on their materials properties, scalability, and recyclability.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description: A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. Educated at the universities of Warwick and Southampton in the United Kingdom, he has previously been affiliated with the Centre for Imperial and Post-Colonial Studies at the University of Southampton, the University of Warwick, and SOAS University of London. Dr Chattha's research focuses on late colonial Punjab, Partition, migration, borders and borderlands, collective violence, and the formation of the early postcolonial Pakistani state. He has written extensively on the long-term consequences of the partitions of 1947 and 1971, with particular attention to displacement, citizenship, internment, property, and state-building. He is the author of Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), which examines the wartime and postwar experiences of Bengalis interned in West Pakistan; The Punjab Borderland: Mobility, Materiality and Militancy, 1947–1987 (Cambridge University Press, 2022); and Partition and Locality: Violence, Migration and Development in Gujranwala and Sialkot, 1947–1961 (Oxford University Press, 2012). His current book project explores the history of evacuee and enemy property in Pakistan.EVENT POSTER TBA _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. events.title: Under Pressure: Attitudes Towards China Among American Foreign Policy Professionals | Lecture by Rory Truex
events.description: How do social norms and professional incentives affect policy discourse within the Washington foreign policy community? We conducted over 50 semi-structured interviews and a survey of nearly five-hundred American foreign policy and national security professionals about their views towards the People's Republic of China. Over one fifth of survey respondents noted instances of professional pressure to voice a more hawkish point of view towards China, and many feared being perceived as naive or compromised by their views on, ties to, and experiences in China. These pressures were particularly acute for foreign policy professionals that are traditionally marginalized from power–those who are younger, non-white, or female. Our interview subjects reported a number of different coping strategies, including trying to communicate their views in the language of the perceived consensus. This "discourse mirroring" is distinct from preference falsification and self-censorship but may still contribute to difficulties in gauging peoples' true attitudes. Speaker BioRory Truex is Associate Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton, where his research and teaching focuses on authoritarianism. He is the host of Civic Forum, a podcast about the big questions facing democracy, in the US and elsewhere.

Talk Summary: This talk will introduce Hannah Shepherd's new book, The Narrowing Sea, via vignettes of the imperial region that developed across the Tsushima Straits between Pusan and Fukuoka in the seven decades from 1876 to 1953. It will offer the imperial region as a useful scale of analysis and connection between other imperial histories, and connect the urbanization of the imperial era with contemporary Japan's urban issues, before ending with a glimpse of new work that continues some of the histories and legacies discussed in The Narrowing Sea. Speaker Bio: Hannah Shepherd is Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Yale University. She received her Ph.D. in History from Harvard University. Before joining the Yale faculty, she was Junior Research Fellow in History at Trinity College, University of Cambridge. At Yale, Shepherd teaches courses on modern Japanese history, Korea and the Japanese Empire, and the history of colonial and imperial cities. Her book, The Narrowing Sea: Fukuoka, Pusan, and the Rise and Fall of an Imperial Region, came out in December 2025, from University of California Press. With Amy Stanley, she is currently working on co-translating and co-editing an English memoir of a former comfort woman, with the working title, The Life of Mun Ok Chu: a Korean woman's story of war and empire.

events.title: Laurent Warlouzet | Liberty, Solidarity and Community: Capitalism and European Integration, 1945 to the Present
events.description: How have European countries coped with the challenge of industrial capitalism and the rise of superpowers? Through an analysis of European integration from 1945 to the present day, Laurent Warlouzet argues that the European response was to create both new institutions, in particular the European Union, and an original framework of governance for capitalism. Beyond the European case, he demonstrates that capitalism is not just a contest between free marketeers and their opponents, those in favour of welfare and environmental policies, because there is a third camp that defends protectionism and assertive defence policies. Hence, the governance of capitalism has three foundational principles– liberty, solidarity, and community. The book explores debates among Europeans about how to address global interdependence in political, economic, and environmental terms. It is based on fresh archival evidence collected in eight countries. Laurent Warlouzet is professor of history at Paris Sorbonne Université. A former postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at the European University Institute (EUI), he works on the international economic history of the post-1919 period, particularly European integration and comparative European history. His previous monograph in English (Governing Europe in a Globalizing World, 2018) was reviewed in Foreign Affairs. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Capitalism. European integration and capitalism is an updated version of Europe contre Europe, originally published in French and reviewed in the mainstream media, including Le Monde, Le Grand Continent and Mediapart. The book will be published in German by Hamburger and in Italian by Luiss UP. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Community is available in open-access on the Cambridge UP here (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/liberty-solidarity-and-community/355531CFEE184AFF8B706B24D25EC368). events.title: Composition Colloquium: Andrea Agostini
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: Andrea Agostini was born on 21 May 1975 in Bologna, Italy. He studied at the Conservatorio Giovanni Battista Martini, where he received a degree in composition in 2000 (studying under Alessandro Solbiati, Giovanni Verrando, and Paolo Aralla), in electronic music in 2001 (studying with Lelio Camilleri), and piano in 2004. Between 1999 and 2006, he also took masterclasses with Ivan Fedele, Brian Ferneyhough, Michael Jarrell, and François Paris. In 2008-2010, he completed his studies with the Cursus (IRCAM's composition and computer music course). He was an IRCAM scholar-in-residence from 2011 to 2013. Andrea Agostini composes instrumental and electroacoustic music, for which he has won numerous prizes and awards, including the Zucchelli Prize in 1999 and in 2000, and the Magone Award in 2001. In 2002, he was a finalist for the Prix international Noroit-Léonce Petitot. In 2003, he won the Concurso Internacional de Composição Electroacústica Música Viva. In 2005 he received third prize for composition in the Seoul International Music Competition and an honorable mention at the Gaudeamus Festival Composers Awards. In 2007 he was a finalist in the Franco Evangelisti International Composition, sponsored by Nuovo Consonanza, and received a Commande d'état (a commission from the French Ministry of Culture) for Musica per il chiostro di Royaumont. His music is performed in festivals across the world, including Festival Musica in Strasbourg, MiTo and Sincronie in Milan, REC in Emilia-Romagna, the IMEB Festival in Bourges, Festival MIA in Annecy, and Northern Spark in Minneapolis. His curiosity for different musical languages led him to explore rock and improvisation, and to study non-Western musical practices. He plays bass with the rock band Frida X, for which he is also an arranger, progammer, and sound engineer. He also composes music for theater, cinema, and radio, and live electronics and motion capture for Project C, a group specialized in sound design for theater performances. He also designs sound environments for visual art installations. With Daniele Ghisi, he created a digital platform for computer-aided composition titled "bach: automated composer's helper". In 2017, during his research residency at IRCAM, he developed a programming language for the Max environment, creating a set of tools based on the bach library. As a musician, Andrea Agostini has collaborated with ensembles such as Icarus and the Orchestre national de la RAI in Turin, for concerts and recordings of works by Fausto Romitelli, Giovanni Verrando, and Oscar Bianchi. In addition, he has given masterclasses and workshops in the conservatories of Bologna, Genoa, and Strasbourg, and in several universities in the United States (Harvard, San Diego, and Stanford). He is currently professor of computer music (algorithmic and computer-aided composition) at the Conservatory of Turin. NOTE: Andrea is in residence at CNMAT for the Fall semester
